body.text: The story of the two Ābhīrīs
body.translated_text: The story of the two <s>Ābhīrīs</s> (cowherd women)

body.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavo 'nyatamasmin gokule dvau ābhīryau prativasataḥ; mātā ca duhtā ca; te abhikṣṇaṃ mathitaghaṭam ādāya grāmāntaṃ gacchataḥ; tayor duhitā śāṭhyasamudācārajātā mātā ṛjukā; duhitā kathayati: amba gṛhāṇa
body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in a certain cattle-herding settlement, two <s>Ābhīrī</s> women were dwelling — a mother and a daughter. They frequently took a pot of churned buttermilk and went to a nearby village. Of them, the daughter was of a deceitful disposition, while the mother was straightforward. The daughter said: 'Mother, hold

the buttermilk pot while I relieve myself.' [The mother] took it and set out. But [the daughter], through her deceitful behavior, lagged behind and did not follow her. In this way, she made her mother carry the buttermilk pot for six <s>krośas</s> (leagues).
  What do you think, monks? She who was that <s>Ābhīrī</s>'s daughter — she is none other than <s>Yaśodharā</s> at that time, in that era. Because she, through deceitful behavior, made her mother carry the buttermilk pot for six <s>krośas</s>, by the ripening of that <s>karma</s>, she carried <s>Rāhula</s> in her womb for six years. Thus, monks, the result of exclusively black <s>karmas</s> is exclusively black, as before, up to: thus should you train, monks.
  The monks, doubts having arisen, asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'What <s>karma</s>, Venerable Sir, did the Venerable <s>Rāhula</s> perform, by the ripening of which he remained in his mother's womb for six years?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'It was <s>Rāhula</s> himself, monks, who performed and accumulated <s>karmas</s>, whose conditions were gathered, whose causes had ripened, which were present like a flood, and which were inevitably bound to occur. Who else would experience the <s>karmas</s> that <s>Rāhula</s> performed and accumulated? Monks, <s>karmas</s> that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen externally in the earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element; rather, <s>karmas</s> performed ripen in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases themselves — both wholesome and unwholesome ones.',

body.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavaḥ vārāṇasyāṃ nātidūre puṣpaphalasaṃpannam āśramapadaṃ nānāvihaganikūjitaṃ viśvastamṛgapakṣiniṣevitam; tatra dvāv ṛṣī bhrātarau prativasataḥ phalamūlāmbubhakṣāv ajinavalkaladhāriṇau śaṅkhaś ca likhitaś ca; śaṅkha upādhyāya likhitaś ca śiṣyaḥ; tau vārāṇasyāṃ sarvalokaprakhyātau; rājñāpi brahmadatte<na> viditau: amuṣminn udyāne dvāv ṛṣī bhrātarau prativasataḥ śaṅkhaś ca likhitaś ca; tatra śaṅkha upādhyāyo likhitaś ca śiṣyaḥ iti; yāvad apareṇa samayena śaṅkha udakasya kuṇḍikāṃ pūrayitvā mūlaphalānām arthe vanaṃ gataḥ; likhitas tu sarātram evotthāya pūrvataraṃ gataḥ; sa puṣpaphalāny ādāya tvaritam āgataḥ; ātmīyām āṭikāṃ pratyavekṣate; svalpaṃ pānīyaṃ; sa tṛṣṇārtaḥ saṃlakṣayati upādhyāyasantakaṃ pānīyaṃ pibāmi iti; tena pītaṃ; yāvat śaṅkha riṣir mūlaphalāny ādāya tṛṣāparyākulīkṛtamukhaḥ āśramaṃ praviṣṭaḥ; kuṇḍikāṃ pratyavekṣate; paśyati riltikāṃ; sa saṃjātāmarṣaḥ kathayati, kena coreṇa pānīyam apahṛtaṃ? iti; likhitaḥ kathayati: upādhyāya ahaṃ coraḥ; mayā pītaṃ; daṇḍaṃ prayaccha iti; sa kathayati: tvaṃ mama bhrātā śiṣyaś ca; yadi pītaṃ supītaṃ yathāsukham iti; sa kathayati: upādhyāya na śaknomy aham etat kaukṛtyaṃ prativinodayituṃ; prayaccha me gurukaṃ daṇḍaṃ yaś corasya pradīyate iti; evam uktaḥ śaṅkha ṛṣiḥ
body.translated_text: In the past, monks, not far from <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, there was a hermitage rich in flowers and fruits, resounding with the songs of various birds, frequented by trusting deer and birds. There two sages who were brothers dwelt — <s>Śaṅkha</s> and <s>Likhita</s> — subsisting on fruits, roots, and water, wearing antelope-skin and bark garments. <s>Śaṅkha</s> was the teacher and <s>Likhita</s> the pupil. Both were renowned throughout <s>Vārāṇasī</s>. Even King <s>Brahmadatta</s> knew of them: 'In such-and-such a garden, two sages who are brothers dwell — <s>Śaṅkha</s> and <s>Likhita</s>; <s>Śaṅkha</s> is the teacher and <s>Likhita</s> is the pupil.' Then, at a later time, <s>Śaṅkha</s>, having filled a water-pitcher, went to the forest for roots and fruits. <s>Likhita</s>, however, had risen the entire night and had gone out earlier. Having gathered flowers and fruits, he came back quickly. He checked his own jug — little water. Afflicted with thirst, he considered: 'I shall drink the water belonging to the teacher.' He drank it. Then the sage <s>Śaṅkha</s>, having gathered roots and fruits, entered the hermitage with his face distressed by thirst. He checked the pitcher and found it empty. Filled with anger, he said: 'What thief has stolen the water?' <s>Likhita</s> said: 'Teacher, I am the thief. I drank it. Impose punishment.' He said: 'You are my brother and my pupil. If you drank it, well drunk — be at ease.' He said: 'Teacher, I cannot dispel this remorse. Impose upon me the severe punishment that is given to a thief.' Thus addressed, the sage <s>Śaṅkha</s>

He said: 'If that is so, stay right here — do not leave until I have returned.' The king, having finished hunting deer, deliberately entered by another gate and did not come out again. On the sixth day, the ministers reported to the king: 'Your Majesty, that sage has been standing in that very spot for six days now. Please issue a command.' The king said: 'Let the punishment be lifted. Let him go — that itself is his punishment.' The ministers told the sage: 'Sage, His Majesty says: the punishment is lifted; go — that itself is your punishment.' He, free from remorse, departed.
  What do you think, monks? He who was King <s>Brahmadatta</s> — he is none other than <s>Rāhula</s> at that time, in that era. Because he, with a corrupted mind, told the sage: 'Stay in that spot — you may not leave' — by the ripening of that <s>karma</s>, he dwelt in his mother's womb for six years. Thus, monks, the result of exclusively black <s>karmas</s> is exclusively black, as before, up to: thus should you train, monks.

children.translated_text: The monks, doubts having arisen, asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'What <s>karma</s>, Venerable Sir, did the Venerable <s>Bhadrika</s> perform, by the ripening of which he became a king among distinguished men?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'It was <s>Bhadrika</s> himself, monks, who performed and accumulated <s>karmas</s>, whose conditions were gathered, whose causes had ripened, which were present like a flood, and which were inevitably bound to occur. Who else would experience the <s>karmas</s> that <s>Bhadrika</s> performed and accumulated? Monks, <s>karmas</s> that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen externally in the earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element; rather, <s>karmas</s> performed ripen in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases themselves — both wholesome and unwholesome ones.',

The women, greedy for flowers and fruits, began to wander about the garden searching for flowers and fruits. Meanwhile, King <s>Brahmadatta</s>, having shaken off the sluggishness of sleep, quickly returned to <s>Vārāṇasī</s>. The ladies of the inner apartments too hastily set out. But one woman, in her confusion, dropped a pearl necklace and departed. Meanwhile, that sweeper (<s>koṭṭamallaka</s>) was wandering about in that garden. He saw the pearl necklace. He reflected: 'What use is this to me? There is a possibility that for the sake of gain I will bring upon myself misfortune.' So he tied it to a vine and left it in the garden, thinking: 'Whoever it belongs to will take it.' Then the ladies of the inner apartments informed the king: 'Your Majesty, such-and-such a woman has left a pearl necklace forgotten in the garden.' The king gave an order to his ministers: 'Sirs, a pearl necklace has been forgotten in the garden — search for it.' They went to the garden and began to search. They found it tied to a vine. They thought: 'Let us first investigate who tied it.' They began to search the garden. They saw the sweeper. They said to him: 'Good man, who tied this pearl necklace to the vine and left it there?' He told them what had happened. The ministers gave the pearl necklace to the king and reported the events. The king said: 'Sirs, summon that sweeper. I wish to see him.' They summoned him. The king asked: 'Good man, why did you tie the pearl necklace to the vine and leave it, rather than taking it for yourself?' He said: 'Your Majesty, I am not entitled to it — it rightly belongs to Your Majesty.' The king, pleased, said: 'Good man, you are worthy of a boon. Tell me — what boon shall I grant you?' body.translated_text: 'You should be vigilant in maintaining order, but you must not strike them.' Meanwhile, a certain man was walking through the middle of the street carrying cakes. The chief of the sweepers snatched the cakes from him. Taking them, he went to a secluded spot. The sweepers followed him. Harassed by them, he crossed the river <s>Vārakā</s> and stood at the foot of a certain tree. In the absence of <s>Buddhas</s> in the world, <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s> (solitary awakened ones) arise — compassionate toward the lowly and wretched, fond of remote beds, seats, and food, worthy of individual offerings to the world. A certain <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> happened to come to that place by chance. The sweeper saw him — pleasing in body and peaceful in deportment. He reflected: 'Surely it is because I have not made offerings to such a truly worthy recipient that, having obtained a human birth, I was born as a sweeper. If this great-souled one would accept cakes from me, I would give them to him.' Then that <s>Pratyekabuddha</s>, having known his mind with his own, extended his bowl out of compassion for him. The sweeper reverently gave him the cakes. The teaching of the <s>Dharma</s> by those great-souled ones is bodily, not verbal. He rose up into the sky and began to perform the supernatural feats of blazing, burning, raining, and illuminating. ) removed the living organisms, and offered it to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> did not accept it, thinking it was not properly prepared. Then the monkey went aside, diluted it with cool water, and offered it to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> accepted it, knowing it was now properly prepared. Then the monkey, knowing 'The <s>Bhagavān</s> has accepted my honey-bowl,' was delighted, joyful, and elated, filled with rapture, happiness, and good cheer. Joining his palms, bowing repeatedly, dancing, paying homage to the <s>Bhagavān</s>, filled with faith in the <s>Bhagavān</s>, gazing at the <s>Bhagavān</s> without looking back, he fell into a well, died, and was reborn in a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> family in <s>Nādikā</s> that was devoted to the six ritual duties. On the very day his conception took place, a rain of honey fell. His father summoned diviners and asked them. They said: 'It is by the spiritual power of this being.' After the passage of eight or nine months, that <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> woman gave birth. A boy was born. On the very day he was born, a rain of honey fell as well. His relatives gathered together and, over twenty-one days of three weeks, performed the extensive birth-celebration. A name was assigned: 'What shall the boy's name be?' The relatives said: 'This boy — on the very day he entered his mother's womb, a rain of honey fell. On the day he was born, a rain of honey fell as well. And he is of the <s>Vāsiṣṭha</s> lineage. Therefore, let the boy's name be <s>Madhuvāsiṣṭha</s>.' The name <s>Madhuvāsiṣṭha</s> was assigned. He was raised and grew up. When he was grown, he went forth in the well-proclaimed <s>Dharma</s>-<s>Vinaya</s>. Even after going forth, three bowls of honey appeared for him every day. He offered one to the <s>Bhagavān</s>, a second to the <s>Saṅgha</s>, and the third he consumed together with his companions.
  The monks, doubts having arisen, asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'Venerable Sir, what <s>karma</s> did the Venerable <s>Madhuvāsiṣṭha</s> perform by the ripening of which three bowls appear for him every day?'   bhikṣavaḥ saṃśayajātāḥ sarvasaṃśayacchettāraṃ buddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ papracchuḥ: kiṃ bhadantāyuṣmatā upālinā karma kṛtaṃ yasya karmaṇo vipākena rājenāpitaḥ saṃvṛttaḥ; bhagavān āha: upālinaiva bhikṣavaḥ aprameyā tathāgatadakṣiṇā iti pūrvam anyāsu jātiṣu karmāṇi kṛtāny upacitāni labdhasaṃbhārāṇi pūrvavad yāvad phalanti khalu dehināṃ.
body.translated_text:
'We have seen it, Venerable Sir.' He who was that monkey — he is this very <s>Madhuvāsiṣṭha</s> at that time, in that era. He offered the honey-bowl to the <s>Tathāgata</s>. By the ripening of that deed, he was reborn in a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> family devoted to the six ritual duties, and at his conception and birth, a rain of honey fell. Even now, day after day, three bowls of honey appear [for him]. Thus, monks, for purely dark deeds the result is purely dark — as before, down to: effort should be made only toward purely bright deeds. And for what reason? If the monk <s>Madhuvāsiṣṭha</s> were formerly to conceive of the great ocean as honey, it too would become honey. Thus, monks, the gift to a <s>Tathāgata</s> is immeasurable.
The monks, having doubts arise, asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'What deed, Venerable Sir, was done by the Venerable <s>Upālin</s>, by the ripening of which deed he became a royal barber?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'For <s>Upālin</s>, monks, the gift to a <s>Tathāgata</s> is immeasurable — in former lives he performed deeds, accumulated them, gathered their provisions — as before, down to: deeds indeed bear fruit for embodied beings.'

What do you think, monks? He who was the nephew of that royal barber — he is this very monk <s>Upālin</s>. Because he shaved the hair and beard of a <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> and made that vow, by the ripening of that deed he became a royal barber. Furthermore, listen to another vow he made.

In the past, monks, a <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> approached a certain royal barber: 'Good sir, shave my hair — there will be merit.' He was on his way to the royal court. He said to his nephew: 'Nephew, shave the hair of this renunciant. I am going to the royal court. Shave it just as you would the king's.' The nephew reflected: 'As my uncle says, there must be merit in this.' Having done it carefully, he shaved the hair and beard. body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in a certain market-town a householder dwelt. He brought a wife from a family of equal standing. He enjoyed, amused, and attended to her. As he enjoyed, amused, and attended to her, a son was born. Again, as he enjoyed, amused, and attended to her, a son was born. Again, as he enjoyed, amused, and attended to her, a son was born — until gradually seven sons were born. He had a friend who was a royal barber. That one was childless. Resting his cheek on his hand, he sat consumed by anxiety: 'I have no son, no daughter. After my death, all my property, being without an heir,

body.text: kathayati: vayasya kathaṃ na cintāparo bhaviṣyāmi yasya me iyat dhanajātaṃ na putro na duhitā, mamātyayāt sarvam etad rājavidheyaṃ bhaviṣyati iti; sa kathayati: yady evam eṣa mama sarvakanīyān putraḥ: sa mayā tava dattaḥ iti; tenāsau pratigṛhītaḥ; yāvad gṛhapatiḥ kālagataḥ; te tasya putrāḥ yadā kenacit sārdhaṃ kaliṃ kurvanti tadā tena paribhāṣyante: yūyam api kaliṃ kurutha yeṣāṃ bhrātā nāpitaḥ iti; te daurmanasyajātāḥ saṃlakṣayanti: yat kiṃcid vayaṃ paribhūtāḥ sarvaṃ tad asya bhrātur doṣāt; sarvathā ācchettavya iti; sa tair ācchinno nāpitaḥ; tena sarvanāpitāḥ kriyākāraṃ kāritāḥ, amukasya gṛhapateḥ putrāṇāṃ na kenacit śmaśrukarma kartavyam iti; te dīrghaśmaśrunakhā jātāḥ; te rājñā dṛṣṭā uktāś ca: bhavantaḥ kimarthaṃ yūyaṃ dīrghaśmaśrunakhās tiṣṭhatha? iti te kathayanti (
body.translated_text: will become subject to the king.' He was seen by that householder, who said: 'Friend, why are you so consumed by anxiety?' He said: 'Friend, how should I not be anxious? I have such great wealth but no son, no daughter. After my death, all of this will become subject to the king.' He said: 'If so, this youngest son of mine — I give him to you.' He accepted him. In time, the householder died. Those sons, whenever they quarreled with anyone, were taunted: 'You too quarrel — you whose brother is a barber!' Filled with displeasure, they reflected: 'Whatever contempt we suffer is all because of that brother's fault. He must be cut off at all costs.' They cut him off as a barber. He then made all the barbers take a vow: 'No one shall perform beard-trimming service for the sons of such-and-such a householder.' They grew long beards and nails. They were seen by the king, who said: 'Sirs, why do you stand about with such long beards and nails?' They said (

): 'This barber has prevented all barbers — none shall perform beard-trimming service for them.' 'For what reason?' They narrated the events as they occurred. The king said: 'A father has the right to give his son. Why did you cut him off? Return him to that very one.' They reluctantly gave him back. Filled with displeasure, and fearing public censure, they wished to kill him. The world has friends, enemies, and neutrals. Others informed him. He then said to that barber: 'They wish to kill me. Give me permission — I shall go forth.' He reflected: 'Better that he go forth than be killed by them.' Knowing this, he said: 'Son, if so, go — go forth. If you attain any collection of virtues, then inform me.' Having received permission, he went forth among the sages. Without a teacher, without a preceptor, he directly realized <s>Pratyekabodhi</s> (Solitary Awakening). He reflected: 'I made a promise to that father — I shall demonstrate [my attainment].' 'Let me go and fulfill that earlier promise.' Having gone to him, he performed the miracles of blazing, heating, raining, and flashing — until, like a tree cut at the root, he fell at his feet and began to make a vow: 'By the merit of having performed service to such a true field of merit, by this wholesome root, may I become a royal barber.' Furthermore, having performed service to five hundred <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s>, he made the vow: 'By this wholesome root, may I become a royal barber.' And again, having performed service to four <s>Samyaksaṃbuddhas</s>, he made the vow: 'By this wholesome root, may I become a royal barber.' By the ripening of that deed, he became a royal barber many times over.
Furthermore, monks, the monks, having doubts arise, asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'What deed, Venerable Sir, was done by <s>Upālin</s> such that he was declared foremost among holders of the <s>Vinaya</s>?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Where did he make the vow?'

At the time of his death, he began to make a vow: 'I have lived the holy life for my entire lifespan under the <s>Bhagavān</s> <s>Kāśyapa</s> the <s>Samyaksaṃbuddha</s>, yet I have not attained any collection of virtues. By this wholesome root, he whom the <s>Bhagavān</s> <s>Kāśyapa</s> the <s>Samyaksaṃbuddha</s> prophesied as the young man named <s>Uttara</s>: "You, young man, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, will be a <s>Tathāgata</s>, an <s>Arhat</s>, a <s>Samyaksaṃbuddha</s> named <s>Śākyamuni</s>" — may I, having gone forth under his teaching, through the abandonment of all afflictions, directly realize <s>Arhatship</s>; and just as my preceptor, the <s>Bhagavān</s> <s>Kāśyapa</s> the <s>Samyaksaṃbuddha</s>, declared me foremost among holders of the <s>Vinaya</s>, so too may that <s>Bhagavān</s> <s>Śākyamuni</s> declare me foremost among holders of the <s>Vinaya</s>.' By the force of that vow, the <s>Tathāgata</s> declared him foremost among holders of the <s>Vinaya</s>. Thus, monks, for purely dark deeds the result is purely dark — as before, down to: effort should be made. Thus, monks, you should train.

Meanwhile, there is nothing that is unknown, unseen, ununderstood, or unrecognized by <s>Buddhas</s> and <s>Bhagavāns</s>. For it is the nature (<s>dharmatā</s>) of <s>Buddhas</s> and <s>Bhagavāns</s> — who are greatly compassionate, engaged in benefiting the world, sole protectors, dwelling in tranquility and insight (<s>śamatha-vipaśyanā</s>), skilled in the three means of taming, who have crossed over the four floods, whose minds are well-established on the ground of the four bases of supernatural power (<s>ṛddhipāda</s>), who have long practiced the four means of gathering disciples (<s>saṃgrahavastu</s>), who have abandoned the five hindrances, who have transcended the five destinies, who are endowed with six factors, who have perfected the six <s>pāramitās</s> (perfections), who are adorned with the blossoms of the seven factors of awakening (<s>bodhyaṅga</s>), who are guides on the Eightfold Path, who are skilled in the nine successive meditative attainments (<s>anupūrvavihāra</s>), who possess the ten powers (<s>daśabala</s>), whose fame fills the ten directions, who are distinguished by a thousand powers — three times in the night and three times in the day, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, knowledge and vision arises: 'Who is declining? Who is progressing? Who has reached difficulty? Who has reached distress? Who has reached constriction? Who is inclined toward the lower realms? Who tends toward the lower realms? Who leans toward the lower realms? Whom shall I, having lifted from the lower realms, establish in heaven and liberation? For whom shall I plant roots of merit not yet planted? For whom shall I ripen those that have been planted? For whom shall I liberate those that have ripened?' And he said:

When the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having conquered <s>Māra</s> the Evil One together with his retinue of thirty-six <s>koṭis</s> (ten millions) of beings, attained unsurpassed knowledge, the people of the inner apartments, ministers, townspeople, and countryfolk were informed: 'Today the ascetic <s>Gautama</s> has died.' King <s>Śuddhodana</s>, together with the inner apartments, princes, ministers, townspeople, and countryfolk, began to mourn. Deities have the ability of vision below. Deities of the <s>Śuddhāvāsa</s> (Pure Abodes) class informed them: 'The <s>Bhagavān</s> has not died; rather, the <s>Bhagavān</s> has attained unsurpassed knowledge.' Then King <s>Śuddhodana</s> attained the highest joy. At that very time, a son was born to <s>Amṛtodana</s>. At his birth, having performed a birth-celebration in full detail, a name was to be assigned: 'What shall the boy's name be?' The kinsmen said: 'This boy was born while joy (<s>ānanda</s>) prevailed; therefore let the boy's name be established as <s>Ānanda</s>.' The boy <s>Ānanda</s> was entrusted to eight nurses: two for carrying, two for play, two for nursing, and two for bathing. While in the care of the nurses, the soothsayers prophesied: 'This boy will serve as attendant to the <s>Bhagavān</s> <s>Śākyamuni</s>.' Having heard that the boy was prophesied by the soothsayers, <s>Amṛtodana</s> reflected: 'If so, the <s>Bhagavān</s> will ordain him; he should not even be brought before him.' In the past, monks, in a certain settlement, a chief of the <s>Kirātas</s> (hunter-folk) dwelt. When <s>Buddhas</s> do not arise in the world, <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s> arise — compassionate toward the lowly and wretched, fond of secluded dwelling and eating places, each individually worthy of offerings to the world. Then a certain <s>Pratyekabuddha</s>, wandering here and there, arrived at the <s>Kirāta</s> settlement. He entered the house of the <s>Kirāta</s> king seeking alms. The king, having become enraged and corrupted his mind, struck him on the back with a ball of clay. That great-souled one, because his pride and conceit had been destroyed, and knowing the king's unfitness for conversion, departed.
  What do you think, monks? He who was that <s>Kirāta</s> king — that is none other than the monk <s>Ānanda</s>. Because he struck the <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> on the back with a clay ball in a fit of anger and with a corrupted mind, by the ripening of that <s>karma</s>, wherever he is born, for five hundred lifetimes a boil appears on his back. He reflected: 'This is the disciple of the ascetic <s>Gautama</s>, the monk <s>Ānanda</s>, who is reputed to be skilled in reading signs. He replied: 'So many hundreds, so many thousands, so many hundred-thousands,' and departed. That <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> removed a few leaves, counted them, and hid them. The Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>, having gone on his alms-round, returned. The <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> said to him again: 'Sir, now tell me — how many leaves are there on this <s>śiṃśapā</s> tree?' body.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavo vārāṇasyām anyatamo brāhmaṇaḥ, tena sadṛśāt kulāt kalatram ānītaṃ; sa tayā sārdhaṃ krīḍati ramate paricārayati; tasya krīḍato ramamāṇasya paricārayataḥ putro jātaḥ; tasya trīṇi saptakāny ekaviṃṣatidivasān vistareṇa jātasya jātimahaṃ kṛtvā kulasadṛśaṃ nāmadheyaṃ vyavasthāpyataṃ; sa unnīto vardhito mahān saṃvṛttaḥ; tena deśāntaraṃ gatvā ṣaṣṭisahasrakaṃ horāśāstram adhītam; evaṃ yāvat saṃsāre saṃsaratā paṃca janmaśatāni horājñānam adhītaṃ; pareṣāṃ copadiṣṭaṃ; tena hetunā tena pratyayena yatra yatropapannaḥ tatra tatra
body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, a certain <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> dwelt. He brought a wife from a family of equal standing. He enjoyed, amused, and attended to her. As he enjoyed, amused, and attended to her, a son was born. After performing the birth celebration in full for twenty-one days — three sets of seven — a name befitting the family was given. He was raised, nourished, and grew to adulthood. Having gone to another country, he studied the science of astrology (<s>horāśāstra</s>) comprising sixty thousand [verses]. Thus, throughout his wanderings in <s>saṃsāra</s>, for five hundred lifetimes he studied the knowledge of astrology, and taught it to others. By that cause and condition, wherever he was born, there

body.text: naimittikānām agro jātaḥ; yāvad etarhy api paścime bhave naimittikānām agro jātaḥ.
body.translated_text: he became the foremost among soothsayers. And even now, in his final existence, he has become the foremost among soothsayers.

The story of the rice, the two patridges and the sugar-cane
(concerning king Prasenajit and a previous birth of him)
body.translated_text:
The story of the rice, the two partridges, and the sugarcane
(concerning King <s>Prasenajit</s> and a previous birth of his)

body.text:
rājñaḥ prasenajitaḥ kośalasya pratidinaṃ bhojanakāle śālyodanaṃ phelāyāṃ nipatati tittirī dvāv ikṣuyaṣṭiś ca; tayor ekaḥ phelāyāṃ dvitīyo bhūmyāṃ; tenāyuṣmata ānandasya niveditaṃ; tena bhikṣūṇām.
  bhikṣavaḥ saṃśayajātāḥ sarvasaṃśayacchettāraṃ buddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ papracchuḥ: kiṃ bhadanta rājñā prasenajitā kośalena karma kṛtaṃ yenāsya bhojanavelāyāṃ śālyodanaṃ phelāyāṃ nipatati tittirī dvāv ikṣuyaṣṭiś ca; tayor ekaḥ phelāyāṃ, dvitīyo bhūmyāṃ? iti; bhagavān āha: rājñaiva bhikṣavaḥ prasenajitā kośalena pūrvam anyāsu jātiṣu karmāṇi kṛtāny upacitāni yenāsya bhojanavelāyāṃ (
body.translated_text:
Every day at mealtime, rice cooked in milk would fall onto King <s>Prasenajit</s> of <s>Kośala</s>'s plate, along with two partridges and a sugarcane stick. Of the two [partridges], one [fell] onto the plate, the second onto the ground. This was reported to the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>, and by him to the monks.
  The monks, doubts having arisen, asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'What <s>karma</s>, Venerable Sir, was performed by King <s>Prasenajit</s> of <s>Kośala</s> that at his mealtime, rice cooked in milk falls onto his plate, along with two partridges and a sugarcane stick — one onto the plate, the second onto the ground?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'It was King <s>Prasenajit</s> of <s>Kośala</s> himself, monks, who in the past, in other births, performed and accumulated <s>karmas</s>, by which at his mealtime (

  bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavo vārāṇasyāṃ nagaryāṃ anyatamo gṛhapatiḥ prativasaty āḍhyo mahādhano mahābhogaḥ; tasya paricārakaiḥ krṣigrāmān navaśālir ānītaḥ; dve tittirī ikṣuṣaṣṭiś ca; asati buddhānām utpāde pratyekabuddhā loka utpadyante hīnadīnānukampakāḥ prāntaśayanāsanabhaktāḥ ekadakṣiṇīyā lokasya; anyatamaḥ pratyekabuddho vārāṇasīm anuprāptaḥ; sa pūrvāhṇe nivāsya pātracīvaram ādāya piṇḍapātam aṭaṃs tasya gṛhapater niveśanaṃ praviṣṭaḥ; sa tena dṛṣṭaḥ kāyaprāsādikaḥ cittaprāsādikaś ca; tena tasmai tatprathamato navānnam ānetavyam iti kṛtvā śālyodanam ikṣuyaṣṭis tittiridvayaṃ dattaṃ; tatraikaḥ pātre nipatito dvitīyo bhūmyāṃ.
  bhagavān āha: kiṃ manyadhve bhikṣavaḥ? yo 'sau gṛhapatir eṣa evāsau rājā prasenajit kośālas tena kālena tena samayena; yad anena pratyekabuddhāya navaṃ śālyodanam ikṣuyaṣṭis tittiridvayaṃ ca dattaṃ tena karmaṇā bahūni varṣāṇī bahūni varṣaśatāni bahūni varṣaśatasahasrāṇi divyamānuṣaṃ saukhyam anubhūtam; etarhy apy asya bhojanavelāyāṃ śālyodanam ikṣuyaṣṭis tittiridvayaṃ ekaḥ phelāyāṃ patati dvitīyo bhūmyāṃ.
  rājñā prasenajitā kośalena śrutaṃ: mama bhagavatā evaṃ karmaplotir vyākṛtā; tad ayaṃ prāktanasya karmaṇaḥ phalavipāka iti viditvā bhagavati saśrāvakasaṃghe prasannaḥ; sa caivaṃ karmavipākāvarjitamatis tiṣṭhati; naimittikena ca vyākṛtam āryānandasya paṭṭabandho bhaviṣyati iti; yāvat prabhātāyāṃ rajanyām āyuṣmata ānandasya lalāṭe piṭako jātaḥ; rājñā prasenajitā kośalena śrutaṃ; tasyaitad abhavat; bhavati dakṣiṇīyeṣu kārān kṛtvā avandhyapuṇyaphalaviśeṣaḥ; yannv aham asya svayam evopasthānaṃ kūryām iti; tena sarvavaidyā āhūtaḥ: āryānandasya cikitsāṃ kuruta iti; te tasya cikitsāṃ kartum ārabdhāḥ; rājñā prasenajitā kośalena āyuṣmata ānandasya svayam eva śataśalākaṃ chatraṃ dhāritaṃ; śirāyāṃ ca muktāyāṃ lalāṭe
body.translated_text:
) rice cooked in milk falls onto his plate, along with two partridges and a sugarcane stick — one onto the plate, the second onto the ground.
  In the past, monks, in the city of <s>Vārāṇasī</s> there dwelt a certain householder, wealthy, of great riches, of great possessions. His servants brought newly harvested rice from the agricultural villages, two partridges, and a sugarcane stick. When <s>Buddhas</s> do not arise in the world, <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s> (solitary awakened ones) arise — compassionate toward the lowly and wretched, fond of secluded dwelling and eating places, each individually worthy of offerings to the world. A certain <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> arrived at <s>Vārāṇasī</s>. In the forenoon, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, he went on alms-round and entered that householder's dwelling. The householder saw him — pleasing in body and pleasing in mind. Thinking 'The first portion of the new harvest should be given to him,' he gave him rice cooked in milk, a sugarcane stick, and a pair of partridges. Of the two, one fell into the bowl and the second onto the ground.
  The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'What do you think, monks? He who was that householder — he is none other than King <s>Prasenajit</s> of <s>Kośala</s> at that time, in that era. Because he gave a <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> newly harvested rice cooked in milk, a sugarcane stick, and a pair of partridges, by the ripening of that <s>karma</s>, for many years, many hundreds of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, he has experienced divine and human happiness. And even now, at his mealtime, rice cooked in milk, a sugarcane stick, and a pair of partridges [appear] — one falls onto the plate, the second onto the ground.'
  King <s>Prasenajit</s> of <s>Kośala</s> heard: 'The <s>Bhagavān</s> has explained my <s>karma</s>-ripening thus.' Knowing 'this is the fruit-ripening of a former <s>karma</s>,' he was pleased with the <s>Bhagavān</s> together with the community of monks led by his disciples. And he remained with his mind won over by the ripening of <s>karma</s>. And the soothsayer had predicted: 'There will be a headband-investiture for the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>.' Indeed, when dawn broke, a boil arose on the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>'s forehead. King <s>Prasenajit</s> of <s>Kośala</s> heard of it. He thought: 'There is indeed a special, never-fruitless merit in performing services for those worthy of offerings. Let me personally attend to him.' He summoned all the physicians: 'Treat the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>.' They began to treat him. King <s>Prasenajit</s> of <s>Kośala</s> personally held a hundred-ribbed parasol over the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>'s head. And when the vein was lanced, on his forehead

  The monks, doubts having arisen, asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'What <s>karma</s>, Venerable Sir, was performed by the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>, by the ripening of which <s>karma</s> King <s>Prasenajit</s> of <s>Kośala</s> personally held a hundred-ribbed parasol over his head, tied a white headband, and attended to him?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'It was the monk <s>Ānanda</s> himself, monks, who in the past, in other births, performed and accumulated <s>karmas</s> — as before, up to: indeed, <s>karmas</s> ripen for embodied beings.'

children.text:
bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavo vārāṇasyām anyatamo vaidyaḥ prativasati; tasya samīpe pratyekabuddho glāna upasaṃkrāntaḥ; sa tena sarvopakaraṇaiḥ pravāritaḥ; svayam eva cikitsā kṛtā upasthānaṃ ca.
  kiṃ manyadhve bhikṣavaḥ? yo 'sau vaidya eṣa evāsau ānanadabhikṣuḥ tena kālena tena samayena; yad anena pratyekabuddhāya kārān kṛtvā praṇidhānaṃ kṛtaṃ tasya karmaṇo vipākena anekāni varṣāṇi varṣaśatāni varṣasahasrāṇi rājāmātyabrāhmaṇagṛhapatibhir asyopasthānaṃ kṛtaṃ; yāvad etarhy asya rājñā prasenajitā kośalena śatiśalākaṃ chatraṃ dhāritaṃ; svayaṃ copasthānaṃ kṛtam iti.
children.translated_text:
In the past, monks, in <s>Vārāṇasī</s> there dwelt a certain physician. A sick <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> approached him. He provided him with all requisites, personally administered the treatment, and personally attended to him.
  What do you think, monks? He who was that physician — he is none other than the monk <s>Ānanda</s> at that time, in that era. Because he performed services for a <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> and made an aspiration, by the ripening of that <s>karma</s>, for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, kings, ministers, <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, and householders have attended to him. And even now, King <s>Prasenajit</s> of <s>Kośala</s> has held a hundred-ribbed parasol for him and personally attended to him.

body.translated_text: Then the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having dwelt at <s>Śrāvastī</s> as long as he wished, set out on his journey toward <s>Śālā</s>. Traveling by stages, he reached <s>Śālā</s>. At that time, many senior elders and great disciples dwelt near the <s>Bhagavān</s> in forest huts — namely, the Venerable <s>Ājñātakauṇḍinya</s>, the Venerable <s>Aśvajit</s>, <s>Bhadrika</s>, <s>Bāṣpa</s>, <s>Mahānāman</s>, <s>Yaśa</s>, <s>Pūrṇa</s>, <s>Vimala</s>, <s>Gavāṃpati</s>, <s>Subāhu</s>, the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s>, the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>, the Venerable <s>Mahākāśyapa</s>, (

  tatra bhagavān bhikṣūn āmantrayate sma: aham asmi bhikṣavaḥ etarhi jīrṇo vṛddho mahallakaḥ, klāmyāmi catasraḥ parṣado 'vavadituṃ bhikṣūn bhikṣuṇīḥ upāsikān upāsikyaḥ; utsāhayata me bhikṣavo bhikṣum upasthāyakaṃ yo mām upasthānaṃ kariṣyati manāpena nāmanāpena, bhāṣitaṃ codgrahīṣyati, svam arthaṃ ca na riṃciṣyati; athāyuṣmān ājñātakauṇḍinya utthāyāsanād ekāṃśam uttarāsaṅgaṃ kṛtvā yena bhagavāṃs tenāñjaliṃ praṇamayya bhagavantam idam avocat*: ahaṃ bhadantam upasthāsyāmi manāpena nāmanāpena, bhāṣitaṃ codgrahīṣyāmi, svaṃ cārthaṃ na riṃciṣyāmi; tvaṃ tāvat kauṇḍinya jīrṇo vṛddho mahallakaḥ; tavaiva tāvad upasthāyakena karaṇīyaṃ; niṣīda tvaṃ kauṇḍinya yathāsvake āsane; niṣaṇṇa āyuṣmān
body.translated_text:
) the Venerable <s>Mahākauṣṭhila</s>, the Venerable <s>Mahākapphina</s>, the Venerable <s>Aniruddha</s>, <s>Nandika</s>, <s>Kimpila</s>, <s>Yaśa</s> the Elder of <s>Śālā</s> monastery, <s>Pūrṇa</s> the Elder of <s>Kuṇḍopadhānīya</s> — these and other senior elders and great disciples dwelt near the <s>Bhagavān</s>.
  There the <s>Bhagavān</s> addressed the monks: 'I am now, monks, old, aged, elderly, and I am weary of instructing the four assemblies — monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. Assign to me, monks, a monk as attendant who will attend to me in a manner that is agreeable and not disagreeable, who will retain what is spoken, and who will not neglect his own spiritual development.' Then the Venerable <s>Ājñātakauṇḍinya</s>, rising from his seat, arranging his upper robe over one shoulder, joining his palms toward the <s>Bhagavān</s>, said this to the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'I, Venerable Sir, shall attend to the <s>Bhagavān</s> in a manner that is agreeable and not disagreeable; I shall retain what is spoken and shall not neglect my own spiritual development.' 'You, <s>Kauṇḍinya</s>, are yourself old, aged, elderly. You yourself need to be attended to. Be seated, <s>Kauṇḍinya</s>, at your own seat.' The Venerable <s>Ājñātakauṇḍinya</s> sat down at his own seat.

Then the Venerable <s>Aśvajit</s>, <s>Bhadrika</s>, <s>Bāṣpa</s>, <s>Mahānāman</s>, <s>Yaśa</s>, <s>Pūrṇa</s>, <s>Vimala</s>, <s>Gavāṃpati</s>, <s>Subāhu</s>, the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s>, the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>, the Venerable <s>Mahākāśyapa</s>, the Venerable <s>Mahākauṣṭhila</s>, the Venerable <s>Mahākapphina</s>, the Venerable <s>Aniruddha</s>, <s>Nandika</s>, <s>Kimpila</s>, <s>Yaśa</s> the Elder of <s>Śālā</s> monastery, and <s>Pūrṇa</s> the Elder of <s>Kuṇḍopadhānīya</s>, each rising from their seats, arranging their upper robes over one shoulder, joining their palms toward the <s>Bhagavān</s>, said this to the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'I, Venerable Sir, shall attend to the <s>Bhagavān</s> in a manner that is agreeable and not disagreeable; I shall retain what is spoken and shall not neglect my own spiritual development.' 'You too, <s>Pūrṇa</s>, are old, aged, elderly. You yourself need to be attended to. Be seated, <s>Pūrṇa</s>, at your own seat.' The Venerable <s>Pūrṇa</s> sat down at his own seat.
  Then the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s> thought: 'Who indeed is the monk the <s>Bhagavān</s> has in mind as his attendant? Let me enter such a <s>samādhi</s> that, with my mind composed, I may observe the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s mind.' (

body.translated_text:
) Then the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s> entered such a <s>samādhi</s> that, with his mind composed, he observed the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s mind. The Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s> saw that the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s mind was settled on the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>: '<s>Ānanda</s> is the monk who shall attend to me in a manner that is agreeable and not disagreeable; he shall retain what is spoken and shall not neglect his own spiritual development.' Having seen this, emerging from that <s>samādhi</s>, he said this to the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s>: 'Know this, Venerable One — the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s mind is settled on the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>: "<s>Ānanda</s> is the monk who shall attend to me in a manner that is agreeable and not disagreeable; he shall retain what is spoken and shall not neglect his own spiritual development." Just as in a gabled house or a long hall, when sunbeams enter through the eastern window, they come to rest against the western wall — in just the same way, the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s mind is settled on the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>: "<s>Ānanda</s> is the monk who shall attend to me in a manner that is agreeable and not disagreeable; he shall retain what is spoken and shall not neglect his own spiritual development." Come, let the two of us go and encourage him.'
  Then the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> and the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s> approached the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>. Having approached, they exchanged warm and cordial words of greeting and inquiry with the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s> and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> said this to the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>: 'Will you undertake to attend to the <s>Bhagavān</s>? A great benefit will come from attending to the <s>Sugata</s>.' 'I am not able, Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s>, to attend to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. For what reason? Because <s>Buddhas</s> and <s>Bhagavāns</s> are difficult to approach, difficult to endure. Just as a blazing fire is difficult to approach and difficult to endure because of the closeness of the flames, even so <s>Buddhas</s> and <s>Bhagavāns</s> are difficult to approach and difficult to endure. I am not able to attend to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Just as a lion, king of beasts,

body.translated_text:
) will retain what is spoken, and will not neglect his own spiritual progress — this is the marvelous and wonderful quality of the monk <s>Ānanda</s>.
  When <s>Ānanda</s> was encouraged by the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Maudgalyāyana</s> as the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s attendant, and was praised by the <s>Bhagavān</s>, then the monks, doubts having arisen, asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'What <s>karma</s>, Venerable Sir, did the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s> perform, by the ripening of which he became the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s brother, attendant, one of great learning, retainer of what is heard, and storer of what is heard?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'It was the monk <s>Ānanda</s> himself, monks, who performed and accumulated <s>karmas</s>, as before, up to: indeed, <s>karmas</s> ripen for embodied beings.'

The story of Bhānumān and Bhānumantaḥ

The story of <s>Bhānumān</s> and <s>Bhānumantaḥ</s>
(concerning a previous birth of <s>Ānanda</s>)

body.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavo vārāṇasyāṃ nagaryāṃ bhānur nāma rājā rājyaṃ kārayati ṛddhaṃ ca yāvad ākīrṇabahujanamanuṣyaṃ ca; sa devyā sārdhaṃ krīḍati ramate paricārayati; tasya krīḍato ramamāṇasya paricārayataḥ putro jātaḥ; tasya jātau jātimahaṃ kṛtvā nāmadheyaṃ vyavasthāpyate, kiṃ bhavatu dārakasya nāmeti; amātyāḥ kathayanti;
body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in the city of <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, a king named <s>Bhānu</s> was exercising sovereignty — it was prosperous, and so on, teeming with a great multitude of people. He sported, enjoyed, and dallied with his queen. As he sported, enjoyed, and dallied, a son was born. At his birth, having performed the birth-celebration, a name was assigned: 'What shall the boy's name be?' The ministers said:

body.text: pitāsya bhānuḥ, tasmād bhavatu dārakasya bhānumān iti nāma; tasya bhānumān iti nāma kṛtaṃ; sa unnīto vardhito mahān saṃvṛttaḥ; pitrā yauvarājye 'bhiṣiktaḥ; bhūyo 'py asya krīḍato ramamāṇasya paricārayataḥ putro jātaḥ; tasyāpi jātau jātimahaṃ kṛtvā bhānumanta iti nāma kṛtaṃ; bhānumān kumāro naiṣkramyābhinandī; sa pitaraṃ paśyati dharmādharmeṇa rājyaṃ kārayantaṃ; sa saṃlakṣayati; aham api pitur atyayād rājā bhaviṣyāmi; aham api dharmādharmeṇa rājyaṃ kārayitvā narakaparāyaṇo bhaviṣyāmi iti; sa pituḥ sakāśam upasaṃkrāntaḥ pādayor nipatya kathayati: deva anujānīhi pravrajāmi iti; sa kathayati: putra yasyārthe yajñā ijyante homā hūyante tapāṃsi tapyante tat tava karatalagataṃ rājyaṃ; kasyārthe pravrajasi iti; sa nivāryamāṇo 'pi nāvatiṣṭhate; rājñā avaśyanirbandhaṃ jñātvā anujñātaḥ; sa ṛṣīṇāṃ madhye pravrajitaḥ; rājñā bhānumantaḥ kumāro yauvarājye abhiṣiktaḥ; bhānumatā ṛṣimadhye pravrajitena ekānte prakramya anācāryakeṇa anupādhyāyakena pratyekabodhiḥ sākṣātkṛtā; so 'pareṇa samayena glānaḥ saṃvṛttaḥ; sa itaś cānutaś ca paribhraman vārāṇasīm anuprāptaḥ; rājñā śrutaṃ; bhānumatā (
body.translated_text: 'His father is <s>Bhānu</s>; therefore let the boy's name be <s>Bhānumān</s>.' He was named <s>Bhānumān</s>. He was brought up and raised until he was grown. He was anointed by his father as crown prince. Once again, as [the king] sported, enjoyed, and dallied, another son was born. At his birth too, having performed the birth-celebration, he was named <s>Bhānumantaḥ</s>. Prince <s>Bhānumān</s> was one who delighted in renunciation. He saw his father ruling the kingdom by both righteous and unrighteous means. He considered: 'I too, after my father's death, will become king. I too, having ruled by both righteous and unrighteous means, will be destined for hell.' He approached his father, fell at his feet, and said: 'Your Majesty, give me permission — I shall go forth.' He said: 'Son, that for the sake of which sacrifices are offered, oblations are poured, and austerities are practiced — that kingdom is in the palm of your hand. For whose sake are you going forth?' Being restrained, he still would not remain. The king, knowing his resolute determination, gave permission. He went forth among the sages. The king anointed Prince <s>Bhānumantaḥ</s> as crown prince. <s>Bhānumān</s>, having gone forth among the sages, having gone to a secluded place, without a teacher, without a preceptor, directly realized <s>Pratyekabodhi</s> (Solitary Awakening). At a later time, he fell ill. Wandering here and there, he arrived at <s>Vārāṇasī</s>. The king heard: '<s>Bhānumān</s> (

body.text: ) pratyekabodhiḥ sākṣātkṛtā, sa ceha iti; sa tasya sakāśam upasaṃkrāntaḥ pādayor nipatya kathayati: maharṣe tvaṃ piṇḍakenārthī, ahaṃ puṇyena; ihaiva madīye udyāne prativasa; ahaṃ te sarvopakaraṇair vaighātaṃ karomi iti; tenādhivāsitaṃ; rājñā tasya bhānumantaḥ kumāraḥ upasthāyako dattaḥ; sa tasyopasthānaṃ kartuṃ pravṛttaḥ; pratyekabuddhena tasya alpalakṣaṇaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ, saptāhasyātyayāt kālaṃ kariṣyatīti; sa tenoktaḥ: bhrātaḥ kimarthaṃ na pravrajasi? iti; sa kathayati: maharṣe pravrajāmi; yady evaṃ gaccha, pitaram avalokya; sa rājñaḥ sakāśaṃ gataḥ; deva anujānīhi māṃ, pravrajāmi; rājā kathayati: tava bhrātā pravrajitaḥ; mamātyayāt tvam eva rājā; kimarthaṃ pravrajasi iti; sa na labhate pravrajyāṃ; sa pratyekabuddhaḥ svayam eva rājñaḥ sakāśam upasaṃkrāntaḥ; upasaṃkramya gāthayā kathayati:
body.translated_text: ) has directly realized <s>Pratyekabodhi</s>, and he is here.' He approached him, fell at his feet, and said: 'Great sage, you need alms-food and I need merit. Dwell right here in my garden. I shall provide you with all requisites.' He consented. The king assigned Prince <s>Bhānumantaḥ</s> as his attendant. He began to attend upon him. The <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> discerned a minor sign in him — he would die after seven days. He said to him: 'Brother, why do you not go forth?' He said: 'Great sage, I shall go forth.' 'If so, go — take leave of your father.' He went to the king and said: 'Your Majesty, give me permission — I shall go forth.' The king said: 'Your brother has gone forth. After my death, you will be king. Why are you going forth?' He did not obtain permission to go forth. The <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> himself approached the king. Having approached, he spoke to him in verse:

children.translated_text: Release, O <s>Bhānu</s>, <s>Bhānumantaḥ</s> — let <s>Bhānumān</s> ordain him.

children.text: pravrajyā śreyasi bhāno yasmāt saṃvarṇitā jinaiḥ // iti;
children.translated_text: Going forth is better, O <s>Bhānu</s>, since it has been praised by the <s>Jinas</s> (Conquerors). //

children.text: rājā kathayati: maharṣe tvaṃ pravrajitaḥ; eṣa mamātyayād rājā bhaviṣyati; ihaiva dānāni dāsyati; puṇyāni kariṣyati; kimarthaṃ pravrajati iti; pratyekabuddho gāthāṃ bhāṣate:
children.translated_text: The king said: 'Great sage, you have gone forth. After my death, this one will be king. Here he will give gifts and perform meritorious deeds. Why is he going forth?' The <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> spoke a verse:

children.text: anyathā cintitā hy arthā anyathā parivartitāḥ /
children.translated_text: Matters were conceived one way, but have turned out another.

children.text: alpakaṃ jīvitaṃ bhāno paraṃ saptāham eva tu //
children.translated_text: The life of <s>Bhānumantaḥ</s> is short, O <s>Bhānu</s> — only seven days more. //

body.text: maharṣe asya saptāhaṃ jīvitaṃ? pratyekabuddhaḥ kathayati, saptāhaṃ; rājā kathayati: maharṣe yady evam anujñāto bhavatu; pravrājaya; sa ātmanaḥ alpakaṃ jīvitaṃ jñātvā tīvreṇa prasādena tasyopasthānaṃ kartum ārabdhaḥ; sa pratyekabuddho vyāvābādhikaḥ; tasya pātraṃ karatale hṛhītvā bhuṃjānasya vāyunā hastaḥ kampate; tatas tena rājakumāreṇa kaṭakam avatārya pātrasya
body.translated_text: 'Great sage, does he have [only] seven days to live?' The <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> said: 'Seven days.' The king said: 'Great sage, if so, he has permission. Ordain him.' Knowing that his life was short, with intense faith, he began to attend upon him [the <s>Pratyekabuddha</s>]. That <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> was suffering from a trembling illness. As he held the bowl in the palm of his hand to eat, the wind made his hand tremble. Then that prince, removing his bracelet, gave it as a support for the bowl.

children.translated_text: The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling at <s>Rājagṛha</s> in the <s>Veṇuvana</s> (Bamboo Grove), at the <s>Kalandakanivāpa</s> (Squirrel Feeding-ground). At that time there was a famine — a hardship, a wilderness, alms-food being difficult to obtain by begging. Those monks who had attained supernatural power (<s>ṛddhi</s>) would go to the great <s>jambū</s> tree from which <s>Jambudvīpa</s> takes its name, take a bowlful of <s>jambū</s> fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, eat them themselves, and share the remainder with other monks. Or else, from the groves of <s>bilva</s> trees, <s>kapittha</s> trees, and <s>āmalakī</s> trees nearby, they would take a bowlful of <s>āmalaka</s> fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, eat them themselves, and share the remainder with other monks. Going to <s>Uttarakuru</s>, they would take a bowlful of rice that grows without cultivation from grain-bearing rice plants, eat it themselves, and share the remainder with other monks. Going to the gods of the <s>Cāturmahārājika</s> (Four Great Kings) and <s>Trāyastriṃśa</s> (Thirty-Three) heavens, they would take a bowlful of divine <s>sudhā</s> (ambrosia), eat it themselves, and share the remainder with other monks. Or, going to whatever prosperous countries, teeming with many people, they would take a bowlful of pure and excellent food and drink, eat it themselves, and share the remainder with other monks.

body.translated_text: Then <s>Devadatta</s> thought: 'Now there is a famine — a hardship, a wilderness, alms-food being difficult to obtain by begging. Those monks who have attained supernatural power go to the great <s>jambū</s> tree from which <s>Jambudvīpa</s> takes its name, take a bowlful of <s>jambū</s> fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, eat them themselves, and share the remainder with other monks. Or else, from the groves of <s>bilva</s> trees, <s>kapittha</s> trees, and <s>āmalakī</s> trees nearby, they would take a bowlful of <s>āmalaka</s> fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, eat them themselves, and share the remainder with other monks. Going to <s>Uttarakuru</s>, they take a bowlful of rice that grows without cultivation from grain-bearing rice plants, eat it themselves, and share the remainder with other monks. Going to the gods of the <s>Cāturmahārājika</s> and <s>Trāyastriṃśa</s> heavens, they take a bowlful of divine <s>sudhā</s>, eat it themselves, and share the remainder with other monks. Or, going to whatever prosperous countries, teeming with many people, they take a bowlful of pure and excellent food and drink, eat it themselves, and share the remainder with other monks. If I too were to attain supernatural power, I too could go to the great <s>jambū</s> tree from which <s>Jambudvīpa</s> takes its name, take a bowlful of <s>jambū</s> fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, eat them myself, and share the remainder with other monks. Or else, from the groves of <s>bilva</s> trees, <s>kapittha</s> trees, and <s>āmalakī</s> trees nearby, take a bowlful of <s>āmalaka</s> fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, eat them myself, and share the remainder with other monks. Going to <s>Uttarakuru</s>, take a bowlful of rice that grows without cultivation from grain-bearing rice plants, eat it myself, and share the remainder with other monks. Going to the gods of the <s>Cāturmahārājika</s> and <s>Trāyastriṃśa</s> heavens, take a bowlful of divine <s>sudhā</s>, eat it myself, and share the remainder with other monks. Or, going to whatever prosperous countries, teeming with many people, take a bowlful of pure and excellent food and drink, eat it myself, and share the remainder with other monks.'

body.translated_text: 'Now, who could teach me the path to supernatural power?' Then <s>Devadatta</s> approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the <s>Bhagavān</s> and stood to one side. Standing to one side, <s>Devadatta</s> said this to the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'May the <s>Bhagavān</s> teach me the path to supernatural power.' body.translated_text: ) 'Apply yourself wisely to higher morality (<s>adhiśīla</s>), <s>Gautama</s>, and supernatural power will come to you, and more besides. Apply yourself wisely to higher mind (<s>adhicitta</s>) and higher wisdom (<s>adhiprajñā</s>), <s>Gautama</s>, and supernatural power will come to you, and more besides.' Then <s>Devadatta</s> thought: 'The <s>Bhagavān</s> will not teach me the path to supernatural power,' and departed. He approached the Venerable <s>Ājñātakauṇḍinya</s>. Having approached, he said to the Venerable <s>Ājñātakauṇḍinya</s>: 'Elder, teach me the path to supernatural power.' Then the Venerable <s>Ājñātakauṇḍinya</s>, having ascertained the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s intention and knowing that this evil desire born of ambition had arisen in <s>Devadatta</s>, said this to <s>Devadatta</s>: 'Apply yourself wisely to form (<s>rūpa</s>), <s>Devadatta</s>, and supernatural power will come to you, and more besides.' Then <s>Devadatta</s> thought: 'Even Elder <s>Kauṇḍinya</s> will not teach me the path to supernatural power.' Knowing this, he approached the Venerable <s>Aśvajit</s>, <s>Bhadrika</s>, <s>Bāṣpa</s>, <s>Mahānāman</s>, <s>Pūrṇa</s>, <s>Vimala</s>, <s>Gavāṃpati</s>, and <s>Subāhu</s> — the five hundred elders. Having approached the five hundred elders, he said: 'Elders, teach me the path to supernatural power.' Then the five hundred elders, having ascertained the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s intention and that of the senior monks, and knowing that this evil desire born of ambition had arisen in <s>Devadatta</s>, said this to <s>Devadatta</s>: 'Apply yourself wisely to form, <s>Devadatta</s>, and supernatural power will come to you, and more besides. Apply yourself wisely to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, <s>Devadatta</s>, and supernatural power will come to you, and more besides.' Then <s>Devadatta</s> thought: 'Even the five hundred elders will not teach me the path to supernatural power. Could it be that these venerable ones have made a prior agreement with the <s>Bhagavān</s>? For none of them will teach me the path to supernatural power.' Then <s>Devadatta</s> thought: 'Now, who could be capable of teaching me the path to supernatural power?'

), he bowed his head at the feet of the Venerable <s>Daśabalakāśyapa</s> and stood to one side. Standing to one side, <s>Devadatta</s> said this to the Venerable <s>Daśabalakāśyapa</s>: 'Elder, instruct me in the path to supernatural power.' Then the Venerable <s>Daśabalakāśyapa</s>, without consulting the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s mind, and without knowing that among the senior monks and in <s>Devadatta</s> himself such an evil desire had arisen, instructed him in the path to supernatural power. Then <s>Devadatta</s>, practicing wakefulness in the first and last watches of the night, based on the first <s>dhyāna</s> (meditative absorption), produced supernatural power. He became many from being one; having become many, he became one again. He experienced appearing and disappearing through knowledge and vision. He passed with unobstructed body through walls, through mountains, through ramparts, as if through space. He dove in and out of the earth as if in water. He walked on water with unbroken surface as if on earth. He traveled through the sky cross-legged like a winged bird. He touched and stroked with his hand the sun and moon, so mighty and so powerful.
Then <s>Devadatta</s> thought: 'Why should I not go to the <s>Jambu</s> tree after which <s>Jambudvīpa</s> is named, and take a bowl-full of <s>jambu</s> fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, eat them myself, and share the remainder with a hundred monks? Or again, near that tree there is a <s>bilva</s> grove, a <s>kapittha</s> grove, an <s>āmalakī</s> grove — should I take a bowl-full of <s>āmalaka</s> fruits endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, eat them myself, and share the remainder with a hundred monks? Or go to <s>Uttarakuru</s> continent and take a bowl-full of unhusked self-growing rice with fruit, eat it myself, and share the remainder with a hundred monks? Or go to the <s>Cāturmahārājika</s> and <s>Trāyastriṃśa</s> heavens and take a bowl-full of divine ambrosia (<s>sudhā</s>), eat it myself, and share the remainder with a hundred monks? Or to those prosperous regions teeming with many people, and take a bowl-full of pure and excellent food, eat it myself, and share the remainder with a hundred monks?'

[He appeared as] a noble thoroughbred horse, and also a tonsured monk clad in the <s>saṃghāṭī</s> robe. And now, appearing as a young boy wearing a golden belt, he climbed onto Prince <s>Ajātaśatru</s>'s lap and rolled, turned, and twisted about. <s>Ajātaśatru</s> embraced, kissed, and hugged the boy. He even put a ball of phlegm into his mouth — and <s>Devadatta</s> ate it, being thus overcome and possessed in mind by gain and honor. Then Prince <s>Ajātaśatru</s> developed an even more wicked false view: 'How much more powerful the noble <s>Devadatta</s> is than the Teacher!' Being devout, he performed acts befitting his devotion: together with five hundred chariots, he went out morning and evening to attend upon him, and five hundred pot-cooked meals were brought to him at each mealtime. <s>Devadatta</s> too sat at the head of the meal together with five hundred monks.

body.translated_text: ) Having heard this, they went on their alms-round in <s>Rājagṛha</s>, finished their meal, attended to their after-meal duties, put away their bowls and robes, washed their feet, and approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the <s>Bhagavān</s> and sat to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said this to the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'Here, Venerable Sir, we monks, having dressed in the forenoon and taken our bowls and robes, entered <s>Rājagṛha</s>. We heard, Venerable Sir, while going on our alms-round in <s>Rājagṛha</s>: "Such gain and honor has arisen for <s>Devadatta</s>! King <s>Ajātaśatru</s> of <s>Magadha</s>, son of <s>Vaidehī</s>, together with five hundred chariots, goes out morning and evening to attend upon him. Five hundred pot-cooked meals are brought to him at each mealtime. <s>Devadatta</s> sits at the head of the meal together with five hundred monks."' 'Do not, monks, envy <s>Devadatta</s>'s gain and honor. And for what reason? Gain and honor are for <s>Devadatta</s>'s destruction. Gain and honor are for <s>Devadatta</s>'s ruin. Just as, monks, a plantain tree bears fruit for its own destruction, bears fruit for its own ruin, so too gain and honor are for

<s>Devadatta</s>'s destruction. Gain and honor are for <s>Devadatta</s>'s ruin. Just as a bamboo or a reed bears fruit for its own destruction, so too gain and honor are for <s>Devadatta</s>'s destruction. Gain and honor are for <s>Devadatta</s>'s ruin. Just as a she-mule conceives for her own destruction, conceives for her own ruin, so too gain and honor are for <s>Devadatta</s>'s destruction. As long as, monks, such gain and honor arises for <s>Devadatta</s>, it will be for that foolish man's long-lasting harm and suffering. Therefore, monks, you should train thus: "We shall overcome gain and honor, and gain and honor that has arisen shall not seize and dominate our minds." Thus, monks, you should train.
Fruit destroys the plantain; fruit destroys the bamboo; fruit destroys the reed; /
honor destroys a man, just as its own offspring destroys the she-mule. // (

body.translated_text: Then, in <s>Devadatta</s>, who was overcome by gain and honor and whose mind was possessed, this evil desire arose: 'Now the <s>Bhagavān</s> is aged, old, and advanced in years. He is weary of admonishing the four assemblies. Would that the <s>Bhagavān</s> would hand over the community of monks to me! I would govern the community of monks. The <s>Bhagavān</s> could dwell with little concern, devoted to the pleasant abiding in the present life.' The very moment that thought arose, <s>Devadatta</s> lost that supernatural power. And having lost it, he did not even know: 'I too have lost it.'

body.translated_text: At that time, the monk <s>Kakuda</s>, son of <s>Kroḍa</s>, a disciple of the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having practiced the holy life in the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s presence and developed the four <s>Brahmavihāras</s> (divine abidings), having abandoned desire for sensual pleasures, and dwelling predominantly in those states, was reborn in the company of the <s>Brahmaloka</s>. At that time, the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s> was dwelling among the <s>Bhārgavas</s> at <s>Śiśumāragiri</s> in the <s>Bhīṣaṇikā</s> forest, in the Deer Park. Then <s>Kakuda</s> the <s>Brahmā</s>, knowing that <s>Devadatta</s> had lost his supernatural power, just as a strong man might extend a bent arm or bend an extended arm, so <s>Kakuda</s> the <s>Brahmā</s> vanished from the <s>Brahmaloka</s> and appeared among the <s>Bhārgavas</s> before the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>. Then <s>Kakuda</s> the <s>Brahmā</s> said this to the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>: 'You should know, Venerable <s>Maudgalyāyana</s>, that in <s>Devadatta</s>, who is overcome by gain and honor and whose mind is possessed, this evil desire has arisen: "Now the <s>Bhagavān</s> is aged, old, and advanced in years. body.translated_text: 'You should approach the <s>Bhagavān</s> and report this very matter in detail, out of compassion.' The Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s> accepted <s>Kakuda Brahmā</s>'s [request] by his silence. Then <s>Kakuda Brahmā</s>, knowing the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>'s acceptance by his silence, bowed his head at the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>'s feet and vanished right there. Then the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>, knowing that <s>Kakuda Brahmā</s> had just recently departed, entered such a <s>samādhi</s> that, with his mind concentrated, he vanished among the <s>Bhārgavas</s> and appeared in <s>Rājagṛha</s>, at the <s>Veṇuvana</s>, the <s>Kalandakanivāpa</s>. Then the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s> approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Having approached, he bowed his head at the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s> reported in detail the entire conversation he had had with <s>Kakuda Brahmā</s>. Thus addressed, the <s>Bhagavān</s> said this to the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>: 'Did you not, <s>Maudgalyāyana</s>, already know <s>Devadatta</s> previously by pervading his mind with your own? Why then was it afterward reported by <s>Kakuda Brahmā</s>?' 'Indeed so, Venerable Sir.' This, then, was the conversation that took place between the <s>Bhagavān</s> and the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>.

body.text: atha devadattaś catubhir bhikṣubhiḥ sahāyakaiḥ kokālikena khaṇḍadravyeṇa kaṭamorakatiṣyeṇa samudradattena ca sārdhaṃ yena bhagavāṃs tenopasaṃkrāntaḥ; adrākṣīd bhagavān devadattaṃ dūrād eva dṛṣṭvā ca punar āyuṣmantaṃ mahāmaudgalyāyanam āmantrayate: rakṣedānīṃ maudgalyāyana, rakṣedānīṃ maudgalyāyana, eṣa gacchati devadattaḥ; idānīṃ eṣa mohapuruṣo mama purastād ātmanaivātmānaṃ vyākariṣyati; athāyuṣmān mahāmaudgalyāyanaḥ bhagavataḥ (
body.translated_text: Then <s>Devadatta</s>, together with his four monk companions — <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamorakatiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s> — approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> saw <s>Devadatta</s> from afar. Having seen him, he addressed the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>: 'Take care now, <s>Maudgalyāyana</s>! Take care now, <s>Maudgalyāyana</s>! Here comes <s>Devadatta</s>. Now this deluded man will declare himself before me by his own mouth.' Then the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>, having bowed at the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s (

bhagavato 'ntike kopaṃ ca dveṣaṃ ca mānaṃ ca mrakṣaṃ ca āghātaṃ ca akṣāntiṃ ca apratyayaṃ ca prāviṣkārṣīt*; atha devadatto hum iti kṛtvā triḥ śiraḥ kampayitva bhagavato antikāt prakrāntaḥ.

body.text: tena khalu samayena āyuṣmān ānando bhagavataḥ pṛṣṭhataḥ sthito 'bhūd vyajanaṃ gṛhītvā ca bhagavantaṃ vījayamānaḥ; tatra bhagavān āyuṣmantam ānandam āmantrayate: gacchānanda yāvanto veṇuvanaṃ kalandakanivāpam upaniśritya viharanti tān sarvān upasthānaśālāyāṃ sannipātaya; evaṃ bhadanta ity āyuṣmān ānando bhagavataḥ pratiśrutya, yāvanto bhikṣavo veṇuvanaṃ kalandakanivāpam upaniśritya viharanti tān sarvān upasthānaśālāyāṃ sannipātya yena bhagavāṃs tenopasaṃkrāntaḥ; upasaṃkramya bhagavataḥ pādau śirasā vanditvā ekānte asthāt*; ekāntasthita āyuṣmān ānando bhagavantam (
body.translated_text: At that time the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s> stood behind the <s>Bhagavān</s>, holding a fan and fanning the <s>Bhagavān</s>. There the <s>Bhagavān</s> addressed the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>: 'Go, <s>Ānanda</s>, and assemble in the assembly hall all those monks who dwell in dependence on the <s>Veṇuvana</s>, the <s>Kalandakanivāpa</s>.' 'Yes, Venerable Sir.' The Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>, having assented to the <s>Bhagavān</s>, assembled in the assembly hall all those monks who dwelt in dependence on the <s>Veṇuvana</s>, the <s>Kalandakanivāpa</s>, and then approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Having approached, he bowed his head at the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s feet and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s> said this to the <s>Bhagavān</s> (

  1) ihaikaḥ śāstā apariśuddhaśīla eva san pariśuddhaṃ me śīlam akliṣṭa iti pratijānīte; tam enaṃ śrāvakāḥ saṃvāsānvayāt pratijānanti: ayaṃ bhagavān śāstā apariśuddhaśīla eva san pariśuddhaṃ me śīlam asaṃkliṣṭa iti pratijānīte; vayaṃ ced enaṃ pareṣām ārocayema tenāsya syād amanāpaṃ; yenāsya syād amanāpaṃ kiṃ vayaṃ tena śāstāraṃ samudācariṣyāmaḥ? eṣa bhagavān śāstā svayam eva pratijānāti; smanvāharaty eṣo 'smān yaduta cīvarapariṇḍapātaśayanāsanaglānapratyayabhaiṣajyapariṣkāraiḥ; ity apy enaṃ śrāvakāḥ śīlavanto 'nurakṣitavyaṃ manyante; evaṃrūpaḥ śāstā śrāvakāṇām antikāt śīlānurakṣanaṃ pratyāśaṃsati; ayaṃ prathamaḥ śāstā san sanvidyamāno loke.
  2) punar aparam ihaikaḥ śāstā apariśuddhajīva eva pariśuddho me ajīvaḥ akliṣṭa iti pratijānīte; tam enaṃ śrāvakāḥ saṃvāsānvayāt pratijānanti: ayaṃ bhagavān śāstā apariśuddhajīva eva san pariśuddho me ājīva asaṃkliṣṭa iti pratijānīte; vayaṃ ced enaṃ pareṣām ārocayema tenāsya syād amanāpaṃ; yenāsya syād amanāpaṃ kiṃ vayaṃ tena śāstāraṃ samudācariṣyāmaḥ? eṣa bhagavān śāstā svayam eva pratijānāti; smanvāharaty eṣo 'smān yaduta cīvarapariṇḍapātaśayanāsanaglānapratyayabhaiṣajyapariṣkāraiḥ; ity apy enaṃ śrāvakāḥ ājīvato 'nurakṣitavyaṃ manyante; evaṃrūpaḥ śāstā śrāvakāṇām antikāt śīlānurakṣanaṃ pratyāśaṃsati; ayaṃ dvitīyaḥ śāstā san sanvidyamāno loke.
  3) punar aparam ihaikaḥ śāstā
body.translated_text:
): 'Venerable Sir, all those monks who dwell in dependence on the <s>Veṇuvana</s>, the <s>Kalandakanivāpa</s>, have sat down and assembled in the assembly hall. Now let the <s>Bhagavān</s> do as he sees fit.'
  Then the <s>Bhagavān</s> approached the assembly hall. Having approached, he sat on a seat prepared before the community of monks. Having sat down, the <s>Bhagavān</s> addressed the monks: 'Monks, there are these five types of teachers existing and found in the world. What five?
  1) Here, one teacher, though his moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>) is impure, claims: "My moral conduct is pure and untainted." His disciples know through living with him: "This venerable teacher, though his moral conduct is impure, claims his moral conduct is pure and untainted. If we were to tell others, that would be displeasing to him. What would be displeasing to him — why should we address the teacher with that?" This venerable teacher himself claims it; he looks after us with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Thus even his virtuous disciples think he should be guarded with respect to moral conduct. Such a teacher expects protection of his moral conduct from his disciples. This is the first type of teacher existing and found in the world.
  2) Furthermore, here one teacher, though his livelihood (<s>ājīva</s>) is impure, claims: "My livelihood is pure and untainted." His disciples know through living with him: "This venerable teacher, though his livelihood is impure, claims his livelihood is pure and untainted. If we were to tell others, that would be displeasing to him. What would be displeasing to him — why should we address the teacher with that?" This venerable teacher himself claims it; he looks after us with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Thus even his disciples think he should be guarded with respect to livelihood. Such a teacher expects protection of his moral conduct from his disciples. This is the second type of teacher existing and found in the world.

This venerable teacher himself claims it; he looks after us with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Thus even his disciples think he should be guarded with respect to knowledge and vision. Such a teacher expects protection of his knowledge and vision from his disciples. This is the third type of teacher existing and found in the world.
  4) Furthermore, here one teacher, though his explanation (<s>vyākaraṇa</s>) is deficient, claims: "My explanation is complete and untainted." His disciples know through living with him: "This venerable teacher, though his explanation is deficient, claims his explanation is complete and untainted. If we were to tell others, that would be displeasing to him. What would be displeasing to him — why should we address the teacher with that?" This venerable teacher himself claims it; he looks after us with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Thus even his disciples think he should be guarded with respect to his complete explanation. Such a teacher expects protection of his complete explanation from his disciples. This is the fourth type of teacher existing and found in the world.
  5) Furthermore, here one teacher, though his <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s> are poorly proclaimed, claims: "My <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s> are well-proclaimed and untainted." His disciples know through living with him: "This venerable teacher, though his <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s> are poorly proclaimed, claims his <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s> are well-proclaimed and untainted. If we were to tell others, that would be displeasing to him. What would be displeasing to him — why should we address the teacher with that?" This venerable teacher himself claims it; he looks after us with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Thus even his disciples think he should be guarded with respect to his well-proclaimed <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s>. Such a teacher expects protection of his well-proclaimed <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s> from his disciples. This is the fifth type of teacher existing and found in the world.

body.translated_text: possessing pure knowledge and vision, I declare: 'My knowledge and vision are pure and undefiled.' My disciples do not think I should be protected on account of my knowledge and vision. I do not expect from my disciples the protection of my knowledge and vision. Indeed, monks, possessing accomplished explanation, I declare: 'My explanation is accomplished and undefiled.' My disciples do not think I should be protected on account of my accomplished explanation. I do not expect from my disciples the protection of my accomplished explanation. Indeed, monks, having a well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, I declare: 'My Dharma and Vinaya are well-proclaimed and undefiled.' My disciples do not think I should be protected on account of my well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. I do not expect from my disciples the protection of my well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. I shall speak to you, monks, with restraint, with persistence — I shall not flatter you, like a potter [testing] unfired vessels. What is of substance will endure. And you are capable of [receiving] the Bhagavān's words.

children.text: atha devadattaḥ kokālikakhaṇḍadravyakaṭamorakatiṣyasamudradattan āmantrayate: eta evaṃ kokālikakhaṇḍadravyakaṭamorakatiṣyasamudradattāḥ; tiṣṭhate eva śramaṇasya gautamasya samagraṃ śrāvakasaṃghaṃ bhetsyāmaḥ; cakrabhedaṃ kariṣyāmaḥ; tad asmākam abhyatītakālagatānāṃ digvidikṣu udāraḥ kalyāṇaḥ kīrtiśabdaślokaḥ abhyudgamiṣyati; tiṣṭhata eva śramaṇasya gautamasya tāvanmahardhikasya tāvanmahānubhāvasya devadattena kokālikena khaṇḍadravyeṇa kaṭamorakatiṣyeṇa samudradattena samagraḥ śrāvakasaṃghaḥ bhinnaś cakrabhedaś ca kriyate iti; te kathayanti: na śakṣyāmo vayaṃ devadatta bhagavataḥ samagraṃ śrāvakasaṃghaṃ bhettuṃ; tat kasya hetoḥ? santy āyuṣman devadatta bhagavataḥ śrāvakāḥ mahardhikā mahānubhāvā divyacakṣuṣaḥ paracittavidaḥ; ye dūrād api paśyanti, antike 'pi na dṛśyante; te cetasā cittaṃ spharitvā manasā mano vijānanti; te asmān parisarpata eva jñāsyanti iti; sa kathayati: asti kokālika upāyaḥ; ete vayaṃ sthavirasthavirān bhikṣūn upasaṃkramāmaḥ sarvopakaraṇaiḥ alpotsukhā bhavantu sthavirā vayaṃ sthavirāṇāṃ sarvopakaraṇair avighātaṃ kariṣyāma iti; navakāṃś ca bhikṣūn upasthāpayāmaḥ upalāḍāyāmaḥ pātreṇa cīvareṇa śikyena saritena kāyabandhanena uddeśena pāṭhena svādhyāyena yogena manasikāreṇa; asty eṣa āyuṣman devadatta upāya iti; tatra devadattaḥ samagrasya saṃghasya bhedāya parākramitum ārabdhaḥ.
children.translated_text: Then <s>Devadatta</s> addressed <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s>: 'Come, <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s>! Even while the ascetic <s>Gautama</s> remains, we shall split the united community of his disciples. We shall bring about a wheel-breaking. Then, when we have passed away and are gone, a great, noble, auspicious fame and renown shall spread in all directions: "Even while the ascetic <s>Gautama</s>, of such great supernatural power and such great majesty, remained, <s>Devadatta</s> together with <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s> split the united community of his disciples and brought about a wheel-breaking."' They said: 'We are unable, Venerable <s>Devadatta</s>, to split the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s united community of disciples. For what reason? Because, Venerable <s>Devadatta</s>, the <s>Bhagavān</s> has disciples of great supernatural power and great majesty, who possess the divine eye and know the minds of others — they see even from afar, yet cannot be seen even close by. They, pervading mind with mind, will know our intentions even while we are merely creeping about.' He said: 'There is a stratagem, <s>Kokālika</s>. We shall approach the senior elder monks and [offer]: "Let the Elders be free from concern about all requisites — we shall provide the Elders with all requisites without hindrance." And we shall attend to the junior monks, winning them over with bowls, robes, slings, belts, body-bands, recitation instruction, text study, oral review, meditation practice, and mental attention.' 'This is indeed a stratagem, Venerable <s>Devadatta</s>.' Thereupon <s>Devadatta</s> began to exert himself toward splitting the united <s>Saṅgha</s>.

  'Let the venerable <s>Saṅgha</s> hear! These — <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka</s>, <s>Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s> — knowing that a monk is striving for the schism of the united <s>Saṅgha</s>, are acting as his followers in the disruptive speech. And they say to the monks: "Do not, venerable ones, say anything to this monk — whether good or bad. And why? This monk, venerable ones, is one who speaks the <s>Dharma</s>, one who speaks the <s>Vinaya</s>. This monk upholds and maintains the <s>Dharma</s> and the <s>Vinaya</s>. This monk speaks with knowledge, not without knowledge. What is agreeable and acceptable to this monk is agreeable and acceptable to us as well." Though admonished by many monks through friendly counsel, they persist in holding firmly to that same matter and insist: "This alone is the truth; all else is delusion." The <s>Saṅgha</s> admonishes <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka</s>, <s>Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s> by the formal act of the fourth motion: "Do not, <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka</s>, <s>Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s>, knowing that a monk is striving for the schism of the united <s>Saṅgha</s> and who, having taken up and maintained a dispute conducive to schism, stands [in it] — be followers of his in the disruptive speech. And do not say to the monks: 'Do not, venerable ones, say anything to this monk — whether good or bad. And why? This monk is one who speaks the <s>Dharma</s>, one who speaks the <s>Vinaya</s>. This monk upholds and maintains the <s>Dharma</s> and the <s>Vinaya</s>. This monk speaks with knowledge, not with ignorance. What is agreeable and acceptable to this monk is agreeable and acceptable to us as well.' And why? This monk is not one who speaks the <s>Dharma</s>, nor one who speaks the <s>Vinaya</s>. This monk upholds and maintains what is contrary to <s>Dharma</s> and contrary to <s>Vinaya</s>. This monk speaks without knowledge, not with knowledge. Let the venerable ones not delight in the schism of the <s>Saṅgha</s>. Let them delight rather in the harmony of the <s>Saṅgha</s>. Let the venerable ones come together with the <s>Saṅgha</s>. For a united <s>Saṅgha</s>, harmonious, in accord, not quarreling, single-minded, reciting as one, united as milk and water, illuminating the Teacher's teaching, dwells in the touch of happiness. Let the venerable ones abandon this conduct that follows the schism of the <s>Saṅgha</s>, this disruptive speech.' Those who consent are to remain silent; those who do not consent should speak. This is the first reading of the motion. Likewise the second and third readings. (
