  devadattena śrutaṃ vyākṛto 'haṃ śramaṇena gautamena pratibalo me bhikṣavo devadattaḥ samagraṃ śrāvakasaṃghaṃ bhettuṃ cakrabhedaṃ ca kartuṃ; tathā cāsya catvāro bhikṣavaḥ sahāyakāḥ anuvartino vyagravāditāyāṃ kokālikakhaṇḍadravyakaṭamorakatiṣyasamudradattāḥ iti; śrutvā ca punaḥ kokālikakhaṇḍadravyakaṭamorakatiṣyasamudradattān āmantrayate:
body.translated_text:
The monks reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'Venerable Sir, we have admonished <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka</s>, <s>Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s> by the formal act of the fourth motion. Though admonished, they persist in holding firmly to that same matter and insist: "This alone is the truth; all else is delusion."' There the <s>Bhagavān</s> addressed the monks: '<s>Devadatta</s> is capable, monks, of splitting the united community of disciples and of creating a wheel-breaking [schism]. He has four monks as allies and followers in the disruptive speech: <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka</s>, <s>Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s>.'
  <s>Devadatta</s> heard: 'I have been declared by the ascetic <s>Gautama</s>: "<s>Devadatta</s> is capable of splitting the united community of disciples and of creating a wheel-breaking [schism]. He has four monks as allies and followers in the disruptive speech: <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka</s>, <s>Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s>."' Having heard, he addressed <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka</s>, <s>Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s>:

body.text:
yat khalu kokālikakhaṇḍadravyakaṭamorakatiṣyasamudradattāḥ jānīyāta, vyākṛto 'haṃ śramaṇena gautamena pratibalo devadattaḥ samagraṃ śrāvakasaṃghaṃ bhettuṃ cakrabhedaṃ ca kartuṃ; tathā cāsya catvāro bhikṣavaḥ sahāyakāḥ kokālikakhaṇḍadravyakaṭamorakatiṣyasamudradattā iti; yannv ahaṃ bhūyasyā matrayā saṃghabhedāya parākrameya iti; sa paṃcabhir bhikṣuśataiḥ sārdham ante ārāmasya gaṇabhojanaṃ bhuṅkte; etat prakaraṇaṃ bhikṣavo bhagavata ārocayanti.
  bhagavān āha: kiṃ manyadhve bhikṣavaḥ? kimarthaṃ tathāgatena trikabhojanam anujñātaṃ; gaṇabhojanaṃ pratikṣiptaṃ? nanu dvāv arthāu saṃpaśyatā, kulodayatāṃ ca pratītya, pāpecchānāṃ (
body.translated_text:
'Know this, <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka</s>, <s>Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s> — I have been declared by the ascetic <s>Gautama</s>: "<s>Devadatta</s> is capable of splitting the united community of disciples and of creating a wheel-breaking [schism]. He has four monks as allies: <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka</s>, <s>Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s>." Why should I not strive even more for the schism of the <s>Saṅgha</s>?' He, together with five hundred monks, ate a group-meal at the edge of the monastery. The monks reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>.
  The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'What do you think, monks? For what purpose did the <s>Tathāgata</s> allow eating in groups of three but prohibit group-meals? Was it not with two purposes in view: consideration for the welfare of families, and (

body.text: SBV II 86
) ca pudgalānāṃ pakṣapralopanārthaṃ; mā haiva pāpecchaḥ pudgalaḥ saṃgham evāgamya, saṃgham evoddiśya, saṃgham evāvedayitvā pāṣaṇḍika iva kṛtvā saṃghenaiva sārdhaṃ vigṛhya vivādaṃ sthāpayet iti.
body.translated_text: ) to prevent persons of evil desires from attracting a faction? Lest a person of evil desires, having approached the <s>Saṅgha</s>, and having designated the <s>Saṅgha</s>, and having informed the <s>Saṅgha</s>, should act in the manner of a sectarian, and having quarreled with the <s>Saṅgha</s> itself, should establish a dispute.'

children.translated_text: <s>Devadatta</s> loses his magical powers

children.text:
yadā āyuṣmatā daśabalakāśyapena devadattasya ṛddher mārgo vyapadiṣṭaḥ, tadāsau bhikṣubhir ucyate: kasmāt tvayā sthavira devadattasya pāpecchasya ṛddher mārgo vyapadiṣṭaḥ? sa kathayati: nāham āyuṣmanto jāne yathāyaṃ pāpeccha iti; yadi mayā jñātam abhaviṣyat ṛkāro 'py asya mayā na vyapadiṣṭo 'bhaviṣyat; prāg eva ṛddher mārgaḥ iti; tato devadattaḥ bhikṣubhiḥ praṇayam āsthāyocyate; devadatta yā kācit śrīsaubhāgyasaṃpat, sarvāsau sthaviraṃ daśabalakāśyapam āgamya; na tvaṃ tasya sakāśam upasaṃkrāmasi iti; te saṃlakṣayanti: apy eva nāmāyam asmābhiḥ prabodhitaḥ tasya sakāśam upasaṃkrāmet; sa evaṃ pratinivartayet iti; sa evaṃ praticoditaḥ kathayati: kiṃ mama tena kṛtaṃ? nanu mayā vīryam ādhāya, pūrvarātrāpararātraṃ jāgarikāyogam anuyuktena viharatā prathamaṃ dhyānaṃ niśritya ṛddhir abhinirhṛtā iti; sa vākpravyāharaṇakālasamanantaram eva tayā akṛtajñatayā ṛddheḥ parihīṇaḥ.
  bhikṣavaḥ saṃśayajātāḥ sarvasaṃśayacchettāraṃ buddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ papracchuḥ: paśya bhadanta devadattaḥ akṛtajñatayā ṛddheḥ parihīṇaḥ iti; bhagavān āha: na bhikṣava etarhi, yathā atīte 'py adhvany eṣaḥ akṛtajñatayā vidyāyāḥ parihīṇaḥ; tac chrūyatāṃ.
children.translated_text:
When the Venerable <s>Daśabalakāśyapa</s> had taught <s>Devadatta</s> the path to supernatural power, the monks said to him: 'Why, Elder, did you teach the path to supernatural power to <s>Devadatta</s>, a man of evil desires?' He said: 'Venerable Ones, I did not know that he was of evil desires. If I had known, I would not have taught him even the letter "ṛ" — let alone the path to supernatural power.' Then the monks, approaching <s>Devadatta</s> with affection, said: '<s>Devadatta</s>, whatever glory and good fortune you have attained, all of that is thanks to the Elder <s>Daśabalakāśyapa</s>. Why do you not go to him?' They thought: 'Perhaps if we admonish him, he will approach him and thus reform.' But when thus urged, he said: 'What has he done for me? Did I not, by exerting effort, keeping vigil in the first and last watches of the night, and dwelling devoted to the practice of wakefulness, produce supernatural power based on the first <s>dhyāna</s> (meditative absorption)?' The very moment he uttered those words, through that ingratitude he lost his supernatural power.
  The monks, doubts having arisen, asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'See, Venerable Sir — <s>Devadatta</s> has lost his supernatural power through ingratitude.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Not only now, monks; in the past too, he lost his magical knowledge through ingratitude. Listen to this.'

body.text:
The story of an out-caste versed in magic and of a brāhmaṇa student
(concerning a previous birth of Devadatta)
body.translated_text:
The story of an outcaste versed in magic and of a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> student
(concerning a previous birth of <s>Devadatta</s>)

body.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavo vārāṇasyāṃ nagaryāṃ brahmadatto nāma rājyaṃ kārayati ṛddhaṃ ca yāvad ākīrṇabahujanamanuṣyaṃ ca; (
body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in the city of <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, a king named <s>Brahmadatta</s> was exercising sovereignty — it was prosperous, and so on, teeming with a great multitude of people. (

body.text: SBV II 87
body.translated_text: SBV II 87

body.text: ) tatra caṇḍālo vidyāmantradharo vidyāmantrakuśalaḥ gāndhārīvidyāṃ parivartya ṛddhyā gandhamādanāt parvatāt akālartukāni puṣpaphalāny ādāya rājñe brahmadattāyopanayati; rājā brahmadattas tasyābhiprasannaḥ abhisāram anuprayacchati; yāvad anyatamo māṇavo mantrārthī mantragavaṣī śravaparampayā janapadāt vārāṇasīm anuprāptaḥ; tato mārgaśramaṃ prativinodya tasya caṇḍālasya vidyāmantradhāriṇaḥ sakāśam upasaṃkrāntaḥ; upasaṃkramya kathayati: icchāmy aham upādhyāyasya śuśrūṣāṃ kartuṃ; kasyārthe? vidyāyāḥ; sa gāthāṃ bhāṣate:
body.translated_text: ) There, a <s>Caṇḍāla</s> (outcaste) who possessed magical spells and was skilled in magical incantations, having mastered the <s>Gāndhārī</s> spell, would fly by supernatural power to Mount <s>Gandhamādana</s>, take flowers and fruits of out-of-season varieties, and present them to King <s>Brahmadatta</s>. King <s>Brahmadatta</s>, pleased with him, gave him an allowance. Then a certain young <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, desirous of spells and seeking incantations, having heard by word of mouth, came from the countryside to <s>Vārāṇasī</s>. Having recovered from the fatigue of travel, he approached that <s>Caṇḍāla</s> who possessed magical spells and said: 'I wish to serve the teacher.' 'For what purpose?' 'For the sake of magical knowledge.' He spoke a verse:

children.text: na vidyā kasyacid deyā martavyaṃ saha vidyayā /
children.translated_text: Magical knowledge should not be given to anyone; one should die with one's knowledge.

children.text: prayacched vidyayā vidyāṃ śuśrūṣābhir dhanena vā // <iti>
children.translated_text: One should give knowledge [only] in exchange for knowledge, service, or wealth. //

body.text: sa kathayati: upādhyāya yady evam ahaṃ śuśrūṣāṃ karomi; kiyantaṃ kālaṃ kartavyā? sa kathayati: dvādaśabhir varṣaiḥ śuśrūṣayā dīyeta vā na vā; so 'tyarthaṃ vidyāpratipannaḥ anujñātavān; tata ārādhanaparamaḥ satkṛtya guruśuśrūṣāṃ kartum ārabdhaḥ; yāvad apareṇa samayenāsau caṇḍālo madyamadākṣipto gṛham āgataḥ; sa māṇavaḥ saṃlakṣayati; ayam upādhyāyaḥ atīva madyamadākṣiptaḥ; pārśve asya śayyā kalpayitavyā iti; yāvad asau caṇḍālaḥ saṃparivartitum ārabdhaḥ; tasya saṃparivartamānasya khaṭvāyā aṅgaṇikā bhagnā; māṇavaḥ śrutvā pratibuddhaḥ; sa saṃlakṣayati: upādhyāyaḥ duḥkhaṃ śayiṣyate; yannv aham aṅgaṇikāyāṃ pṛṣṭhaṃ datvā avasthitaḥ; dharmatā hy eṣā śauṇḍānāṃ yo balavāṃs tasya vāntir bhavati; tasya prathame yāme madyaṃ vigacchati; tena tīkṣṇamadyavegāt māṇavasya pṛṣṭhe vāntaṃ; sa saṃlakṣayati: yady ahaṃ kāyaṃ cālayeyaṃ vācaṃ vā niścārayeyaṃ sthānam etad vidyate yad upādhyāyaḥ śabdaṃ śrutvā pratibuddho na punaḥ śayyāṃ kalpayet; sa pratisaṅkhyānena avasthitaḥ; yāvad caṇḍālaḥ svayam eva pratibuddhaḥ paśyati taṃ tathā viprakṛtaṃ; tataḥ pṛcchati, ko 'yaṃ; sa kathayati: upādhyāya ahaṃ somaśarmā; vatsa (
body.translated_text: He said: 'Teacher, if so, I shall perform service. For how long must it be done?' He said: 'Through twelve years of service, it may or may not be given.' He, being exceedingly eager for the knowledge, consented. Then, with the utmost devotion, he began to serve the teacher respectfully. At a later time, that <s>Caṇḍāla</s> came home intoxicated with liquor. The young <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> considered: 'The teacher is extremely intoxicated. A bed must be arranged beside him.' Then the <s>Caṇḍāla</s> began to toss about. As he tossed about, a leg of the cot broke. The young man, hearing it, awoke. He considered: 'The teacher will sleep uncomfortably. Let me put my back against the broken leg and stay thus.' For it is the nature of drunkards that the strong one vomits. In the first watch, his drunkenness passed; and due to the force of the strong liquor, he vomited on the young man's back. He considered: 'If I move my body or utter a sound, there is a possibility that the teacher, hearing the noise, will wake up and not settle back to sleep.' So he remained steady through careful reflection. Then the <s>Caṇḍāla</s> himself woke up and saw him thus mistreated. He asked: 'Who is this?' He said: 'Teacher, I am <s>Somaśarman</s>.' 'Child, (

body.text: SBV II 88
body.translated_text: SBV II 88

body.text:
) kim asy evaṃsthitaḥ? tena yathāvṛttaṃ samākhyātaṃ; so 'bhiprasannaḥ kathayati: vatsa parituṣṭo 'haṃ; gatvā snātvā āgaccha; vidyāṃ tubhyam anuprayacchāmi iti; somaśarmā āgataḥ; tena tasmai vidyā dattā; capalā brāhmaṇā bhavanti; sa vegam asahamānaḥ cintayati; ihaiva tāvad enāṃ vidyāṃ jijñāsayāmi, tato 'nyatra gamiṣyāmi iti; tena sā vidyā parivartitā; bhavanatalam utpatya, āśv eva gandhamādanaṃ parvataṃ gatvā, akālartukāni puṣpāny ādāya āgataḥ; tena tāni rājñaḥ purohitāya dattāni; tenāpi rājñe brahmadattāya; rājā kathayati: kutas tavaitāni; sa kathayati: viprakṛṣṭād deśān māṇavo 'bhyāgataḥ; tenaitāni mama dattāni; sa cātyarthaṃ vidyāmantradhārī akāmakaraṇīyaś ca brāhmaṇaḥ; kim anena caṇḍālena sarvalokapratyākhyātena? tasya vṛttim ācchidya asmai māṇavāya dīyatām iti; rājā kathayati: evaṃ kāraya iti; tataḥ purohitena caṇḍālād vṛttim ācchidya tasmai brāhmaṇāya dattā; sa tayā akṛtajñatayā tasya vidyāyāḥ parihīṇaḥ.
  kiṃ manyadhve bhikṣavaḥ yo 'sau caṇḍālaḥ eṣa evāsau daśabalakāśyapaḥ tena kālena tena samayena; so 'sau māṇavaḥ eṣa eva asau devadattaḥ tena kālena tena samayena; tadāpy eṣa vidyāyāḥ parihīṇaḥ; adyāpy eṣa ṛddheḥ parihīṇaḥ; tasmāt tarhi bhikṣavaḥ evaṃ śikṣitavyaṃ yat kṛtajñā bhaviṣyāmaḥ; svalpam api kṛtaṃ na nāśayiṣyāmaḥ prāg eva prabhūtataram; ity evaṃ vo bhikṣavaḥ śikṣitavyaṃ.
body.translated_text:
) why were you standing like this?' He narrated the events as they had occurred. Pleased, he said: 'Child, I am satisfied. Go, bathe, and come back; I shall give you the magical knowledge.' <s>Somaśarman</s> returned. He gave him the knowledge. <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> are fickle by nature. Unable to contain his eagerness, he thought: 'Let me first test this knowledge right here, then I shall go elsewhere.' He practiced the spell. Rising from the ground of the house, he quickly flew to Mount <s>Gandhamādana</s>, took out-of-season flowers, and returned. He gave them to the king's chaplain. The chaplain [gave them] to King <s>Brahmadatta</s>. The king said: 'Where did you get these?' He said: 'A young man has arrived from a distant land. He gave them to me. He is exceedingly skilled in magical spells and does whatever is commanded — and he is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>. What use is that <s>Caṇḍāla</s>, who is despised by all the world? Let his allowance be taken away and given to this young man.' The king said: 'Do so.' Then the chaplain, having taken the allowance away from the <s>Caṇḍāla</s>, gave it to that <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>. Through that ingratitude, he lost his knowledge of that spell.
  What do you think, monks? He who was that <s>Caṇḍāla</s> — he is none other than <s>Daśabalakāśyapa</s> at that time, in that era. He who was that young <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> — he is none other than <s>Devadatta</s> at that time, in that era. At that time too, he lost his magical knowledge. Now too, he has lost his supernatural power. Therefore, monks, you should train thus: 'We shall be grateful. We shall not destroy even a small favor, let alone a greater one.' Thus should you train, monks.

body.text: The Buddha goes to Gayā
body.translated_text: The <s>Buddha</s> goes to <s>Gayā</s>

body.text: atha bhagavān yathābhiramyaṃ rājagṛhe vihṛtya bhikṣugaṇaparivṛtaḥ bhikṣusaṃghapuraskṛtaḥ, magadheṣu janapadeṣu cārikāṃ caran gayām anuprāptaḥ gayāyāṃ viharati;
body.translated_text: Then the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having dwelt at <s>Rājagṛha</s> as long as he wished, surrounded by a community of monks and preceded by a community of monks, wandering through the <s>Magadha</s> territories, arrived at <s>Gayā</s> and dwelt there.

body.text: rājñā bimbisāreṇa bhagavataḥ parṇopagūḍhasya śāleḥ paṃcamātrāṇi śakaṭaśatāni prāpitāni; devadattena ajātaśatrur abhihitaḥ: paśya vṛddharājā śramaṇasya gautamasya kīdṛśān kārān karoti; aham api janapadacārikāṃ cariṣyāmi; asmākam api tvayā piṇḍakena avighātaḥ karaṇīyaḥ. (
body.translated_text: King <s>Bimbisāra</s> sent five hundred cartloads of rice covered with leaves for the <s>Bhagavān</s>. <s>Devadatta</s> said to <s>Ajātaśatru</s>: 'See how the old king performs such services for the ascetic <s>Gautama</s>. I too shall wander through the countryside. You must provide me with alms-food without obstruction.' (

children.text:
The story of a mango tree
(concerning a previous birth of prince Ajātaśatru)
children.translated_text:
The story of a mango tree
(concerning a previous birth of Prince <s>Ajātaśatru</s>)

children.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavaḥ anyatamasminn agrāmake araṇyāyatane ṛṣīṇām āśramapadaṃ, nānāpuṣpaphalasalilasaṃpannaṃ; tatra ṛṣayaḥ prativasanti phalamūlāmbhubhakṣāḥ, jaṭāvalkaladhāriṇaḥ, pramuktaphalabhojinaḥ; yāvat tasminn āśramapade āmravṛkṣaḥ phalabhārāvanataśākhaḥ pakvaphalas tiṣṭhati; Ṛśayaḥ phalāni yācante; yā tasmin vṛkṣe adhyuṣitā devatā sā mātsaryābhibhūtā na prayacchati; tatas te ṛṣayaḥ mūlārthinaḥ ekam ṛṣim āśramapade sthāpayitvā bhrāntāḥ; tatsamanantaram eva paṃca coraśatāny āśramapadam anuprāptāni; tair asau vṛkṣo dattaḥ; te kathayanti: katham asmāt phalāni paribhoktavyāni iti; corasenāpatiḥ kathayati: vṛkṣaṃ paraśunā mūle chitvā phalāni bhakṣayata iti; evam ukte devatayā sarvāṇi phalāni bhūmyāṃ pātitāni; corā yāvadāptaṃ bhakṣayitvā prakrāntāḥ; ṛṣaya āgatāḥ pṛcchanti: kena tāny āmraphalāni bhakṣitāni? coraiḥ; sa ṛṣir gāthāṃ bhāṣate:
children.translated_text: In the past, monks, in a certain uninhabited forest region, there was a hermitage of sages, rich in various flowers, fruits, and water. There the sages dwelt — subsisting on fruits, roots, and water, wearing matted locks and bark garments, eating only fallen fruits. In that hermitage, a mango tree stood, its branches bent with the weight of fruit, bearing ripe fruit. The sages asked for the fruits. But the deity inhabiting that tree, overcome by stinginess, would not give them. Then those sages, being in need of roots, left one sage in the hermitage and went off. Immediately thereafter, five hundred thieves arrived at the hermitage. The tree was given to them [by the deity]. They said: 'How shall we eat the fruits from this tree?' The chief of the thieves said: 'Cut the tree at the root with an axe and eat the fruits.' When this was said, the deity cast down all the fruits onto the ground. The thieves ate to their fill and departed. The sages returned and asked: 'Who has eaten those mango fruits?' 'The thieves.' The sage spoke a verse:

children.text: dadāti vṛkṣo na phalaṃ śāntānāṃ brahmacāriṇāṃ /
children.translated_text: The tree does not give its fruit to the peaceful celibates,

children.text: dadāti tu phalaṃ teṣāṃ corāṇāṃ pāpakāriṇāṃ // iti
children.translated_text: but it gives its fruit to those thieves, the evildoers. //

children.text:
te pṛcchanti: ṛṣe kim etat? tena yathāvṛttaṃ samākhyātaṃ; te avadhyātum ārabdhāḥ; mātsaryābhibhūtayā devatayā phalāni ṛṣīṇāṃ na dattāni; apātrāṇāṃ corāṇāṃ dattāni iti.

body.translated_text: Then the <s>Bhagavān</s>, wandering through the <s>Magadha</s> territories, arrived at <s>Rājagṛha</s> and dwelt in the <s>Veṇuvana</s> (Bamboo Grove) at the <s>Kalandakanivāpa</s> (Squirrel Feeding-ground). <s>Devadatta</s> continually committed offenses against the people dwelling in <s>Rājagṛha</s>. Whoever was offended against would send a complaint to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. There the <s>Bhagavān</s> addressed the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>: 'Go, <s>Ānanda</s>, taking your outer robe (<s>saṃghāṭī</s>)

body.text: ādāya anyatamena bhikṣuṇā paścācchramaṇena rājagṛhe rathyāvīthīcatvaraśṛṅgāṭakeṣu brāhmaṇagṛhapatīnām ārocaya yad devadatto vā, devadattapakṣiko vā aparādhaṃ karoti; na tena buddho vā dharmo vā saṃgho vā saṃbadhyate iti; yadi kathayanti: mahardhiko devadatto mahānubhāvaḥ iti, vaktavyāḥ: āsīn mahardhikaḥ; idānīṃ parihīṇas tasyā ṛddheḥ iti; tena gatvā rājagṛhe nagararathyāvīthīcatvaraśṛṅgāṭakeṣu brāhmaṇagṛhapatīnām ārocitaṃ, te na bhūyo bhagavata upālambhaṃ preṣayanti.
body.translated_text: and accompanied by a monk as your attendant, and announce to the <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> and householders in the streets, lanes, crossroads, and intersections of <s>Rājagṛha</s> that whatever offense <s>Devadatta</s> or a follower of <s>Devadatta</s> commits, the <s>Buddha</s>, the <s>Dharma</s>, and the <s>Saṃgha</s> are not implicated in that.' If they say: '<s>Devadatta</s> is of great supernatural power and great might,' they should be told: 'He was formerly of great supernatural power; now he has lost that power.' He went and announced this to the <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> and householders in the streets, lanes, crossroads, and intersections of <s>Rājagṛha</s>. After that, they no longer sent complaints to the <s>Bhagavān</s>.

An illness arose in the <s>Bhagavān</s>. <s>Jīvaka</s> brought <s>nārāca</s> ghee (medicated clarified butter) to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. There the <s>Bhagavān</s> addressed <s>Jīvaka</s>, the king of physicians: 'Is it wonderful, <s>Jīvaka</s>?' 'It is wonderful, <s>Bhagavān</s>.' 'Is it marvelous, <s>Jīvaka</s>?' 'It is marvelous, <s>Bhagavān</s>.' 'Do you know, <s>Jīvaka</s>?' 'I know, <s>Bhagavān</s>.' 'Do you not know, <s>Jīvaka</s>?' 'Nor do I, <s>Sugata</s>.' 1) 'What is wonderful, <s>Jīvaka</s>?' '<s>Bhagavān</s>, cows graze on grass and drink water. From that this nectar is produced, from which this <s>nārāca</s> ghee is prepared.' 2) 'What is marvelous?' '<s>Bhagavān</s>, the arising of a <s>Buddha</s>, the teaching of the true <s>Dharma</s>, and the good practice of the <s>Saṅgha</s>.' 3) 'What do you know?' '<s>Bhagavān</s>, one who is born must surely die.' 4) 'What do you not know?' '<s>Bhagavān</s>, by whom and where one will die.'
The monks, having doubts arise, asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'See, Venerable Sir, <s>Jīvaka</s> understood the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s riddle.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Not only now, monks — in the past too he understood my riddle. Listen to that.' (

body.text:
The story of a gṛhapati and his son
(concerning a previous birth of Jīvaka)
body.translated_text:
The story of a householder and his son
(concerning a previous birth of <s>Jīvaka</s>)

body.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavo 'nyatamasmin karvaṭake gṛhapatiḥ prativasati, āḍhyo mahādhano mahābhogaḥ; tena sadṛśāt kulāt kalatram ānītaṃ; sa tayā sārdhaṃ krīḍati ramate paricārayati; tasya krīḍato ramamāṇasya paricārayataḥ kālāntareṇa patnī āpannasatvā saṃvṛttā; sā aṣṭānāṃ va nāvānāṃ vā māsānām atyayāt prasūtā; dārikā jātā; tasyās trīṇi saptakāny ekaviṃṣatidivasān jātāyāḥ jātimahaṃ kṛtvā valayeti nāmadheyaṃ vyavasthāpitaṃ; bhūyo 'py asya krīḍato ramamāṇasya paricārayataḥ putro jātaḥ; tasyāpi kulasadṛśaṃ nāmadheyaṃ vyavasthāpitaṃ; sa saṃlakṣayati: jāto me ṛṇaharo dhanaharaś ca; gacchāmi paṇyam ādāya deśāntaram iti; bhūyaḥ sa saṃlakṣayati: iyaṃ mama patnī rūpavatī; yady aham asyāḥ prabhūtān kārṣāpaṇān datvā gacchāmi, sthānam etad vidyate yat parapuruṣaiḥ sārdhaṃ vikariṣyati; yannv aham asyāḥ svalpān kārṣāpaṇān datvā gaccheyam iti; sa tasyāḥ stokān kārṣāpaṇān datvā, avaśiṣṭaṃ suvarṇakalaśe prakṣipya, grīvāyāṃ muktāhāraṃ baddhvā śmaśāne aśvakarṇasya mūle nikhanya paṇyam ādāya deśāntaraṃ gataḥ; tasya tatra prabhūto lābhaḥ saṃpannaḥ; sa tatraiva dārasaṅgrahaṃ kṛtvā avasthitaḥ; tasya ca bahavaḥ putrā jātāḥ; tatas tayā pūrvikayā patnyā valayā sa ca dārakaḥ hastabalena jñātibalena ca pāyitau, poṣitau, saṃvardhitau; tau kathayataḥ: amba pitā asmākaṃ kva gataḥ? sā kathayati: putra asmin deśe amukam adhiṣṭhānaṃ tatra tiṣṭhati
body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in a certain market-town a householder dwelt — wealthy, of great riches and great possessions. He brought a wife from a family of equal standing. He enjoyed, amused, and attended to her. As he enjoyed, amused, and attended to her, after some time his wife became pregnant. After the passage of eight or nine months, she gave birth. A girl was born. Over the twenty-one days of three weeks, having performed the birth-celebration, the name <s>Valayā</s> was established. Again, as he enjoyed, amused, and attended to her, a son was born. A name befitting the family was established for him too. He reflected: 'A debt-repayer and wealth-bringer has been born to me. Let me go, take goods, and travel to another country.' He further reflected: 'This wife of mine is beautiful. If I give her many <s>kārṣāpaṇas</s> and go, it is possible she will be unfaithful with other men. Let me rather give her only a few <s>kārṣāpaṇas</s> and go.' Having given her a small sum of <s>kārṣāpaṇas</s>, he placed the rest in a golden pitcher, tied a pearl necklace around its neck, buried it at the foot of an <s>aśvakarṇa</s> tree in the cremation ground, took his goods, and went to another country. He gained much profit there. Having taken a wife in that very place, he settled there. Many sons were born to him. Then <s>Valayā</s>, his first wife, and that boy were raised, nourished, and brought up by the strength of her hands and the support of her kinsmen. They said: 'Mother, where has our father gone?' She said: 'Son, he lives in such-and-such a place in such-and-such a country

body.text: tasya ca mahatī dhanasaṃpattiḥ śrūyate, gaccha yadi kiṃcid asyojjīvanopāyas te bhaviṣyati iti; sa pitaraṃ samanveṣamāṇaḥ anupūrveṇa tasya sakāśaṃ gataḥ; sa vīthyām anvāhiṇḍamānaḥ pitrā mukhabimbakena pratyabhijñātaḥ; śabdayitvyā abhihitaḥ: kutas tvam ihāgacchasi? kutra vā gantum? iti; tena vistareṇa samākhyātaṃ; sa saṃlakṣayati: eṣa evāsau mama putraḥ iti; sa tena svagṛhītaḥ uktaś ca: putra na te kasyacid ākhyeyaṃ, mamāyaṃ pitā iti; sa tasyātyarthaṃ snehaṃ kartuṃ ārabdhaḥ; (

Wandering through the street, he was recognized by his father from his facial resemblance. Having called out to him, he said: 'Where have you come from? Where are you going?' He narrated the full account. He reflected: 'This is indeed my son.' He took him into his own house and said: 'Son, you must not tell anyone that I am your father.' body.translated_text: ) Then those other sons said: 'Father, who is this boy?' He said: 'This is the son of my friend.' They observed: 'The way he shows such great affection to this one — surely he is his own son.' They began to whisper among themselves: 'This is another brother.' He reflected: 'I shall send him away. Co-wife rivalry is well-known as one of the most bitter quarrels. It is possible they will have him killed. And if I give him anything, they will kill him on the road for the sake of the inheritance. Let me send him in such a way [that he will be safe].' Having decided, he wrote a note and gave it:

Having thus worked out the meaning of the verse, he went to the cremation ground at a time when no one was about. Nearby he saw the <s>aśvakarṇa</s> tree. He removed the pearl necklace and gave it to <s>Valayā</s>.
What do you think, monks? He who was that householder — that was none other than myself at that time, in that era. He who was his son — that is this very <s>Jīvaka</s> at that time, in that era. Even then he understood my riddle.

body.translated_text: He took the note and set out. On the road, he was seized by his half-brothers. They said: 'What did you receive from father?' He said: 'Nothing — only this note.' They reflected: 'He has been disinherited by father. Let him go.' They released him. He gradually arrived at his own home and was recovering from the fatigue of travel. His mother said: 'What did you receive from your father?' He said: 'Nothing at all, only this note.' She said: 'You have been disinherited by him. The journey has fatigued you, and nothing has come of it.' He said: 'Mother, he is a great soul. He will not disinherit me.' <s>Devadatta</s> thought: 'I too shall drink ghee.' He asked <s>Jīvaka</s>: '<s>Jīvaka</s>, how much ghee was drunk by the ascetic <s>Gautama</s>?' He said: 'Thirty-two <s>palas</s>.' He said: 'I too shall drink thirty-two <s>palas</s>.' <s>Jīvaka</s> said: 'The <s>Bhagavān</s>'s body is like a diamond and is large. He is able to digest that amount. You, however, will not be able to digest it.' He said: 'I too have a diamond body. Why should I not digest it?' He forcibly drank a dose of thirty-two <s>palas</s>. In the <s>Bhagavān</s>, it was properly digested. In <s>Devadatta</s>, it was not digested. The very next day, <s>Jīvaka</s> gave the <s>Bhagavān</s> <s>maṇḍa</s> (whey). <s>Devadatta</s>, out of rivalry, thinking 'The <s>Bhagavān</s> drinks it too,' drank <s>maṇḍa</s> while the ghee was still undigested. ), he experienced painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable feelings. He could not sleep either by night or by day.
The Venerable <s>Ānanda</s>, who was affectionate toward his kinsmen, reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Then the <s>Bhagavān</s>, extending his arm, which resembled the trunk of an elephant, pierced through <s>Gṛdhrakūṭa</s> (Vulture Peak) mountain, and placing on <s>Devadatta</s> his hand — which bore the <s>cakra</s> (wheel), <s>svastika</s>, and <s>nandyāvarta</s> marks, which was generated by hundreds of merits, and which reassures the frightened — made a declaration of truth (<s>satyopayācana</s>): 'By the truth that my mind is equally disposed, neither more nor less, toward my dear son <s>Rāhulabhadra</s> and toward <s>Devadatta</s> — by that truth, may the pain subside.' Immediately upon the declaration of truth, <s>Devadatta</s>'s pain was pacified. He, having recovered his breath as if from the dead, looked at the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s hand. He recognized it. He reflected: 'This is the hand of the ascetic <s>Gautama</s>.' He, consumed by deep-rooted habitual arrogance, deceit, pride, and haughtiness — yet with his pain pacified by the majesty of the <s>Buddha</s> — said: 'Well done, <s>Siddhārtha</s>, you have mastered the medical art! You will be able to make a living from it.' The word spread in the vicinity: '<s>Devadatta</s>, who was overwhelmed by excruciating pain and about to die, has been restored to health by the <s>Bhagavān</s> through a declaration of truth.' Hearing this, even <s>Devadatta</s>'s partisans, no matter how utterly committed, expressed wonder at the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'How perfectly cultivated is his <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness)! How well-developed is his <s>karuṇā</s> (compassion) toward beings!'
The monks said to <s>Devadatta</s>: '<s>Devadatta</s>, you were restored to health by the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Otherwise you would have died.' He said: 'He knows a bewitching trick by which he draws the world around himself.' The monks said: '<s>Devadatta</s>, enough of this boasting. Regain your senses. You were restored to health by the <s>Bhagavān</s>.' He said: 'What did he do for me? The pain subsided when the ghee was digested.'
'He is ungrateful and unacknowledging' — thinking thus, they departed. They approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Having approached, with doubts arisen, they asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'See, Venerable Sir, <s>Devadatta</s> is ungrateful and unacknowledging.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Not only now, monks

children.text:
The story of a Sage and of an ungrateful elephant
(concerning a previous birth of Devadatta)
children.translated_text:
The story of a sage and of an ungrateful elephant
(concerning a previous birth of <s>Devadatta</s>)

children.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavo 'nyatamasminn agrāmake araṇyāyatane nānāvidhapuṣpaphalasalilasaṃpannam udyānaṃ; tasmin kauśikasagotro ṛṣiḥ prativasati; pramuktaphalabhojī mūlaphalāmbubhakṣaḥ ajinavalkalavāsāḥ; tasyāśramapadasamantake viśvastā mṛgapakṣiṇo yatheṣṭaṃ viharanti; tasya nātidūre hastinī prasūtā; tatprasavasamanantaraṃ siṃhena nādo muktaḥ; sā bhītā trastā kalabhaṃ parityajya mūtrapurīṣam utsṛjantī niṣpalāyitā; yāvad asau ṛṣir āśramapadān niṣkramya āśramapadasāmantakena diśo vyavalokayan saṃparibhramitum ārabdhaḥ; yāvat paśyati tam abhinavajātaṃ hastikalabhakaṃ; tato 'sau ṛṣiḥ kāruṇyād ākampitahṛdayaḥ tanmātṛsamanveṣaṇābhiniviṣṭabuddhiḥ samantato vyavalokayitum ārabdhaḥ; yadā sarvāvasthaṃ na paśyati tadā tam ādāyāśramapadaṃ praviṣṭaḥ; sa tena putravad āpāyitaḥ poṣitaḥ saṃvardhitaḥ; mahān saṃvṛttaḥ; tadā tasya ṛṣer āśramapade aparādhyate; puṣpaviṭapān utpāṭayati; phalavṛkṣān śākhāḥ bhinatti; etāni cānyāni cāparādhasahasrāṇi karoti; sa ṛṣis taṃ tarjayati; ṛṣiṇā santarjitaḥ saṃkocam āpadyate; sa yadā saṃjātarāgaḥ saṃvṛttaḥ tadā santarjyamāno 'py avajñāṃ karoti; yāvad apareṇa samayena ṛṣiṇā bhṛśaṃ tarjitaḥ, tam eva ṛṣiṃ hantuṃ pradhāvitaḥ; sa ṛṣer dehaikadeśaṃ bhaṅktvā niṣpalāyitaḥ; devatā gāthāṃ bhāṣate: (
na saṃgatiḥ kāpuruṣeṇa bhadrika kṛtaghnasatvena sudāruṇena /
children.translated_text: Do not associate with a base person, O good one — an ungrateful being, most terrible;

children.text: cirānuyāto 'pi karoti pāpikaṃ nāgo yathaivāśramakauśikasya // iti
children.translated_text: even one long followed, he does evil — as the elephant did to the hermit <s>Kauśika</s>. //

children.text: kim ādarād durjanaṃ sevase tvam annena pānena tathobhayena /
children.translated_text: Why do you out of regard serve a wicked one with food and drink and both?

children.text: avaśyam ante sa nihanti mitraṃ nāgo yathaivāśramakauśikasya // iti
children.translated_text: In the end he inevitably strikes down his friend — as the elephant did to the hermit <s>Kauśika</s>. //

In the past, monks, in a certain uninhabited wilderness tract, there was a garden endowed with various flowers, fruits, and water. In it dwelt a sage of the <s>Kauśika</s> lineage, who ate only wild fruits, subsisting on roots, fruits, and water, clothed in antelope skins and bark. In the vicinity of his hermitage, deer and birds dwelt in trust and roamed as they pleased. Not far from him, a female elephant gave birth. Immediately after her delivery, a lion roared. Frightened and terrified, she abandoned her calf and fled, voiding urine and excrement. Then that sage, having come out of the hermitage, began to wander about the hermitage environs, looking in all directions. He saw that newborn elephant calf. Then that sage, his heart shaken with compassion, his mind intent on searching for its mother, began to look in all directions. When he saw her nowhere, he took the calf and entered the hermitage. He fed, nourished, and raised it like his own son. When it grew up, it began to cause damage in the sage's hermitage — uprooting flowering branches, breaking the boughs of fruit trees, committing these and thousands of other offenses. The sage threatened it. Threatened by the sage, it shrank back. But when it reached maturity and became lustful, even when threatened it showed contempt. Then at a later time, when severely threatened by the sage, it charged at that very sage to kill him. Having broken a part of the sage's body, it fled. A deity spoke these verses: (

children.text: bhagavān āha: kiṃ manyadhve bhikṣavaḥ? yo 'sau ṛṣir aham eva saḥ tena kālena tena samayena; yo 'sau hastināgaḥ eṣa evāsau devadattaḥ tena kālena tena samayena; tadāpy eṣa akṛtajña akṛtavedī; etarhy apy eṣa akṛtajña akṛtavedī; punar api yathaiṣa akṛtajña akṛtavedī, tac chrūyatāṃ.
children.translated_text: The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'What do you think, monks? He who was that sage — that was none other than myself at that time, in that era. He who was that bull elephant — that is none other than <s>Devadatta</s> at that time, in that era. Even then he was ungrateful and unappreciative; now too he is ungrateful and unappreciative. Listen further to how he is ungrateful and unappreciative.'

The story of Mahendrasena
(concerning a previous birth of Devadatta)
body.translated_text:
The story of <s>Mahendrasena</s>
(concerning a previous birth of <s>Devadatta</s>)

body.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavaḥ atīte 'dhvani vārāṇasyāṃ nagaryāṃ mahendrasena nāma rājā rājyaṃ kārayati ṛddhaṃ ca sphītaṃ ca kṣemaṃ ca subhikṣaṃ cākīrṇabahujanamanuṣyaṃ ca; tasya candraprabhā nāma devī satyasvapnā; yat kiṃcit svapne paśyati sarvaṃ tat tathaiva bhavati; tasya ca rājño vijite suvarṇapārśvo nāma bodhisatvaḥ mṛgeṣūpapanno mṛgāṇām adhipatiḥ; so 'cintanīyarūpaprabhāvayogāt sarvalokamanonayanaprahlādanakaraḥ, prārthanīyaś ca; yas taṃ paśyati sa nirīkṣamānas tatraiva tiṣṭhati; so 'tyartham abhivīkṣyamānaḥ śaṅkī saṃvṛttaḥ; sa lubdhakabhayād anyalokabhayāc ca bhītaś carati; dharmatā hy eṣā aciravyativṛtte lokasanniveśe tiryañco 'pi vākpravyāharaṇasamarthā bhavanti; athānyataraḥ kākas
body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in the city of <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, a king named <s>Mahendrasena</s> was exercising sovereignty — it was prosperous, thriving, secure, well-provisioned, and teeming with many people. He had a queen named <s>Candraprabhā</s>, who had truthful dreams: whatever she saw in a dream, all of that came true exactly so. In that king's realm, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> had been born among deer as a deer named <s>Suvarṇapārśva</s> ('Golden-Flanked'), and was their chief. Through the power of his inconceivably beautiful form and splendor, he delighted the eyes and minds of all the world, and was longed for. Whoever saw him would stand gazing, transfixed. Being gazed at so intensely, he became suspicious. Frightened of hunters and of other people, he moved about fearfully. For it is the nature of things that soon after the arrangement of the world, even animals are capable of articulate speech. Then a certain crow

body.text: tasya samīpam upasaṃkrāntaḥ; sa tena sārdhaṃ premapraṇayasaukhyaḥ kathayati: bho mātula kasmāt tvam evaṃ bhītabhītaś carasi? iti; sa kathayati: bhāgineya mamedaṃ rūpaṃ sarvalokaśubhaṃ saṃprārthanīyaṃ ca; so 'haṃ lokabhayāl lubdhakabhayāc ca bhītabhītaś (
body.translated_text: approached him. The deer spoke with him in a spirit of love, affection, and friendship: 'O uncle, why do you go about so fearfully?' He replied: 'Nephew, this form of mine is beautiful to all the world and longed for. Therefore, out of fear of the world and fear of hunters, I go about fearfully.' (

body.translated_text: ) The crow said: 'I too have great fear of owls. Let us protect each other. I shall guard you by day; you guard me by night.' The two, having established this agreement, settled down. Then a certain man was seized by his enemies, bound tightly with his arms behind his back, and cast into a river that was newly filled with water, swift-flowing, with a golden color, adorned with golden garlands. As he was being carried along, he wailed with an anguished voice and lamented:

children.text: bhavāmi kasya dāso 'haṃ kasya vā paricārakaḥ /

children.translated_text: By chance, that lord of deer, surrounded by his herd of deer, had come from the water-place to the bank of the river. Then, hearing the man's cry, those deer scattered in all directions. For it is the nature of <s>Bodhisattvas</s> that even though their bodies may fall, their minds do not waver. Then that lord of deer, his heart stirred by compassion, began to plunge headlong into the river. The crow, mindful of their prior agreement, followed close behind him for protection. Knowing that the lord of deer was determined to rescue the man, the crow said: 'Enough, enough, lord of deer! Do not act rashly! These humans are ungrateful — they do not appreciate kindness.' But <s>Bodhisattvas</s> and great beings are irrevocable. Disregarding the crow's words, he entered the river and, like a dear only son, had the man climb onto his back. Reaching the riverbank, he freed his bonds, let him rest for a moment, and said: 'Go, child, by this path wherever you wish.' Then that man, with joined palms, fell at his feet and said:

children.text: tava dāso hy ahaṃ tāta tavaiva paricārakaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'I am your slave indeed, dear one, and your very servant.

children.text: tvayā me jīvitaṃ dattaṃ yal lokeṣu sudurlabham // iti
children.translated_text: By you my life was given — that which is so hard to obtain in the world! //'
The deer said:

children.text: ma me tvam adya dāsaḥ syāḥ mā caiva paricārakaḥ /

children.text: na vācyas tv aham anyebhyo hanyur māṃ carmakāraṇāt //
children.translated_text: But you must not tell others about me — they would kill me for the sake of my hide. //'

body.translated_text: ) three times, fell at his feet, and departed. Then at a later time, Queen <s>Candraprabhā</s>, wearied by the exertions of love-play, fell into a deep sleep on her great couch. In the last watch of the night, she saw in a dream a supremely beautiful lord of deer, seated on a lion-throne in a great royal assembly, teaching the <s>Dharma</s>. Having seen this, delighted as if by a waking vision, overjoyed at the dream, she quickly rose from the great couch and reported it to the king. Having heard, the king, knowing her dreams to be truthful, was utterly astonished: 'How could one born in an unfortunate destiny sit on a lion-throne and teach the <s>Dharma</s> in a great royal assembly?' Then Queen <s>Candraprabhā</s>, through the skillful use of sweet, charming, and artful conversation, cajoled the king for a moment and said: 'Your Majesty, make an effort to bring that deer.' Then the king gave a command to his ministers

body.text: ājñā dattā: bhavanto yāvanto madviṣayanivāsino mṛgalubdhakās tiṣṭhanti te sarve matsakāśam upaneyāḥ iti; amātyaiḥ pratiprativiṣayeṣu rājapuruṣāṇām ājñā dattā: devaḥ samājñāpayati madviṣayanivāsibhir mṛgalubdhakair ihāgantavyam iti; tad yuṣmābhiḥ sarvamṛgalubdhakā iha preṣayitavyāḥ iti; taiḥ sarve viṣayanivāsino mṛgalubdhakā rājñaḥ sakāśaṃ preṣitāḥ; amātyai rajñe upanītāḥ; rājā kathayati: bhavanto śrutaṃ mayā madvijite paramaramaṇīyarūpavigraho mṛgo 'stīti; sa yuṣmābhir mṛduśithilabandhanopanibaddho matsakāśam akhedita upaneyaḥ iti; te kathayanti: deva vayaṃ tajjīvina eva; iyatā kālena devasya vijite paryaṭadbhir na kadācid evaṃvidho mṛgavaraḥ śrutapūrvaḥ; kimuta dṛṣṭaḥ tam arhati devaḥ śravaparamparayā samanveṣya amuṣmin deśe tiṣṭhatīti; asmākam ājñātum; evaṃ devasya vayaṃ niyatam ājñāṃ saṃpādayāmaḥ iti; tato rājñā amātyānām ājñā dattā: bhavanto vārāṇasyāṃ ghaṇṭāvaghoṣaṇaṃ kārayata samājñāpayati devaḥ; atiramaṇīyavigraho mṛgādhipatir asti; yo me tasya pravṛttiṃ nivedayati tam ahaṃ mahatā satkāreṇa satkaromi; paṃca cāsmai grāmavarān prayacchāmi iti; amātyai rājñaḥ pratiśrutya vārāṇasyāṃ ghaṇṭāvaghoṣaṇaṃ kāritaṃ: śṛṇvantu bhavanto vārāṇasīnivāsinaḥ paurā nānādeśābhyāgatāś ca janāḥ; deva evaṃ samājñāpayati madvijite atiparamaramaṇīyavigraho mṛgādhipatir asti; yo me tasya pravṛttiṃ nivedayati tam ahaṃ mahatā satkāreṇa satkaromi; paṃca cāsmai grāmavarān prayacchāmi iti; tatas taddarśinaḥ puruṣasya etad abhavat: kiṃ tāvat kuṭumbam anupālayāmi, āhosvit kṛtajñatām? iti; kāmān khalu pratisevamānasya (
body.translated_text: : 'Sirs, bring before me all the deer-hunters dwelling in my realm.' The ministers gave orders to the royal officers throughout every district: 'His Majesty commands that all deer-hunters dwelling in his realm must come here. You must send all the deer-hunters here.' They sent all the deer-hunters from the realm before the king. The ministers presented them. The king said: 'Sirs, I have heard that in my realm there is a deer-chief of supremely beautiful form. He must be brought before me gently, bound with soft and loose bonds, without causing him distress.' They replied: 'Your Majesty, we live by that very livelihood. In all this time, wandering through Your Majesty's realm, we have never even heard of such a noble deer, let alone seen one. May Your Majesty, having investigated through a chain of reports, ascertain in which region he dwells. Then we shall surely fulfill Your Majesty's command.' Then the king gave a command to his ministers: 'Sirs, have a bell-proclamation made in <s>Vārāṇasī</s>: His Majesty commands — there is a deer-chief of supremely beautiful form. Whoever reports his whereabouts to me, him I shall honor with great honor and grant five excellent villages.' The ministers, having assented to the king, had a bell-proclamation made in <s>Vārāṇasī</s>: 'Let the citizens of <s>Vārāṇasī</s> hear, and people who have come from various lands! His Majesty thus commands: In my realm there is a deer-chief of supremely beautiful form. Whoever reports his whereabouts to me, him I shall honor with great honor and grant five excellent villages.' Then that man who had seen the deer reflected: 'Which shall I maintain — my household or my gratitude?' 'For one who indulges in desires, (

) nāsti kiṃcit pāpakaṃ karma akaraṇīyam iti sa kāmanidānotthena dveṣavahnitīvreṇa santāpitahṛdayaḥ saṃlakṣayti: tiṣṭhatu kṛtajñatā; śatror vairaniryātanāya samupasthitaḥ kālaḥ; kiṃ mayā punas tādṛśī avasthā prāpayitavyā? tasya tāvad vairaniryātanaṃ karomi iti; sa prabhātāyāṃ rajanyāṃ rājñaḥ parṣadi sanniṣaṇṇasya rājakāryam adhitiṣṭhataḥ, anivārite rājakuladvāre nānāvicitrasurabhipuṣpāṇy ādāya dauvārikāmātyaparaṃparayā rājānaṃ saṃśrāvya parṣadam abhyavagāhya satkāravidhipūrvakeṇa rājño niveditayati: amuṣmin deśe nānātaruṣaṇḍamaṇḍite viśvastamṛgapakṣiṇi suvarṇapārśvo mṛgādhipatir anekamṛgagaṇaparivṛtas tiṣṭhati; ahaṃ taṃ devasya atiramaṇīyavigrahaṃ mṛgavaram upadarśayāmi iti; tato rājā tacchravaṇasaṃjanitasaumanasyaḥ anekāmātyaśatasahasraparivṛtaḥ kutūhalajātenānyena nānādeśābhyāgatena vārāṇasīnivāsinā ca paurajānapadena saṃpuraskṛtaḥ, deśitamārgas tena puruṣeṇa, anupūrveṇa taṃ pradeśam anuprāptaḥ; yāvad asau kākaḥ bodhisatvasya kṛtāvadhiḥ diśām avalokakaḥ tasmin vanaṣaṇḍavṛkṣaśikhare niṣaṇṇaḥ; yāvat paśyati vanaṣaṇḍābhimukhaṃ
body.translated_text: ) there is no evil deed that cannot be done.' With a heart inflamed by the fierce fire of hatred born from desire, he reflected: 'Let gratitude stand aside. The time has come for repaying my enemy's debt. Why should I ever again be brought to such a state? Let me first take my revenge on him.' At dawn, when the king was seated in his assembly attending to royal business, and while the royal palace gate was unguarded, the man took various beautiful fragrant flowers and, through the chain of doorkeepers and ministers, informed the king and, entering the assembly with proper marks of respect, reported to the king: 'In such and such a region, in a place adorned with various groves of trees, where deer and birds dwell in trust, the deer-chief <s>Suvarṇapārśva</s>, surrounded by many herds of deer, dwells. I shall show Your Majesty that supremely beautiful noble deer.' Then the king, overjoyed at hearing this, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of ministers, accompanied by a great crowd of curious people who had come from various lands and citizens and countryfolk of <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, guided along the road by that man, traveled by stages and reached that region. Meanwhile, the crow, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>'s appointed sentinel, who kept watch over the directions, was sitting on the treetop of that forest grove. He saw approaching toward the grove

bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavaḥ aniyatarāśyavasthito bodhisatvaḥ anyatamasminn agrāmake araṇyāyatane parvatagiriguhāpravaṇe puṣpaphalasamṛddhe pakṣiṣūpapanno dārukoṭako babhūva; tasminn eva ca parvataikadeśe siṃho mṛgarājaḥ yatheṣṭapracāravihāratayā mṛgān praghātya praghātya bhakṣayati; tasyāpareṇa samayena māṃsaṃ bhakṣayataḥ asthi dantāntareṇa praviṣṭaṃ; sa śūlarujoparuddhyamānavigraho (

body.translated_text: ) though free from fear and terror, had become enfeebled. He was unable to obtain food. By chance, that woodpecker, through his habit of moving from tree to tree, arrived at the place where the lord of beasts was. He saw the lion afflicted by painful feeling and said: 'Uncle, why are you so feeble?' He replied: 'Nephew, I am afflicted by painful feeling.' 'What kind of suffering do you have?' He explained in detail. The woodpecker said: 'Uncle, I shall treat you. You are the lord of all four-footed creatures and are able to render all kinds of service. In return, you must carry loads of provisions for me from time to time.' He said: 'Very well. I shall do so.' The woodpecker reflected: 'I shall treat him in such a way that he does not know when the treatment has been performed, but knows when he is well.' He remained attentive to finding the right moment by observing the lion's habits and resting patterns. Eventually, the lord of beasts, his jaws relaxed by a pleasant breeze, placed his left cheek on a great rock-slab and fell asleep. Then the woodpecker approached the lord of beasts. He observed that he was lying in that deeply relaxed state. He reflected: 'This is the time for the treatment.' Knowing this, after careful examination, he swiftly extracted a bone lodged between the teeth by a rapid pecking motion, and having come out through the mouth-opening, sat perched on a tree watching him. Then the lord of beasts, his spirits revived by the removal of the bone-splinter, shook off his drowsiness, arose, and set out. Then the woodpecker, knowing that the lord of beasts was freed from suffering and distress, with a joyful mind approached him and said: 'Uncle, this is the bone that was the cause of your suffering.' The lord of beasts was struck with great astonishment and said: 'Nephew, I must certainly repay you for this service. Come to me from time to time.' 'Very well, so be it,' said the woodpecker, and departed. Then at a later time,

body.text: bhagavān āha: kiṃ manyadhve bhikṣavaḥ? yo 'sau dārukoṭakaḥ aham eva saḥ tena kālena tena samayena; yo 'sau siṃho mṛgarājaḥ eṣa evāsau devadattaḥ tena kālena tena samayena; tadāpy eṣa akṛtajñaḥ akṛtavedī; etarhy apy eṣa akṛtajña akṛtavedī; punar api yathaiṣa akṛtajña akṛtavedī tac chrūyatāṃ.
body.translated_text: The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'What do you think, monks? He who was the woodpecker — that was I at that time, in that era. He who was the lion, king of beasts — he is none other than <s>Devadatta</s> at that time, in that era. At that time too he was ungrateful and unacknowledging; even now he is ungrateful and unacknowledging. And hear further how he is ungrateful and unacknowledging.'

body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in the city of <s>Vārāṇasī</s> there dwelt a certain poor man. He made his livelihood by selling firewood. At a later time, having risen early in the morning, he took his axe and hook and went to the forest in search of firewood. A great untimely storm arose, preceded by a flash of rain, wind, and lightning. That man, thinking 'Is this a proper or improper [shelter]?', went from tree to tree searching for a place. Yet still the rain poured down heavily. Moving from tree to tree, he gradually entered a mountain cave. In that cave dwelt a bear. Seeing it, he was terrified and began to flee. The bear said: 'Child, why are you frightened? There is no danger from me. Stay.' Though suspicious, he was unable to leave out of fear. Then the bear embraced him in his arms and held him. He satisfied him with roots and fruits. A seven-day storm arose — the rain-god kept raining and would not stop. After the passage of seven days, on the eighth day, when the sky was clear and the clouds had dispersed, the bear, having surveyed the four directions, gave him abundant roots and fruits, and said to the man: 'Child, the storm has passed. The sky is clear. The clouds have dispersed. Go in comfort.' The man fell at his feet and said: 'Father, I am going. But I must repay you for your kindness.' He said: (

body.translated_text: ) 'Child, this much is done for me — that you do not reveal me to anyone.' He said: 'Father, very well, so be it.' Having circumambulated him and fallen at his feet, he departed. As he was entering <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, a certain hunter was going out to kill game. He saw the man and said: 'Friend, after so long you have come here! Your wife and children have become distraught. They wailed terribly: "You have been killed by the seven-day untimely storm or by a wild beast!" Many deer and birds were killed by the seven-day untimely storm. But how did you escape?' He told him everything as it had happened. The hunter said: 'Friend, however I manage to make a living, I shall never enter the forest again.' The king reflected: 'Worship must be rendered to him.' The monks said: 'Your Majesty, this <s>Bodhisattva</s> belongs to the <s>Bhadrakalpa</s> (Fortunate Aeon). Arrangements should be made for his worship.' Then King <s>Brahmadatta</s>, together with his inner palace, princes, ministers, townspeople, and countryfolk, taking all kinds of fragrant wood, went to that place. He had all the meat, bones, and remains gathered together and said: 'Sirs, build a pyre of all fragrant woods and cremate him with great honor.' A great <s>stūpa</s> was established at that place. Parasols, banners, and flags were raised, and a great festival was held. And all those who performed acts of devotion there became destined for liberation.
  What do you think, monks? He who was the bear — that was I at that time, in that era. He who was the ungrateful man — he is none other than <s>Devadatta</s> at that time, in that era. At that time too he was ungrateful and unacknowledging; even now he is ungrateful and unacknowledging. And hear further how he is ungrateful and unacknowledging.

body.translated_text: Having spoken thus, he died. Then those men, having butchered him and divided the meat into shares, said to the ungrateful man: 'Take your double share of meat.' He stretched out his hands to take it — and they fell to the ground. The hunter, seeing him so afflicted, cried 'Alas, how terrible! How terrible!' and, abandoning even his own shares, departed. Hearing of this extraordinary event, a great crowd of people gathered at that place. King <s>Brahmadatta</s>, driven by curiosity, went there himself. body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in the city of <s>Vārāṇasī</s> there dwelt a certain poor man. He made his livelihood by selling firewood. At a later time, having risen early in the morning, he took his axe and hook and went to the forest in search of firewood. In that mountainous region, adorned with thickets of various trees and abundant with various flowers and fruits, the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, in an irregular state of existence, was born among bears. Then that woodcutter, while searching for firewood, was charged by a tiger in a certain place. Terrified by the fear of death, by chance he climbed (

body.text: ca: bho mahātmann ete manuṣyāḥ kṛṣṇaśirasaḥ akṛtajñāḥ bhavanti; pātayainaṃ; bhakṣayitvā gacchāmi iti; prāyaḥ śaraṇāgatavatsalā anya 'pi manuṣyāḥ; prāgeva bodhisatvāḥ; sa kathayati: mamāyaṃ śaraṇāgataḥ; nāham etaṃ pātayāmi iti; tathāpy asau vyāghraḥ māṃsaśoṇitābhilāṣī tiṣṭhaty eva; na tasmād viprakrāmati; athāsau ṛkṣas taṃ puruṣam āha: śrānto 'haṃ; tvaṃ tāvat tiṣṭha; ahaṃ viśramāmi iti; sa tasyotsaṅganiṣaṇṇaḥ śramakheditapariṣrāntaś ca middham avakrāntaḥ; sa vyāhgraḥ kathayati: bhoḥ puruṣa kiyantaṃ kālaṃ tvayātra sthātavyaṃ? pātayainaṃ; bhakṣayitvā gamiṣyāmi: iti; sa nirghṛṇahṛdayaḥ pāpakarmā tyaktaparalokaḥ saṃlakṣayati: śobhanam eṣa kathayati; kiyantaṃ kālaṃ mayātra sthātavyaṃ? pātayāmi iti; sa tena pātitaḥ; tena mahātmanā patatābhihitaṃ hā nai vā te hā kiṃ cit dus se mi ity uktvā patitaḥ; vyāghreṇānayena vyasanam āpāditaḥ; sa tasya saṃdhāya bhāṣitaṃ śrutvā saṃlakṣayati: mamāyaṃ kenacit saṃvibhāgaṃ kartukāmaḥ, yenaivaṃ kathayati iti; tasya tṛṣṇāndhasya pralāpo lagnaḥ; kṣiptacittas tena tenānvāhiṇḍann evam āha: hā nai vā te hā kiṃ cit dus se mi iti; sa jñātibhir gṛhaṃ nītaḥ; pralapaty eva na santiṣṭhate; te vidyāmantradhāriṇo bhūtacikitsakān anyāṃś ca śramaṇabrāhmaṇān suhṛtsambandhibāndhavān pṛcchati; te bahudhā kathayanti; na kaścit cikitsāṃ karoti; tena khalu samayena vārāṇasyāṃ nātidūre āśramapade vividhataruṣaṇḍamaṇḍite puṣpaphalasalilasaṃpanne anekavihaganikūjite ṛṣiḥ paṃcābhijñaḥ prativasati; tasya puruṣasya jñātayas taṃ puruṣan ādāya tasya ṛṣeḥ sakāśaṃ gatāḥ pādayor nipatya kathayanti: maharṣe ayam asmākaṃ jñātiḥ; muhur muhur evaṃ pralapati; kim asya kartavyam iti; pāpakārī ayaṃ satvaḥ; anena durātmanā kṛtopakārī bodhisatvo vyāghrasya purastāt pātitaḥ; tena mahātmanā cintitam asmai dharmaṃ deśayāmi iti; so 'nena pātitaḥ; tasya patato bhrāntasya daśānāṃ ślokānām ekaikam akṣaraṃ pratibhātaṃ hā nai vā te hā kiṃ cit dus se mi iti; tasya ṛṣeḥ śiṣyaḥ (
body.translated_text: and said: 'Great-souled one, these black-headed humans are ungrateful. Drop him down — I shall eat him and go.' Most people are tender toward those who have come for refuge, how much more so the <s>Bodhisattvas</s>. He said: 'This one has come to me for refuge. I will not drop him.' Yet that tiger, craving flesh and blood, remained standing right there and did not go away. Then that bear said to the man: 'I am tired. You stay watch for now — I shall rest.' He sat on the man's lap, and exhausted and weary from his effort, was overcome by drowsiness. The tiger said: 'Good man, how long are you going to stay here? Drop him down — I shall eat him and go.' That man, merciless of heart, a doer of evil deeds, heedless of the next world, reflected: 'This is a fine idea. How long must I stay here? I shall drop him.' And he dropped him. But as the great-souled one was falling, he cried out: 'Alas! Do not! Alas! Something bad will befall you!' — and having said this, he fell. The tiger brought him to ruin through this betrayal. The bear, having heard his purposeful words as he fell, reflected: 'This one wants to share something with me, since he speaks thus.' That utterance stuck in the mind of the one blinded by craving. Disturbed in mind, wandering here and there, he kept saying: 'Alas! Do not! Alas! Something bad will befall you!' He was taken home by his kinsmen. He kept babbling and would not settle down. They consulted exorcists, spirit-healers, other <s>śramaṇas</s> and <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, friends, relatives, and kinsmen. They gave various opinions. No one could cure him. At that time, not far from <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, in an ashram adorned with groves of various trees, abundant in flowers, fruits, and water, resounding with the songs of many birds, there dwelt a sage possessed of the five supernatural knowledges. The kinsmen of that man took him to that sage, fell at his feet, and said: 'Great sage, this is our kinsman. Again and again he babbles thus. What should be done for him?' This being was an evildoer. The wicked man had pushed down the <s>Bodhisattva</s> — who had done him a kindness — before the tiger. That great-souled one had thought: 'Let me teach him the <s>Dharma</s>.' But he was pushed down by this man. As he fell, confused, one syllable of each of ten verses came to him: 'Alas! Do not! Alas! Something bad will befall you!' The sage's disciple (

body.translated_text: ) and teeming with a great multitude of people. That king was faithful, virtuous, of good intentions, devoted to his own welfare, compassionate, great-souled, devoted to <s>Dharma</s>, affectionate toward his subjects, a giver of all things, one who renounced all things, one who gave without attachment, and he abided in great generosity. There was nothing that he had not given, nothing that he had not renounced — to <s>śramaṇas</s>, <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, the destitute, beggars, travelers, and supplicants. But for the most part, his custom was to attend to the sick. Rising early each morning, he would pay respects to his parents, make the rounds of visiting the sick, and then sit at the tribunal for hearing cases. Then a certain man fell ill. Abandoned by all physicians, hopeless about his life, facing death, he wandered here and there and arrived at the royal capital of <s>Śibighoṣā</s>. At that time, when the spring season had arrived and the trees were in full bloom, the king, together with his inner apartments, set out for the garden grounds — to a forest grove resounding with the cries of geese, herons, peacocks, parrots, <s>śārikā</s> birds, cuckoos, and <s>jīvañjīvaka</s> birds. That sick man, his body wracked with acute pain and the distress of affliction, frequently sighing with difficulty in breathing, eyes brimming with tears, leaning on a staff, slowly and gradually approached the king. Having bowed his head, he said: 'Your Majesty, save me from this illness! Grant me life!' Then King <s>Śibi</s>, hearing those words uttered by the sick man in tones that were compassionate, wretched, and halting, his heart shaken with pity, turned back right there and addressed his ministers: 'Summon all the physicians residing in my dominion.' All the physicians were summoned by them and brought before the king. Then the king, having summoned that man, said: 'Sirs, treat this man.' The physicians, having deliberated, said unanimously: 'Your Majesty, if a man who has never been angry at anyone since birth — if his blood is used to prepare a gruel and the patient is fed it, then this man will recover. There is no other way.' Having heard this, the king reflected: 'What use is such a life to me, or sovereignty, lordship, and dominion? If I, being what I am, cannot bring peace to others who are suffering.' Having reflected thus, the king began to examine his own history. He asked his wet-nurse: 'Mother, have I ever been angry at anyone?' She said: 'Your Majesty, when

He himself opened veins in his five limbs. A vessel was filled with blood. Then, having prepared a gruel from it, it was given [to the sick man]. The king was beloved of his townspeople and countryfolk. The inner apartments, princes, ministers, townspeople, and countryfolk began to cry out. And people who had come from various lands began to protest: 'How can so many beings be abandoned for the sake of one ordinary being?' Then the king reassured those people. By that method, for six months, veins were opened in his five limbs and gruel was fed [to the sick man]. King <s>Śibi</s>'s body became like a sieve. His vitality began to decline. The deities of the <s>Śuddhāvāsa</s> (Pure Abodes) reflected: 'If the <s>Bodhisattva</s> of this auspicious <s>kalpa</s> declines thus, that is not good.' They provided him with vital essence daily, by which he sustained himself. When that man's illness subsided, King <s>Śibi</s> granted him five excellent villages. He became one of the foremost and most respected in <s>Vārāṇasī</s>. Then the report spread in the surrounding regions: 'King <s>Śibi</s> opened veins in his five limbs; with his own blood he attended to the sick man for so long a time; and the man was restored to health.' Then people, aroused by curiosity, came and asked that man: 'Good man, is it true that King <s>Śibi</s> attended to you for so long a time?' He said: 'What has he done for me? Whether his corrupted blood is thrown on the ground or given to someone else, what is so wonderful about that?' The very moment those words ended, fire fell upon his house, and his entire house and property were burned.
  What do you think, monks? He who was King <s>Śibi</s> — that was I at that time, in that era. He who was the ungrateful man — that is none other than <s>Devadatta</s> at that time, in that era. At that time too he was ungrateful and unappreciative. Now too he is ungrateful and unappreciative. Furthermore, hear about how he is ungrateful and unappreciative.

body.translated_text: endowed with all major and minor limbs. At his birth, thousands of auspicious omens appeared. At his birth, having performed the birth-celebration, a name was assigned: 'What shall the boy's name be?' The ministers said: 'Your Majesty, at his birth thousands of auspicious omens appeared. Therefore let the boy's name be <s>Kalyāṇakārī</s> (Doer of Good).' He was named <s>Kalyāṇakārī</s>. The boy <s>Kalyāṇakārī</s> was entrusted to eight nurses — two body-nurses, two milk-nurses, two washing-nurses, and two play-nurses. Raised by eight nurses with milk, curds, butter, ghee, skimmed ghee, and other choice provisions, he grew quickly like a lotus in a lake. Once again, the king sported, enjoyed, and dallied with his queen. As he sported, enjoyed, and dallied, the queen became pregnant. After the passage of eight or nine months, she gave birth. A boy was born. At his birth too, thousands of inauspicious omens appeared. He was named <s>Akalyāṇakārī</s> (Doer of Evil). He too was raised and grew up. Prince <s>Kalyāṇakārī</s> was one whose nature was loving-kindness, compassionate, merciful toward all beings, fond of giving and delighting in generosity. He gave gifts to ascetics, <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, the destitute, beggars, and mendicants. His father told him: 'Son, do not constantly give gifts. Where will such great wealth come from that I should give every day like this?' For it is the nature of a generous giver that he becomes dear and agreeable to many people; and in all directions, his noble and auspicious fame and renown spread abroad. A king of another territory, having heard of his virtues and greatness, gave him his daughter. The king received her with great pomp. <s>Kalyāṇakārī</s> said: 'I shall not take a wife until I have earned wealth. Please grant permission, father — I shall voyage across the great ocean.' He said: 'Do so.' He set out for the great ocean with merchandise. His brother <s>Akalyāṇakārī</s> thought: 'He is dear and agreeable to many people. If he returns from the great ocean with a ship full of riches, he will become even more beloved by many (

body.translated_text: let him gather merchandise suitable for the ocean voyage.' Many hundreds of merchants gathered merchandise suitable for the ocean voyage. Then the caravan-leader <s>Kalyāṇakārī</s>, together with his brother <s>Akalyāṇakārī</s>, having performed the auspicious rites and benedictions, accompanied by many hundreds of merchants, taking abundant ocean-going merchandise on carts, loads, bundles, baskets, camels, oxen, and donkeys, set out. Gradually, inspecting the market-towns in various villages, towns, and royal capitals, he arrived at the seashore. Having built a ship for five hundred <s>purāṇas</s> (coins) and engaged five crew members — an inloader, an outloader, a sailor, a fisherman, and a helmsman — and having had a bell-proclamation made three times, he embarked upon the great ocean. When the ship had set sail, he said to his brother <s>Akalyāṇakārī</s>: 'If the ship is wrecked in mid-ocean, cling to my neck. Do not panic.' He said: 'Very well, so be it.' Then the ship, driven by favorable winds, arrived at Jewel Island. The helmsman said: 'Let the merchants of <s>Jambudvīpa</s> hear! That which is known as Jewel Island, the source of diamonds, <s>vaiḍūrya</s>, sapphires, emeralds, and other gems — we have reached it. Gather jewels to your hearts' content.' Then the ship turned back. Not far from shore, by an ill-fortune caused by a <s>makara</s> sea-creature, it met with disaster. Then <s>Akalyāṇakārī</s> clung to <s>Kalyāṇakārī</s>'s neck. He, with great effort, rescued him. So exhausted was he that he was overcome by deep sleep. As he tossed about, <s>Akalyāṇakārī</s> saw the jewels tied to his waist. He thought: 'This one will take the jewels and leave. I shall leave empty-handed.'
Knowing this, he stole the jewels from him while he was deep in sleep, and gouged out his eyes with thorns. Having abandoned him blind on the seashore, he departed. By chance, cowherds grazing cattle arrived at that spot. They saw him and asked: 'Sir, who are you in this condition?' He narrated the events as they had occurred. Hearing this, compassion arose in them. They took him to the house of a cowherd-chief. He began to play the <s>vīṇā</s> (lute) there. The cowherd-chief's wife, seized by the intoxication of youth, hearing the sound of the <s>vīṇā</s>, began to desire him. He, recalling the treacherous conduct [of his brother], covered his ears and stayed thus — he would not consent. For those absorbed in sensual desires, there is nothing they will not do. She stirred up her husband against him: 'This blind man is making advances toward me!'

body.translated_text: ) and there met with misfortune. Now suitors are coming for you. Whoever I do not give you to will be displeased. What should be done about this?' She said: 'Father, if so, arrange a city-festival. I shall descend for a <s>svayaṃvara</s> (self-choice ceremony).' The king said: 'Daughter, do so.' Then in various lands and various domains, the <s>svayaṃvara</s> was announced. That city was cleared of stones, gravel, and rubbish, sprinkled with sandalwood water, adorned with fragrant incense-burners, with raised banners and pennants, festooned with silk-banner garlands, strewn with various flowers — beautiful, like the <s>Nandana</s> garden of the gods. A bell-proclamation was made: 'Let the citizens dwelling in the city hear, and the people who have come from various lands! Tomorrow the princess will descend for the <s>svayaṃvara</s>. Therefore you should all assemble according to your means.' Then, at dawn, the princess, adorned with various ornaments, surrounded by many maidens, like a forest deity in the midst of a blossoming grove, resplendent with great pomp, descended for the <s>svayaṃvara</s> in the middle of the city, before hundreds of thousands of assembled beings. <s>Kalyāṇakārī</s> stood at a certain spot, playing the <s>vīṇā</s>. Indeed, <s>karmas</s> are what connect beings to one another. Even a strong cause looks to its corresponding condition. Then the princess, her heart captivated by the sound of the <s>vīṇā</s>, was drawn to the <s>vīṇā</s>-player <s>Kalyāṇakārī</s>. She cast her garland upon him [saying]: 'This is my husband.' The people became displeased. Some, unable to contain their indignation, began to criticize: 'How can it be that, rejecting princes, sons of ministers and chaplains who have come from various lands, and other eminent citizens, the princess — endowed with such beauty, youth, and accomplishments — has chosen a blind man as her husband!' The servants, having overcome their displeasure, reported to the king: 'Your Majesty, the princess, having descended for the <s>svayaṃvara</s>, has chosen a husband.' The king said: 'What sort of man?' 'Your Majesty, a blind man.' He too, upon hearing, became displeased. He summoned her and said: 'Daughter, there are kings, wealthy men, guild-masters, caravan-leaders, sons of ministers, and sons of chaplains

) is chosen.' 'You have not done well. What are you thinking? He is blind. I shall enjoy myself with other men.' She said: 'I am not one to commit such a deed.' He said: 'How is it known?' She began to make a declaration of truth (<s>satyopayācana</s>): 'By the truth, by this true utterance, that desire has arisen only for you, the beneficent prince, and for no other — by this truth, by this true utterance, may one of your eyes become as before.' Immediately upon the declaration of truth, one of his eyes became as before. He said: 'I am indeed that benefactor. I have been brought to this state by my ungrateful brother.' She said: 'How is it known that you are indeed that benefactor?' He too began to make a declaration of truth: 'By the truth, by this true utterance, that when he was plucking out my eyes, not even the subtlest anger arose in my mind — by this truth, by this true utterance, may my second eye become as before.' Together with his declaration of truth, his second eye became as before. Then that princess, taking the benefactor whose senses were now whole, went to the king and said: 'Father, this is indeed the benefactor.' The king did not believe it. He narrated the events as they occurred. The king was struck with the utmost astonishment. Then the king married his daughter to him with great magnificence. And that benefactor, with a great army, went to that city, deposed the ungrateful one, and was established in his ancestral kingdom.
What do you think, monks? He who was that benefactor — that was none other than myself at that time, in that era. He who was the ingrate — that is this very <s>Devadatta</s> at that time, in that era. At that time too he was ungrateful and unacknowledging. Now too he is ungrateful and unacknowledging. Hear further how he is ungrateful and unacknowledging.

body.translated_text: reflected: 'Better the loss of one's own life than the harming of another's life. What is to be done? Let me take my wife and flee.' He took his wife and fled. His wife, from lack of food and drink and from the weariness and fatigue of travel, became extremely agitated and said: 'Noble husband, I am about to die.' <s>Viśākha</s> reflected: 'I saved her from among demons. If she now dies, it is not fitting.' He cut the flesh of his own thigh and gave it to her to eat. He also pierced his arms above her head and made her drink the blood. Gradually, taking her, he came to the foot of a certain mountain. There they subsisted on roots and fruits. Near that mountain, a river flowed. In it, a man, his hands and feet mutilated by an enemy, had been cast into the current. Carried away by the current, he cried out in a piteous voice. <s>Viśākha</s> was in a certain place gathering roots. He heard that man's cry. With his heart shaken by compassion, he climbed the mountain and began to look around from all sides. He saw that man being carried away. Quickly, very quickly, he descended from the mountain, plunged into the river, hoisted that man onto his back, crossed the river, placed him on the bank, and, his heart pained by the other's suffering, said: 'Son, what happened?' He narrated the events as they had occurred. Then <s>Viśākha</s> consoled him, nourished him with roots and fruits, and entrusted him to his wife. She attended to him. While attending to him, through friendly intimacy, she approached him repeatedly and attended to him with various conversations. For it is the nature of <s>Bodhisattvas</s> that they are by nature of mild passion. <s>Viśākha</s> sometimes attended to her and sometimes did not. And by the power of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, those roots and fruits were exceedingly potent. She, consuming them, through the force of her afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>), began to desire that man whose hands and feet were mutilated. He did not comply. He said: 'I have just barely survived, my life hanging by a thread. If I do such a thing, it is possible that your husband will kill me outright.' She was requested by her again and again. Afflictions are hard to conquer. He consented with her. She, out of her utter infatuation with him, would not go to <s>Viśākha</s> even when sent. He reflected: 'The way she (

He conferred with her: 'If your husband learns of our union, he will certainly harm you and kill me.' She reflected: 'He speaks well. Precautionary measures must be taken.' He asked: 'Good lady, what is this?' She said: 'Noble husband, I am suffering terribly from a headache.' <s>Viśākha</s> said: 'What is to be done about it?' She had seen a rock-breaking herb (<s>pāṣāṇabhedaka</s>) on the front slope of the mountain. She

body.text: kathayati: āryaputra pūrvam apy eṣā śirorujā āsid vaidyena pāṣāṇabhedako vyapadiṣṭaḥ; tena svasthīkṛtā iti; viśākhaḥ kathayati: pāśāṇabhedakaṃ samanveṣāmi iti; sā kathayati: āryaputra eṣa parvataprāgbhāre dṛśyate; ahaṃ tvāṃ rajvā dhārayāmi; tvam utpāṭaya iti; ṛjuko 'sau mahātmā tasyāḥ śāṭhyaṃ na vetti; sa pratipannaḥ: evaṃ bhavatu dhāraya utpāṭayāmi iti; sa tayā rajvā osāritaḥ; tena caikena pāṇinā rajjur muktā; tayā ca muktā; nadyāṃ patitaḥ; dīrghāyuḥ sa satvaḥ; rājyasukhaṃ ca pratyanubhavitavyaṃ; na mṛtaḥ; srotasā uhyamānaḥ anyatamāṃ rājadhānīm anuprāptaḥ; tatra ca rājā aputraḥ kālagataḥ; amātyāḥ sapaurajānapadāḥ sarve sannipatya vicārayanti: bhavanto rājā kālagataḥ; kam idānīṃ rājye pratiṣṭhāpayāmaḥ iti; tair lakṣaṇajñāḥ puruṣāḥ prayuktāḥ: bhavantaḥ samanveṣata; yaḥ puṇyamaheśākhyaḥ satvaḥ taṃ rājye pratiṣṭhāpayāmaḥ iti; te samnatataḥ samanveṣitum ārabdhāḥ;
body.translated_text: said: 'Noble husband, this headache occurred before too. The physician prescribed the rock-breaking herb, and I was cured by it.' <s>Viśākha</s> said: 'I shall search for the rock-breaking herb.' She said: 'Noble husband, it is visible on the front slope of the mountain. I shall hold you with a rope. You pull it up.' That great-souled, honest man did not perceive her deceit. He agreed: 'Very well. Hold on — I shall pull it up.' She lowered him with the rope. Then, with one hand, he released the rope — and she too released it. He fell into the river. That being had a long lifespan. And he was destined to experience the happiness of kingship. He did not die. Carried by the current, he arrived at a certain royal capital. There a king without an heir had died. The ministers, together with townspeople and countryfolk, all gathered and deliberated: 'Sirs, the king has died. Whom shall we now establish as king?' They appointed men skilled in reading marks: 'Sirs, search; whoever is a being marked by great merit, him we shall establish as king.' They began to search in all directions.

body.translated_text: ) came to that spot and saw that great-souled one, endowed with the marks of kingship. Delighted in mind, they went to the ministers and said: 'We have found a being marked by great merit who is worthy of kingship.' Then those ministers, having arranged the beautification of the road and the city, brought him into the city with great magnificence and, at the proper day, hour, and constellation, anointed him as king. Since he had no queen, the ministers, chaplains, kings of neighboring lands, and other wealthy men, guild-heads, and caravan leaders, all brought their own daughters, adorned with every ornament, to that city, thinking: 'The king will choose.' But that king, having been deceived by a woman, would not consent. The ministers said: 'Your Majesty, kings are such as have inner apartments, princes, ministers, townspeople, and countryfolk, and wealth. Please establish your inner apartments. Prominent men from various regions and kings from neighboring lands have prepared their daughters and are waiting. Please meet them.' Even so, he would not consent. He was exceedingly disgusted with women. Through the power of a being's merit, enjoyments become potent and abundant. When the <s>Bodhisattva</s> was freed from the treacherous woman on that mountain, the roots and fruits on that mountain became meager and lost their potency. Then that woman, fearing famine, drought, and death, hoisted the man with mutilated hands and feet onto her shoulders and came to the outskirts of a village. In the streets, lanes, crossroads, and intersections she begged for alms. When asked, she said: 'I am devoted to my husband.' And it is the way of the world that a woman who is devoted to her husband is honored in the world. Wherever she entered, she received alms. Gradually she arrived at that royal capital.
