atha nāgapūrvī devaputro vaṇig iva labdhalābhaḥ sasyasaṃpanna iva kārṣakaḥ śūra iva jitasaṃgrāmaḥ sarvarogaparimukta ivāturo yayā vibhūtyā bhagavatsakāśam upasaṃkrāntaḥ tayaiva vibhūtyā svabhavanaṃ gataḥ
  bhikṣavaḥ pūrvarātrāpararātraṃ jāgarikānuyogam anuyuktā viharanti; tair dṛṣṭo bhagavato 'ntike udāro 'vabhāsaḥ; yaṃ dṛṣṭvā bhagavantaṃ papracchuḥ: kiṃ bhagavan imāṃ rātriṃ bhagavantaṃ darśanāya brahmā sabhāṃpatiḥ śakro devendraḥ catvāro lokapālā upasaṃkrāntāḥ bhagavān āha: na bhikṣavo brahmā sabhāṃpatiḥ na śakro devānām indraḥ nāpi catvāro lokapālāḥ māṃ darśanāyopasaṃkrāntāḥ; api tu yuṣmābhir bhikṣavaḥ sa dhanapālo hastināgaḥ, tāvac caṇḍaḥ tāvad rabhaso yas tathāgatasya vadhāya parākrāntaḥ dṛṣṭo bhadanta: mayā vinītaḥ sa mamāntike cittam abhiprasādya kālagataḥ cāturmahārājijeṣu deveṣūpapannaḥ; sa imāṃ rātriṃ matsakāśam upasaṃkrāntaḥ; tasya mayā dharmo deśitaḥ; sa dṛṣṭasatyaḥ svabhavanaṃ gataḥ iti
  bhikṣavaḥ saṃśayajātāḥ sarvasaṃśayacchettāraṃ buddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ papracchuḥ: kiṃ bhadanta dhanapālakena karma kṛtaṃ

yasya karmaṇo vipākena tiryakṣūpapannaḥ; kiṃ karma kṛtaṃ yena cāturmahārājikeṣu deveṣūpapannaḥ satyadarśanaṃ ca kṛtam iti; bhagavān āha: dhanapālakenaiva hi bhikṣavaḥ karmāṇi kṛtāny upacitāni labdhasaṃbhārāṇi pariṇatapratyayāny oghavat pratyupasthitāny avaśyabhāvīni; dhanapālena karmāṇi kṛtāny upacitāni ko 'nyaḥ pratyanubhaviṣyati? na bhikṣavaḥ karmāṇi kṛtāny upacitāni

) By the ripening of that deed, he was reborn among animals. Because he had performed service to the <s>Saṅgha</s>, by the ripening of that deed he became one who obtained food and drink. Because he died with a mind of serene faith toward me, he was reborn among the <s>Cāturmahārājika</s> (Four Great Kings') gods. Because while ordained under <s>Kāśyapa</s> the <s>Samyaksaṃbuddha</s> he had studied, recited, and developed skill in the aggregates (<s>skandha</s>), skill in the elements (<s>dhātu</s>), skill in the sense-bases (<s>āyatana</s>), skill in dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>), and skill in what is possible and impossible (<s>sthānāsthāna</s>) — therefore, having become a deity, he saw the truth in my presence. Thus indeed, monks, for purely dark deeds, as before, down to: effort should be made only toward purely bright deeds. Thus, monks, you should train.
  Summary verse (<s>uddāna</s>):
  'The goose, <s>Aṭṭa</s>, and the released one, /
  the deer, the putrid one, the monkey, the elephant, /
  the cat, the bull, the moon-stone, /
  the elephant, the jackal, and the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>.' //
  The monks, having doubts arise, asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'See, Venerable Sir, the <s>Bhagavān</s> was abandoned by five hundred monks, yet the Venerable <s>Ānanda</s> did not abandon him.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Not only now, monks — in the past too, I was abandoned by them, but <s>Ānanda</s> did not abandon me. Listen to that.'

In the past, monks, in this very auspicious <s>kalpa</s> (aeon), when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a teacher named <s>Kāśyapa</s> arose in the world — endowed with knowledge and conduct, Well-gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Charioteer of Persons to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, <s>Buddha</s>, <s>Bhagavān</s>. He dwelt near the city of <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, at the <s>Ṛṣivadana</s> Deer Park. In his dispensation, there was one who had gone forth and served as an attendant (<s>vaiyāpṛtyakara</s>). But he showed disregard for the minor and subsidiary training rules. (

body.translated_text:
The story of King <s>Dhṛtarāṣṭra</s>, and his faithful captain <s>Pūrṇamukha</s>, etc.
(concerning a previous birth of <s>Ānanda</s>, etc.)
  In the past, monks, at the great lake <s>Anavatapta</s>, there was a lord of geese named <s>Dhṛtarāṣṭra</s>. He had two sons: <s>Pūrṇa</s> and <s>Pūrṇamukha</s>. <s>Pūrṇa</s> was the elder; <s>Pūrṇamukha</s> was the younger. Now <s>Pūrṇa</s> was fierce, (

body.text: SBV II 193

) rabhasaḥ karkaśaḥ; nityam eva haṃsān bhartsayati; keṣāṃcit pakṣān utpāṭayati; keṣāṃcin nakharikābhiḥ kṣataṃ karoti; etāni cānyāni ca upadravaśatāni karoti; te haṃsāḥ pratidinam āgamya dhṛtarāṣṭrasya haṃsādhipater nivedayanti; sa saṃlakṣayati: pūrṇaś caṇḍo rabhasaḥ karkaśaḥ; yady aham enaṃ yauvarājye pratiṣṭhāpayāmi mamātyayād eṣa haṃsayūthaṃ nāśayiṣyati; tad upāyasaṃvidhānaṃ kartavyam iti; tena pūrṇaḥ pūrṇamukhaś ca ubhāv apy uktau; yaḥ utsān sarāṃsi taḍāgāni cāvalokya agrato matsakāsam āgacchati tam ahaṃ haṃsādhipatiṃ sthāpayāmi iti; tāv anyonyaṃ spardhayā paṃcaśataparivārau prankrāntau; tāv itaś cāmutaś ca utsān sarāṃsi taḍāgāni ca avalokayantāv
body.translated_text: ) violent, and harsh. He constantly bullied the geese — plucking the wings of some, scratching others with his claws — and inflicted hundreds of such harassments. The geese came daily to report to <s>Dhṛtarāṣṭra</s>, the lord of geese. He reflected: '<s>Pūrṇa</s> is fierce, violent, and harsh. If I establish him as crown prince, after my passing he will destroy the flock of geese. A stratagem must be devised.' He told both <s>Pūrṇa</s> and <s>Pūrṇamukha</s>: 'Whichever of you surveys the springs, lakes, and ponds and comes before me first — him I shall establish as lord of geese.' The two, in rivalry with each other, set out with retinues of five hundred each. Surveying springs, lakes, and ponds here and there,

body.translated_text: they gradually reached the city of <s>Vārāṇasī</s>. At that time, in <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, a king named <s>Brahmadatta</s> was exercising sovereignty — it was prosperous, and teeming with a great multitude of people. Not far from his garden in <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, there was a lotus-pond named <s>Brahmāvatī</s>, renowned as surpassing even a great lake. In it, various kinds of aquatic flowers had been planted. On its banks, on all four sides, thousands of flowering and fruit-bearing trees had been planted. It was covered with blue lotuses, white water-lilies, and white lotuses, adorned with many groves of trees, and resounding with the songs of many kinds of birds. Having seen its splendor, the goose <s>Pūrṇa</s> with his retinue of five hundred descended and began to sport about freely. <s>Pūrṇamukha</s> too was urged by his flock-mates: 'You too should descend and play.' He said: 'Let me first secure the kingship. Afterwards I shall come back and play.' Going swiftly, he secured the kingship. Then, with his retinue of five hundred, he came to <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, descended into the <s>Brahmāvatī</s> lotus-pond, and began to sport. Seeing him disporting thus, the people were overcome with wonder: 'What a supremely beautiful lord of geese has arrived here from somewhere! Having adorned the <s>Brahmāvatī</s> lotus-pond, surpassing all aquatic birds in beauty of form, he arouses the admiration of the people and dwells freely.' Having heard, all the inhabitants of <s>Vārāṇasī</s> surrounded the <s>Brahmāvatī</s> lotus-pond on all sides and stood watching his confident deportment and beauty of form. The ministers reported to the king: 'Your Majesty, a lord of geese has come from somewhere. Having descended into the <s>Brahmāvatī</s> lotus-pond with a retinue of many hundreds of geese, surpassing all aquatic birds in beauty of form, (

You must capture him alive, unharmed, with snares, and bring him to me.' He was caught with the most delicate of snares. He spoke a verse:

body.translated_text: Four hundred and ninety-nine fled. One did not flee. He stood there, grieving for the bound one. The bird-catchers, seeing this, were overcome with supreme wonder. Out of fear of the king, they did not bind him. Nor did they kill him. They took the lord of geese to the king's presence. The second one, unbound, fettered by the bonds of affection, followed of his own accord. The lord of geese was brought before the king. The king said: 'Sirs, why has this second one been brought?' They said: 'Your Majesty, he was not bound by us. He came of his own accord.' The king, overcome with supreme wonder, said: 'Surely this is his wife.

Go — release this lord of geese together with his wife. And none of you shall kill them.' The bird-catchers said: 'Your Majesty, others will kill them. Let an announcement be made to the people.' The king gave a command to his ministers: 'Go, sirs — have a bell-proclamation made throughout the city of <s>Vārāṇasī</s>: "His Majesty commands thus: No one dwelling in my domain shall kill aquatic birds."' They had the bell-proclamation made.
  What do you think, monks? He who was <s>Pūrṇamukha</s>, the lord of geese — that was I myself at that time, in that era. She who was his wife — that is this very <s>Ānanda</s> at that time, in that era. Those four hundred and ninety-nine geese — those are these very four hundred and ninety-nine monks. Even then I was abandoned by them as geese, and <s>Ānanda</s> as a goose did not abandon me. Now too I was abandoned by them, and the monk <s>Ānanda</s> did not abandon me. body.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavo vārāṇasyāṃ nagaryām aṭṭo nāma rājā rājyaṃ kārayati ṛddhaṃ ca sphītaṃ ca yāvad ākīrṇabahujanamanuṣyaṃ ca; tasya paṃcāmātyaśatāni yeṣām anubhāvāt prātisīmaiḥ koṭṭarājabhir nābhibhūyate; yāvad dakṣiṇāpathāt karadaṇḍī nāma sahasrayodhī abhyāgataḥ; so 'nyatamenāmātyena rājñaḥ sakāśam upanītaḥ; deva ayaṃ karadaṇḍī nāma sahasrayodhī; devam uddiśya dakṣiṇāpathād āgataḥ; tad arhati devo 'sya parigrahaṃ kartum iti; sa rājñā parigṛhītaḥ; bhogaiḥ saṃvibhaktaḥ; yāvad apareṇa samayena aṭṭasya rājñaḥ bhūmyantarā rājānaḥ upacittabalasādhanāḥ saṃvṛttāḥ; te caturaṅgabalakāyaṃ sannāhya hastikāyam aśvakāyaṃ rathakāyaṃ pattikāyam aṭṭaṃ rājānam abhigatāḥ yuddhāya; aṭṭo 'pi rājā caturaṅgabalakāyaṃ sannāhya hastikāyam aśvakāyaṃ rathakāyaṃ pattikāyaṃ bhūmyantarān rājñaḥ pratyabhiniryāto yuddhāya; aṭṭena rājñā bhūmyantarā rājanaḥ jītāḥ bhītaḥ bhagnāḥ parājitāḥ parāpṛṣṭhīkṛtāḥ svaksvakān viṣayān gatāḥ; taiḥ punar api sannipatya aṭṭasya rājñaḥ paṃcāmātyaśatāni upaskāreṇa bhagnāni: āgacchata yūyaṃ; yuṣmān prativiśiṣṭaraiḥ bhogaiḥ saṃvibhajāmaḥ iti; te saṃpratipannāḥ; tato bhūmyantarā rājanaḥ punar api caturaṅgabalakāyaṃ sannāhya hastikāyam aśvakāyaṃ rathakāyaṃ pattikāyam aṭṭam rājānam abhigatā yauddhāya; aṭṭo 'pi nāma caturaṅgabalakāyaṃ sannāhya hastikāyam aśvakāyaṃ rathakāyaṃ pattikāyaṃ bhūmyantarān rājñaḥ pratyabhiniryāto yuddhāya; aṭṭasya rājñaḥ paṃca amātyaśatāni yuddhe vartamāne pratinivartya karaṇḍdinā sahasrayodhena sārdhaṃ yoddhum ārabdhāni
body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in the city of <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, a king named <s>Aṭṭa</s> was exercising sovereignty — it was prosperous, thriving, and teeming with a great multitude of people. He had five hundred ministers, by whose power he was not overcome by neighboring vassal kings. Then from the southern regions, a thousand-warrior named <s>Karadaṇḍī</s> arrived. He was brought to the king's presence by a certain minister: 'Your Majesty, this is <s>Karadaṇḍī</s>, a thousand-warrior. He has come from the southern regions for Your Majesty's sake. Your Majesty should extend his patronage to him.' He was taken under the king's patronage and shared in the royal enjoyments. Then at a later time, neighboring kings of King <s>Aṭṭa</s> had built up their forces and resources. Having marshaled their four-division army — elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry — they marched against King <s>Aṭṭa</s> for battle. King <s>Aṭṭa</s> too, having marshaled his four-division army — elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry — marched out against the neighboring kings for battle. King <s>Aṭṭa</s> defeated, routed, broke, and vanquished the neighboring kings, and sent them fleeing back to their own territories. But they regrouped and, through bribery, won over King <s>Aṭṭa</s>'s five hundred ministers: 'Come over to us — we shall share with you even finer enjoyments.' They accepted. Then the neighboring kings once again marshaled their four-division army — elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry — and marched against King <s>Aṭṭa</s> for battle. King <s>Aṭṭa</s> too marshaled his four-division army — elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry — and marched out against the neighboring kings for battle. In the midst of battle, King <s>Aṭṭa</s>'s five hundred ministers turned against him and began to fight alongside <s>Karadaṇḍī</s> the thousand-warrior against him.

The story of a bull that got entangled other bulls into trouble by bad counsels
(concerning a previous life of the Buddha and Devadatta)

bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavo dvau sārthavāhau paṃcabhiḥ śakaṭaśataiḥ sārdham anuvyaharamāṇau kāntāramārgaṃ pratipannau; tavyoḥ kāntāramārgapratipannayoḥ kadācid balīvardānāṃ parītto yavaso bhavati; pānīyaṃca kadācit parīttaṃ bhavati; kadācin nāsty eva; tato 'sau sārthaḥ saha balīvardaiḥ atīva pariśrāntaḥ kṛcchreṇa kāntāmārgaṃ pratipannaḥ paśyati anyatarasmin pradeśe haritaśādvalaṃ salilasaṃpannaṃ ca snātāḥ; prabhūtaṃ ca pānīyaṃ pītaṃ; tatas te balīvardāḥ parīttena pānyena yavasena ca parikhinnāḥ, paryāptaṃ yavasaṃ pānīyaṃ ca pītvā viśrāntāḥ; teṣāṃ yaḥ pradhāno balīvardaḥ sa tān prabodhayati: bhavanto vayaṃ parīttena yavasena parīttena ca pānīyena parikheditāḥ; ayaṃ pradeśo haritaśādvalaḥ salilasaṃpannaś ca; yadi bhavatām abhipretam ihaiva haṭhaṃ kṛtvā tiṣṭhāmaḥ iti; dvitīyaḥ pradhānabalīvardaś ca yūthyān kathayati: bhavanto balavanto manuṣyāḥ durdāntadamakāḥ; yathaiva vayaṃ vahāmas tathaiva vahata; mā anarthaṃ prāpayiṣyatha iti; evam ukte pradhānabalīvardo ruṣitaḥ svayūthyān kathayati: bhavantaḥ kena candrasya pṛṣṭhaṃ
body.translated_text: In the past, monks, two caravan-leaders, traveling together with five hundred carts, set out on a wilderness road. As they traveled on the wilderness road, sometimes there was scanty fodder for the bullocks, sometimes the water was scanty, and sometimes there was none at all. Then that caravan, together with the bullocks, utterly exhausted and with difficulty traveling the wilderness road, saw in a certain place a green meadow well-supplied with water. They bathed, and drank abundant water. Then those bullocks, wearied by the scanty water and fodder, having drunk their fill of fodder and water, rested. Their chief bullock roused them: 'Sirs, we have been wearied by scanty fodder and scanty water. This place has a green meadow and is well-supplied with water. If it pleases you, let us stubbornly remain right here.' The second chief bullock said to his herd: 'Sirs, humans are powerful, tamers of the untamed. Just as we have been pulling, so pull on — lest you come to ruin.' When this was said, the chief bullock, angered, said to his herd: 'Sirs, who has seen the back of the moon?

body.text: dṛṣṭam ebhir yuṣmābhir na voḍhavyam iti; yāvat sārthikā balīvardān yojayitum ārabdhāḥ; te balīvardair bhreṣaṇarūpā avasthāpitāḥ; sārthikā prabhūtān prahārān datvā pratodayaṣṭibhir ātāḍya ātāḍya rudhireṇa pragharatā śakaṭe yojitāḥ; anye tūṣṇīṃ voḍhum ārabdhāḥ; teṣāṃ na kiṃcit kṛtaṃ; devatā gāthāṃ bhāṣate
body.translated_text: These [carts] need not be drawn by you.' Then the caravan-men began to yoke the bullocks. The bullocks stood in a posture of refusal. The caravan-men, having struck them with many blows and beaten them with goads, yoked them to the carts while blood flowed. The others began to draw in silence. Nothing happened to them. A deity spoke a verse:

) bullock who led the others astray — that was <s>Devadatta</s> at that time, in that era. Even then, those who heeded my word crossed the wilderness road safely and securely. Those who heeded <s>Devadatta</s>'s word came to ruin and calamity. Now too, those who have adopted my view have safely and securely crossed the wilderness road of <s>saṃsāra</s>. Those who have adopted <s>Devadatta</s>'s view have come to ruin and calamity.
  The monks, having doubts arise, asked the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, who cuts through all doubts: 'See, Venerable Sir, <s>Devadatta</s> is a fool with a retinue of fools.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Not only now, monks — in the past too <s>Devadatta</s> was a fool with a retinue of fools. Listen to that.'

The story of the leader of the monkeys

children.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavaḥ anyatamasmin araṇyāyatane markaṭayūthapatiḥ prativasati; tena paribhramatā kūpe candrabimbakaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ; yūthapatiḥ kathayati: bhavantaḥ candraḥ kūpe patitaḥ; uddharāmaḥ; kim acandrako loko bhaviṣyati? iti; te kathayanti: śobhanam; uddharāmaḥ iti; te saṃjalpaṃ kartum ārabdhāḥ: katham atra uddhartavyaḥ? iti; apare kathayanti: kim atra jñāyate? markaṭarajjuṃ kṛtvā samuddharāmaḥ iti; tair markaṭarajjuḥ kṛtā; ekaḥ śākhāyāṃ lagnaḥ; tasya pucche aparo lagnaḥ; tasyāpy aparo lagna ity evaṃ sarve lagnāḥ; śākhā atibhārā jātā; te pānīyaṃ vikṣobhayitum ārabdhāḥ; candrapratibimbakaṃ naṣṭaṃ; śākhā bhagnā; sarve kūpe patitāḥ; anayena vyasanam āpannāḥ; devatā gāthāṃ bhāṣate
children.translated_text: In the past, monks, in a certain forest region, a monkey troop-leader dwelt. While roaming about, he saw the reflection of the moon in a well. The troop-leader said: 'Sirs, the moon has fallen into the well! Let us pull it out — shall the world be without a moon?' They said: 'Excellent! Let us pull it out.' They began to deliberate: 'How shall it be pulled out?' Others said: 'What is there to consider? Let us make a monkey-chain and pull it out.' They made a monkey-chain. One clung to a branch; another clung to that one's tail; yet another clung to his — and so all of them clung on. The branch became overburdened. They began to stir the water. The moon's reflection vanished. The branch broke. They all fell into the well and came to ruin and calamity. A deity spoke a verse:

children.text: yeṣām iha hi mūrkāṇāṃ mūrkho bhavati nāyakaḥ /
children.translated_text: Those fools here whose leader is a fool —

children.text: sarve te nidhanaṃ yānti candroddhārā iva vānarāḥ // iti
children.translated_text: they all go to destruction, like the monkeys trying to retrieve the moon. //

children.text: kiṃ manyadhve bhikṣavo yo 'sau markaṭayūthapatiḥ devadattaḥ saḥ tena kālena tena samayena; tadāpy eṣa mūrkho mūrkhaparivāraḥ; etarhy apy eṣa mūrkho mūrkhaparivāraḥ
children.translated_text: What do you think, monks? He who was the monkey troop-leader — that was <s>Devadatta</s> at that time, in that era. Even then he was a fool with a retinue of fools. Now too he is a fool with a retinue of fools.

body.text: bhagavān śrāvastyāṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍadasyārāme; atha bhagavata etad abhavat: tathāgatasya saṃbhṛtasaṃbhārāṇi karmāṇi kṛtāny upacitāni labdhasaṃbhārāṇi pariṇatapratyayāny oghavat pratyupasthitāny
body.translated_text: The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling at <s>Śrāvastī</s> in the <s>Jetavana</s>, the park of <s>Anāthapiṇḍada</s>. Then the <s>Bhagavān</s> reflected: 'The deeds of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, performed and accumulated, whose provisions have been gathered, whose conditions have ripened, which stand present like a flood,

body.text: avaśyabhāvīni; tathāgatenaiva karmāṇi (
body.translated_text: which are inevitably bound to occur — the deeds (

body.text: SBV II 203
body.translated_text: SBV II 203

) performed and accumulated by the <s>Tathāgata</s> himself — who else would experience them? For deeds performed and accumulated do not ripen externally in the earth element,' and so on as before up to 'they indeed bear fruit for embodied beings.' '<s>Devadatta</s> will inevitably split the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s <s>Saṅgha</s>.'
  The <s>Saṅgha</s> is split by five causes. First, the <s>Saṅgha</s> does not split at the beginning. As long as a <s>Buddha</s> has arisen in the world, the world remains facing him: 'A <s>Buddha</s>, sirs, has arisen in the world.' After the Teacher has passed into <s>parinirvāṇa</s>, the <s>Saṅgha</s> splits. Whoever should say 'I alone am the Teacher' — to him it should be said: 'When the <s>Bhagavān</s> was alive, enduring, persisting, and carrying on, where were you?' When no abscess has arisen, the <s>Saṅgha</s> does not split — neither a view-abscess nor a conduct-abscess. When no pair of disciples has been designated, the <s>Saṅgha</s> does not split. Why? Because when the <s>Saṅgha</s> has been split, a pair of disciples necessarily reunites it. When the boundary has not been bound, the <s>Saṅgha</s> does not split. Why? Because the <s>Saṅgha</s> splits within the boundary, not outside the boundary.

children.text: atha bhagavata etad abhavat: mama nirarbude bhikṣusaṃghe arbudam utpannaṃ śīlārbudaṃ dṛṣṭyarbudaṃ ca; śīlārbudam utpāditaṃ sudattena kalantakaputreṇa; dṛṣṭyarbudam ariṣṭena bhikṣuṇā; avaśyaṃ ca devadattena saṃgho bhettavyaḥ; yannv ahaṃ rājagṛhe varṣām upagaccheyam; atha bhagavata etad abhavat: yadi tāvat śaikṣāśaikṣaiḥ pudgalaiḥ sārdhaṃ rājagṛhaṃ gamiṣyāmi na śakṣyati devadattaḥ saṃghabhedaṃ kartuṃ; yannv ahaṃ pṛthagjanakalyāṇakaiḥ pudgalaiḥ sārdhaṃ gaccheyam; iti viditvā āyuṣmatā rāhulena upasthāyakena paṃcabhir bhikṣuśataiḥ sārdhaṃ yathābhiramyaṃ śrāvastyāṃ vihṛtya yena rājagṛhaṃ tena cārikāṃ prakrāntaḥ; anupūrveṇa cārikāṃ caran rājagṛham anuprāptaḥ iti (

children.translated_text: SBV II 204

Then the <s>Bhagavān</s> reflected: 'In my <s>Bhikṣusaṃgha</s>, which was free from abscesses, an abscess has arisen — a conduct-abscess and a view-abscess. The conduct-abscess was created by <s>Sudatta Kalantakaputra</s>; the view-abscess by the monk <s>Ariṣṭa</s>. And <s>Devadatta</s> will inevitably split the <s>Saṅgha</s>. Let me spend the rains retreat in <s>Rājagṛha</s>.' Then the <s>Bhagavān</s> reflected: 'If I go to <s>Rājagṛha</s> together with individuals who are learners and beyond-learners, <s>Devadatta</s> will not be able to cause a schism in the <s>Saṅgha</s>. Let me rather go together with ordinary persons of good character.' Having determined this, together with the Venerable <s>Rāhula</s> as his attendant and five hundred monks, having dwelt in <s>Śrāvastī</s> as long as he wished, he set out on a wandering tour toward <s>Rājagṛha</s>. Wandering by stages on his tour, he arrived at <s>Rājagṛha</s>. (

buddho bhagavān rājagṛhe varṣā upagato veṇuvane kalandakanivāpe; tena khalu samayena durbhikṣam abhūt; kṛcchraḥ kāntāraḥ durlabhaḥ piṇḍako yācanakena; tatra bhagavān bhikṣūn āmantrayate sma: icchāmy ahaṃ bhikṣavaḥ imāṃ traimāsīṃ pratisaṃlātuṃ; na me kenacid bhikṣuṇā upasaṃkramitavyaṃ sthāpayitvā piṇḍapātanirhārakaṃ; tad eva poṣadham iti; bhikṣusaṃghena kriyākāraḥ kṛtaḥ na kenacid asmākam imāṃ traimāsīṃ bhagavantaṃ darśanāyopasaṃkramitavyaṃ sthāpayitvā piṇḍapātanirhārakaṃ; tad eva poṣadham iti
  tena khalu samayena āyuṣmantau śāriputramaudgalyāyanau dakṣiṇāgiriṣu varṣā upagatau; devadattena traimāsīṃ bhikṣusaṃghaḥ pravāritaḥ cīvarapiṇḍapātaśayanāsanaglānapratyayabhaiṣajyapariṣkāraiḥ; sa trayāṇāṃ va dvikānāṃ vā māsānām atyayād bhikṣūn āmantrayate sma: śramaṇa āyuṣmanto gautama evaṃ śrāvakāṇāṃ dharmaṃ deśayati; āraṇyakatvena bhikṣuḥ śudhyati mucyati niryāti sukhaduḥkhaṃ vyatikrāmati sukhaduḥkhavyatikramaṃ cānuprāpnoti; piṇḍapātikatvena pāṃsukūlikatvena
body.translated_text:
The <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s> took up the rains retreat at <s>Rājagṛha</s> in the <s>Veṇuvana</s> <s>Kalandakanivāpa</s>. At that time there was a famine — a harsh wilderness, difficult to obtain alms by begging. Then the <s>Bhagavān</s> addressed the monks: 'I wish, monks, to go into seclusion for this three-month period. No monk is to approach me, except the one who brings the alms-food offering — that is the <s>Poṣadha</s>.' The <s>Bhikṣusaṃgha</s> made the formal act: 'None of us is to approach the <s>Bhagavān</s> for a visit during this three-month period, except the one who brings the alms-food offering — that is the <s>Poṣadha</s>.'
  At that time, the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Maudgalyāyana</s> had taken up the rains retreat in the southern hills. <s>Devadatta</s> provided the <s>Bhikṣusaṃgha</s> for the three-month period with robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicine and supplies for the sick. After the passage of two or three months, he addressed the monks: 'The ascetic <s>Gautama</s>, sirs, teaches the <s>Dharma</s> to his disciples thus: a monk is purified by dwelling in the forest, is freed, escapes, transcends pleasure and pain, and attains the transcendence of pleasure and pain; by eating only alms-food, by wearing only rag-robes,

body.text: traicīvarikatvena ābhyavakāśikatvena śudhyati mucyati niryāti sukhaduḥkhaṃ vyatikrāmati sukhaduḥkhavyatikramaṃ cānuprāpnoti; yasya cāyuṣmantaḥ imāni paṃca vratapadāni na rocante na kṣamante na saṃprakhyānti sa śramaṇasya gautamasya ārād bhavatu durād bhavatu; śalākaṃ gṛhṇātu iti; paṃcabhir bhikṣuśataiḥ śalākā gṛhītāḥ; devadatta utthāyāsanāt prakrāntaḥ; paṃca bhikṣuśatāni pṛṣṭhataḥ pṛṣṭhataḥ samanubaddhāni; āyuṣmān rāhulo dvāre tiṣṭhati; tena tāni devadattasya pṛṣṭhataḥ pṛṣṭhataḥ samanubaddhāni dṛṣṭāni; sa kathayati: āyuṣmantaḥ kimarthaṃ tathāgatam arhantaṃ samyaksaṃbuddham apahāya asya pāpecchasya pṛṣṭhataḥ pṛṣṭhataḥ samanugacchata? iti; te kathayanti: āyuṣman rāhula evaṃvidhe durbhikṣe kṛcchre kāntāre bhagavān adarśano vyavasthitaḥ; vayaṃ (
body.translated_text: by wearing only the triple robe, and by dwelling in the open air, one is purified, freed, escapes, transcends pleasure and pain, and attains the transcendence of pleasure and pain. Whoever among you, sirs, does not approve of, accept, or acknowledge these five ascetic practices — let him be far away, far away from the ascetic <s>Gautama</s>! Let him take a voting-stick.' Five hundred monks took the voting-sticks. <s>Devadatta</s> rose from his seat and departed. The five hundred monks followed close behind him. The Venerable <s>Rāhula</s> stood at the door. He saw the five hundred monks following close behind <s>Devadatta</s>. He said: 'Sirs, why do you abandon the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the <s>Arhat</s>, the Perfectly Awakened One, and follow close behind this one of evil desires?' They said: 'Venerable <s>Rāhula</s>, in such a famine, in this harsh wilderness, the <s>Bhagavān</s> has remained out of sight. We, (

) devadattānubhāvāt prāṇair na viyuktāḥ; yadi devadattena traimāsīṃ bhikṣusaṃgho na pratipādito 'bhaviṣyat, ekaḥ bhikṣur na jīvito 'bhaviṣyad iti
  yadā devadattena tathāgatena śrāvakasaṃgho bhinnaḥ, tadā mahān pṛthivīcalo jātaḥ; ulkāpātā diśodāhāḥ; devadundubhayaḥ abhinadanti; niyamānavakrāntā niyamaṃ nāvakrāmanti; phalaṃ na prāpnuvanti; vairāgyaṃ na gacchati; āsravān na kṣapayanti; noddiśanti; na paṭhanti; na svādhyāyanti; sūtravinayadharābhidhārmikāraṇyakāḥ sūtravinayābhidharmāraṇyakacintāyāṃ na prayujyante; na śrāvakabodhau bījam āropayanti; na pratyekāyāṃ bodhau; nānuttarāyāṃ samyaksaṃbodhau; sadevamānuṣaṃ jagad vyākulaṃ vartate; trisahasramahāsahasre lokadhātau dharmacakraṃ viṣṭhitaṃ na satvasantāne vartate
body.translated_text:
) by <s>Devadatta</s>'s power, have not been separated from our lives. If <s>Devadatta</s> had not provided for the <s>Bhikṣusaṃgha</s> during the three-month period, not a single monk would have survived.'
  When the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s community of disciples was split by <s>Devadatta</s>, a great earthquake arose; meteors fell, the horizons blazed; celestial war-drums resounded; those approaching the fixed course of certainty no longer entered it; they did not attain the fruits; dispassion did not arise; they did not exhaust the defilements; they did not teach; they did not recite; they did not study; those who upheld <s>Sūtra</s>, <s>Vinaya</s>, <s>Abhidharma</s>, and the forest-dwelling practice did not engage in contemplation of <s>Sūtra</s>, <s>Vinaya</s>, <s>Abhidharma</s>, and forest-dwelling; they did not sow the seed for <s>Śrāvaka</s> awakening, nor for <s>Pratyeka</s> awakening, nor for unsurpassed perfect awakening. The world with its gods and humans was thrown into confusion. In the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system, the Wheel of <s>Dharma</s>, though established, did not turn in the continuity of beings.

body.translated_text: <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Maudgalyāyana</s> visit the <s>Buddha</s> and promise to him to restore the congregation

body.text: āyuṣmantau śāriputramaudgalyāyanau saṃlakṣayanti: kimartham ayaṃ mahāpṛthivīcālaḥ? iti; samanvāhṛtyārhatāṃ jñānadarśanaṃ na pravartate; tau samanvāhartuṃ pravṛttau; paśyataḥ: devadattena bhagavataḥ śrāvakasaṃghaṃ bhinnaṃ; tayor etad abhavat: gaccāvaḥ bhagavataḥ śrāvakasaṃghaṃ pratisandhātum iti; athāyuṣmantau śāriputramaudgalyāyanau trayāṇāṃ vārṣikāṇāṃ māsānām atyayāt kṛtacīvarau niṣṭhitacīvarau samādāya pātracīvaraṃ yena rājagṛhaṃ tena cārikāṃ prakrāntau; anupūrveṇa cārikāṃ carantau rājagṛham anuprāptau; athāyuṣmantau śāriputramaudgalyāyanau pātracīvaraṃ pratiśamayya pādau prakṣālya yena bhagavāṃs tenopasaṃkrāntau; tena khalu samayena āyuṣmān rāhulo dvare tiṣṭhate; athāyuṣmān rāhulaḥ āyuṣmantaṃ śāriputram idam avocad upādyāya devadattena bhagavataḥ śrāvakasaṃgho bhinnaḥ iti; (
body.translated_text: The Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Maudgalyāyana</s> reflected: 'For what reason has this great earthquake occurred?' They investigated with the knowledge and vision of <s>Arhats</s>, but it did not reveal itself. They began to investigate further, and they saw: '<s>Devadatta</s> has split the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s community of disciples.' The thought occurred to them: 'Let us go to reunite the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s community of disciples.' Then the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Maudgalyāyana</s>, at the end of the three months of the rainy season, having finished their robes, taking up their bowls and robes, set out on a walking tour toward <s>Rājagṛha</s>. Wandering by stages, they arrived at <s>Rājagṛha</s>. Then the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Maudgalyāyana</s>, having put away their bowls and robes and washed their feet, approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>. At that time, the Venerable <s>Rāhula</s> was standing at the gate. Then the Venerable <s>Rāhula</s> said this to the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s>: 'Preceptor, <s>Devadatta</s> has split the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s community of disciples.' (

body.translated_text: SBV II 206

body.translated_text: ) He said: 'Venerable one, it is for this very purpose that we have come. Be at ease; we shall effect the reunification.' Having said this, they entered the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s presence. Having entered, they bowed their heads at the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable

body.text: śāriputramaudgalyāyanau bhagavantam idam avocatāṃ: gachāmo vayaṃ bhadanta tathāgatasya bhinnaṃ śrāvakasaṃghaṃ sandhātum iti
body.translated_text: <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Maudgalyāyana</s> said this to the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'We wish to go, Venerable Sir, to reunite the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s split community of disciples.'

children.translated_text: The sermon on the four meritorious men

children.text:
bhagavān āha: sādhu sādhu śāriputramaudgalyāyanau; bahu sa puṇyaṃ prasūyate apramāṇam asaṃkhyeyaṃ yas tathāgatasya bhinnaṃ śrāvakasaṃghaṃ pratisandhatte, tadyathā śatachinnaṃ vālaṃ yaḥ koṭyā koṭiṃ pratisandadhyāt; evam eva sa bahu puṇyaṃ prasūyate aprameyam asaṃkhyeyaṃ yas tathāgatasya bhinnaṃ śrāvakasaṃghaṃ pratisandhatte
  catvāra ime śāriputramaudgalyāyanau brāhmaṃ puṇyaṃ prasavanti; katame catvāraḥ? 1) yaḥ pudgalaḥ apratiṣṭhitapūrve pṛthivīpradeśe tathāgatasya śārīraṃ stūpaṃ pratiṣṭhāpayati; ayaṃ prathamaḥ pudgalaḥ brāhmaṃ puṇyaṃ prasavati; kalpaṃ svargeṣu modate; 2) punar aparaṃ yaḥ pudgalaḥ apratiṣṭhitapūrve pṛthivīpradeśe caturdiśasya bhikṣusaṃghasya vihāraṃ pratiṣṭhāpayati; ayaṃ dvitīyaḥ pudgalaḥ brāhmaṃ puṇyaṃ prasavati; kalpaṃ svargeṣu modate; 3) punar aparaṃ yaḥ pudgalaḥ tathāgataśrāvakasaṃghaṃ bhinnaṃ sandhatte; ayaṃ tritīyaḥ pudgalaḥ brāhmaṃ puṇyaṃ prasavati; kalpaṃ svargeṣu modate; 4) punar aparaṃ yaḥ pudgalaḥ maitrīsahagatena cittena avaireṇa asapatnena avyābādhena vipulena mahadgatena apramāṇena subhāvitena ekāṃ diśam adhimucya spharitvā upasaṃpadya viharati; tathā dvitīyāṃ tathā tṛtīyāṃ tathā caturthīm; ity ūrdhvam adhaḥ tiryak sarvaśaḥ sarvam imaṃ lokaṃ maitrīsahagatena cittena avaireṇa asapatnena avyābādhena vipulena (

children.text: ) mahadgatena apramāṇena subhāvitena adhimucya spharitvā upasaṃpadya viharati; evaṃ karuṇāmuditaupekṣāsahagatena cittena avaireṇa asapatnena avyābādhena vipulena mahadgatena apramāṇena subhāvitena adhimucya spharitvā upasaṃpadya viharati; tathā dvitīyāṃ tathā tṛtīyāṃ tathā caturthīm; ity ūrdhvam adhaḥ tiryak sarvaśaḥ sarvam imaṃ lokaṃ upekṣāsahagatena cittena avaireṇa asapatnena avyābādhena vipulena mahadgatena apramāṇena subhāvitena ekāṃ diśam adhimucya spharitvā upasaṃpadya viharati; ayaṃ caturthaḥ pudgalaḥ brāhmaṃ puṇyaṃ prasavati; kalpaṃ svargeṣu modate
children.translated_text: ) exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading, resolving, and dwelling in it; likewise with a mind accompanied by <s>karuṇā</s> (compassion), <s>muditā</s> (sympathetic joy), and <s>upekṣā</s> (equanimity), free from enmity, free from hostility, free from malice, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading, resolving, and dwelling in it; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; above, below, across, everywhere, all this world — with a mind accompanied by <s>upekṣā</s>, free from enmity, free from hostility, free from malice, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading one direction, resolving, and dwelling in it — this fourth person generates <s>brāhma</s> merit and rejoices in the heavens for an aeon.'

The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Excellent, excellent, <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Maudgalyāyana</s>! Great is the merit — immeasurable, incalculable — generated by one who reunites the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s split community of disciples; just as if one were to rejoin, tip to tip, a hair cut into a hundred pieces — even so, great is the merit — immeasurable, incalculable — generated by one who reunites the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s split community of disciples.
  There are these four persons, <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Maudgalyāyana</s>, who generate <s>brāhma</s> (divine) merit. Which four? (1) The person who, in a place where one has not been established before, establishes a <s>stūpa</s> for the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s relics — this first person generates <s>brāhma</s> merit and rejoices in the heavens for an aeon. (2) Furthermore, the person who, in a place where one has not been established before, establishes a monastery for the community of monks of the four directions — this second person generates <s>brāhma</s> merit and rejoices in the heavens for an aeon. (3) Furthermore, the person who reunites a split community of the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s disciples — this third person generates <s>brāhma</s> merit and rejoices in the heavens for an aeon. (4) Furthermore, the person who, with a mind accompanied by <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness), free from enmity, free from hostility, free from malice, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading one direction, resolving and dwelling in it; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; above, below, across, everywhere, all this world — with a mind accompanied by <s>maitrī</s>, free from enmity, free from hostility, free from malice, vast, (

body.text: Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana visit Devadatta and exhort the misguided monks to return to the true doctrine
body.translated_text: <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s> visit <s>Devadatta</s> and exhort the misguided monks to return to the true doctrine

body.text: āthāyuṣmantau śāriputramaudgalyāyanau bhagavato bhāṣitam abhinandyānumodya bhagavataḥ pādau śirasā vanditvā bhagavato 'ntikāt prakrāntau; tena khalu samayena devadatto dakṣiṇāgiriṣu buddhalīlayā anudharmaṃ deśayati; kokāliko 'sya dakṣiṇe pārśve niṣaṇṇaḥ; khaṇḍadravyaḥ vāme; adrākṣīd devadattaḥ śāriputramaudgalyāyanau dūrād eva; dṛṣṭvā ca punaḥ saṃlakṣayati: mahāśrāvakā api mayā anvāvartitāḥ; idānīm ahaṃ sarvajñaḥ; kokālikaṃ khaṇḍadravyaṃ ca bāhubhyāṃ
body.translated_text: Then the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>, having rejoiced in and approved of the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s words, bowed their heads at the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s feet and departed from the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s presence. At that time, <s>Devadatta</s> was teaching the <s>Dharma</s> in imitation of the <s>Buddha</s>'s manner in the southern hills. <s>Kokālika</s> was seated at his right side, and <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s> at his left. <s>Devadatta</s> saw <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Maudgalyāyana</s> from afar. Having seen them, he reflected: 'Even the great disciples have been won over by me. Now I am omniscient.' He nudged <s>Kokālika</s> and <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s> with his arms,

body.text: ghaṭṭayati uttiṣṭhottiṣṭheti; tau saṃlakṣayataḥ eṣa evāsmākaṃ doṣo yad asmābhir asya saṃghabhede sāhāyyaṃ kalpitam; uttiṣṭhāmaḥ; yadi prahāraṃ dadāti, balavān eṣa niyatam asmān hanti iti; tāv utthitau; āyuṣmān śāriputro dakṣiṇe pārśve niṣaṇṇaḥ; āyuṣmān maudgalyāyanaḥ uttare iti; tatra devadattaḥ āyuṣmantam śāriputram āmantrayate pratibhātu te śāriputra bhikṣūṇāṃ dharmyāṃ kathāṃ kathayituṃ; pṛṣṭhī me āvilāyati; tat tāvad āyāmayiṣye iti; adhivāsayaty āyuṣmān śāriputraḥ devadattasya tūṣṇīṃbhāvena; atha devadattaś caturguṇam uttarāsaṅgaṃ prajñapya dakṣiṇena pārśvena śayyāṃ kalpayitvā middham avakrāntaḥ; āyuṣmatā śāriputreṇa (
body.translated_text: saying: 'Get up, get up.' Those two reflected: 'This is indeed our fault, that we provided assistance to him in splitting the community. Let us rise. If he strikes, he is strong — he will surely kill us.' They rose. The Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> sat on the right side, and the Venerable <s>Maudgalyāyana</s> on the north. Then <s>Devadatta</s> addressed the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s>: 'May it please you, <s>Śāriputra</s>, to give a talk on the <s>Dharma</s> to the monks. My back is aching; I shall recline for a while.' The Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> consented to <s>Devadatta</s> by silence. Then <s>Devadatta</s>, having spread his upper robe folded in four, lying down on his right side, fell asleep. The Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> used his supernatural power so that (

body.text: ) tathādhiṣṭhito yathottānakaḥ kāyena krathamanena avasthitaḥ; tatra āyuṣmān śāriputro bhikṣūn āmantrayate sma: paśyata āyuṣmantaḥ śāstur avasthām: uttānakaḥ kāyena krathamānena middham avakrāntaḥ iti; athāyuṣmān śāriputraḥ āyuṣmantaṃ mahāmaudgalyāyanam idam avocat: saṃvejaya āyuṣman mahāmaudgalyāyana parṣadam iti; athāyuṣmān mahāmaudgalyāyanas tadrūpaṃ samādhiṃ samāpannaḥ yathā samāhite citte pūrvasyāṃ diśy upari vihāyasam abhyudgamya caturvidham īryāpathaṃ kalpayati caṃkramyate tiṣṭhati niṣīdati śayyāṃ kalpayati; tejodhātum api samāpadyate; tejodhātusamāpannasya āyuṣmato mahāmaudgalyāyanasya vividhāny arciṃṣi kāyān niścaranti nīlāni pītāni lohitāny avadātāni māñjiṣṭhāni sphaṭikavarṇāni; yamakāny api prātihāryāṇi vidarśayati; adhaḥ kāyaḥ prajvalati uparimāt kāyāt śītalā vāridhārā syandate; uparimaḥ kāyaḥ prajvalati addhaḥkāyāt śītalā vāridhārā syandate; yathā pūrvasyāṃ diśi evaṃ dakṣiṇasyāṃ paścimāyām uttarasyāṃ diśi; iti caturdiśaṃ caturvidhaṃ ṛddhiprātihāryaṃ vidarśya tān ṛddhyabhisaṃskārān pratiprasrabhya prajñapta evāsane niṣaṇṇaḥ; āyuṣmantā ca mahāmaudgalyāyanena te bhikṣavaḥ saṃvejitāḥ; tata āyuṣmatā śāriputreṇa teṣāṃ bhikṣūṇāṃ tathāvidho dharmo deśitaḥ; yaṃ śrutvā devadatte nirapekṣāḥ saṃvṛttāḥ; uktāś ca: yeṣāṃ vaḥ āyuṣmantaḥ śāstā priyaḥ te uttiṣṭhantu; gacchāmaḥ iti
body.translated_text: ) <s>Devadatta</s> lay supine with his body thrashing. Then the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> addressed the monks: 'See, Venerable ones, the state of your teacher — he has fallen asleep lying supine with his body thrashing.' Then the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> said this to the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>: 'Inspire awe in the assembly, Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>.' Then the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s> entered such a <s>samādhi</s> (concentration) that, with his mind composed, he rose into the sky in the eastern direction and displayed the four modes of deportment — walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. He also entered the fire-element <s>samādhi</s>. Having entered the fire-element <s>samādhi</s>, various rays issued from the Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s>'s body — blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and crystal-colored. He also displayed the miracle of the pairs: the lower body blazed with fire while from the upper body a cool stream of water flowed; the upper body blazed with fire while from the lower body a cool stream of water flowed. As in the eastern direction, so in the southern, western, and northern directions — thus in the four directions he displayed the fourfold miraculous wonder of supernatural power. Having displayed those feats of supernatural creation, he descended and sat upon his prepared seat. The Venerable <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s> thus inspired awe in those monks. Then the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> taught such a <s>Dharma</s> to those monks that, having heard it, they became indifferent to <s>Devadatta</s>. And he said: 'Let those of you, Venerable ones, to whom the Teacher is dear, rise. Let us go.'

body.text: Many misled monks are led back to the Buddha and readmitted into the order without a word of reproach
body.translated_text: Many misled monks are led back to the <s>Buddha</s> and readmitted into the order without a word of reproach

body.text: āyuṣmantau śāriputramahāmaudgalyāyanau saṃprasthitau; bhikṣavaḥ pṛṣṭhataḥ pṛṣṭhataḥ samanubaddhāḥ; kokālikena devadattaḥ utthāpyate: utthiṣṭhottiṣṭha; mahāśrāvakais te parṣad apahriyate iti; athāyuṣmataḥ śāriputrasya etad abhavad: yadi devadattasa apaśyataḥ parṣadaṃ neṣyāmi sthānam etad vidyate yad uṣṇaṃ rudhiraṃ chardayitvā kālaṃ kariṣyati; paśyata eva netavyā iti; tau mandagatipracāratayā saṃghasametau gacchataḥ; devadatto 'pi tīvreṇa paryavasthānena akṣiṇī saṃparimārjan pradhāvitaḥ; āyuṣmatā śāriputreṇa atiparamabhīṣaṇapātālaprakhyā
body.translated_text: The Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Mahāmaudgalyāyana</s> set out. The monks followed behind them. <s>Kokālika</s> roused <s>Devadatta</s>: 'Get up, get up! The great disciples are taking away your assembly!' Then the thought occurred to the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s>: 'If I lead away the assembly while <s>Devadatta</s> is not watching, there is the possibility that he will vomit hot blood and die. They should be led away in his sight.' They went slowly, walking at a gentle pace, together with the community. <s>Devadatta</s> too, with intense agitation, rubbing his eyes, rushed after them. The Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> created an extremely terrifying, abyss-like

body.text: gartā nirmitā; devadattaḥ kokālikakhaṇḍadravyakaṭamorakatiṣyasamudradattaiḥ sārdhaṃ samantatas tāṃ gartāṃ paribhramitum ārabdhaḥ; na śaknoty uttartuṃ; sa saṃlakṣayati: (
body.translated_text: chasm. <s>Devadatta</s>, together with <s>Kokālika</s>, <s>Khaṇḍadravya</s>, <s>Kaṭamoraka</s>, <s>Tiṣya</s>, and <s>Samudradatta</s>, began to circle around that chasm on all sides. He was unable to cross it. He reflected: (

body.text: SBV II 209
body.translated_text: SBV II 209

body.text:
) na ca parṣadam ārāgayiṣyāmi; atha ca punar anayena vyasanam āpatsyāmi; iti viditvā pratinivṛttaḥ; āyuṣmantāv api śāriputramaudgalyāyanau bhikṣusaṃgham ādāya yena bhagavāṃs tenopasaṃkrāntau; atha te bhikṣavaḥ ālekhajātāḥ madgubhūtāḥ srastaskandhā adhomukhā bhagavatsakāśam upasaṃkrāmanti: kathaṃ vā vayaṃ bhagavantam aprameyaguṇasamanvāgatam apahāya pāpecchaṃ devadattaṃ saṃsṛtāḥ iti; atha bhagavān teṣāṃ bhikṣūṇāṃ cetasā cittam ājñāya bhikṣūn āmantrayate sma: svāgataṃ vo bhikṣavaḥ supravrajitaṃ; sulabdho vo manuṣyapratilambhaḥ; kadācit karhicid āryāyatane pratyājātiḥ indriyair avikalatā ajaḍatā aneḍamūkatā ahastasaṃvācikatā pratibalatā subhāṣitadurbhāṣitānāṃ dharmāṇām artham ājñātuṃ; kadācit karhicit tathāgatā arhantaḥ samyaksaṃbuddhā loka utpadyante; kadācit karhicit tathāgatapraveditasya dharmavinayasya loke dharmadeśanā prajñāyate; tad idaṃ bhikṣavaḥ sudurlabhaṃ sudurlabhaṃ yaduta āryāyatane pratyājātiḥ, indriyair avikalatā ajaḍatā aneḍamūkatā ahastasaṃvācikatā pratibalatā subhāṣitadurbhāṣitānāṃ dharmāṇām artham ājñātuṃ; ahaṃ caitarhi śāstā loka utpannaḥ tathāgato 'rhan samyaksaṃbuddhaḥ vidyācaraṇasaṃpannaḥ sugato lokavid anuttaraḥ puruṣadamyasārathiḥ śāstā devamanuṣyāṇāṃ buddho bhagavān; dharmaś ca deśyate aupaśamikaḥ pārinirvāṇikaḥ saṃbodhigāmī saugatapratisaṃveditaḥ yaduta asmin sati idaṃ bhavati; asyotpādād idam utpadyate;
yaduta avidyāpratyāyāḥ saṃskārāḥ; saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānaṃ vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpaṃ nāmarūpapratyayaṃ ṣaḍāyatanaṃ ṣaḍāyatanapratyayaḥ sparśaḥ sparśapratyayā vedanā vedanāpratyayā tṛṣṇā tṛṣṇāpratyaym upādānaṃ upādānapratyayo bhavaḥ bhavapratyayā jātiḥ jātipratyayāḥ jarāmaraṇaśokaparidevaduḥkhadaurmanasyopāyāsāḥ saṃbhavanti; evam asya kevalasya mahato duḥkhaskandhasya samudayo bhavati; yaduta asminn asati na bhavati; asya nirodhād idaṃ nirudhyate; yaduta avidyānirodhāt saṃskāranirodhaḥ saṃskāranirodhād vijñānanirodho vijñānanirodhān nāmarūpanirodho nāmarūpanirodhāt ṣaḍāyatananirodhaḥ ṣaḍāyatananirodhāt sparśanirodhaḥ sparśanirodhād vedanānirodhaḥ vedanānirodhāt (
body.translated_text:
) nor shall I please the assembly; moreover, I shall meet with calamity through this wrongdoing.' Having realized this, he turned back. The Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Maudgalyāyana</s> too, taking the community of monks, approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Then those monks, ashamed, dejected, with drooping shoulders and downcast faces, approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s presence, thinking: 'How could we have abandoned the <s>Bhagavān</s>, who is endowed with immeasurable virtues, and followed the evil-intentioned <s>Devadatta</s>?' Then the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having known the thoughts in those monks' minds with his own mind, addressed the monks: 'Welcome, monks! Well gone forth! Well obtained is your human birth! Rare is rebirth in a noble realm, completeness of faculties, freedom from dullness, freedom from being mute and deaf, the ability to understand the meaning of well-spoken and ill-spoken teachings. Rare is the arising in the world of <s>Tathāgatas</s>, <s>Arhats</s>, perfectly awakened ones. Rare is the appearance in the world of the teaching of the <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s> proclaimed by a <s>Tathāgata</s>. Therefore, monks, this is extremely rare, extremely rare — namely, rebirth in a noble realm, completeness of faculties, freedom from dullness, freedom from being mute and deaf, the ability to understand the meaning of well-spoken and ill-spoken teachings. And now I, the Teacher, have arisen in the world — a <s>Tathāgata</s>, <s>Arhat</s>, perfectly and fully awakened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed, charioteer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a <s>Buddha</s>, a <s>Bhagavān</s>. And the <s>Dharma</s> is being taught — leading to peace, leading to complete <s>nirvāṇa</s>, conducive to awakening, proclaimed by the <s>Sugata</s> — namely: when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises;
that is, from <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) as condition arise <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations); from <s>saṃskāras</s> as condition arises <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness); from <s>vijñāna</s> as condition arises <s>nāmarūpa</s> (name-and-form); from <s>nāmarūpa</s> as condition arise the <s>ṣaḍāyatanas</s> (six sense-bases); from the <s>ṣaḍāyatanas</s> as condition arises <s>sparśa</s> (contact); from <s>sparśa</s> as condition arises <s>vedanā</s> (feeling); from <s>vedanā</s> as condition arises <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving); from <s>tṛṣṇā</s> as condition arises <s>upādāna</s> (clinging); from <s>upādāna</s> as condition arises <s>bhava</s> (becoming); from <s>bhava</s> as condition arises <s>jāti</s> (birth); from <s>jāti</s> as condition arise <s>jarāmaraṇa</s> (aging-and-death), sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair. Thus there is the arising of this entire great mass of suffering. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; from the cessation of this, that ceases —

body.text: SBV II 210
body.translated_text: SBV II 210

body.text: ) tṛṣṇānirodhaḥ tṛṣṇānirodhād upādānanirodhaḥ upādānanirodhād bhavanirodho bhavanirodhāj jātinirodhaḥ jātinirodhāj jarāmaraṇaśokaparidevaduḥkhadaurmanasyopāyāsā nirudhyante evam asya kevalasya mahato duḥkhaskandhasya nirodho bhavati; tasmāt tarhi
body.translated_text: ) that is, from the cessation of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) comes the cessation of <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations); from the cessation of <s>saṃskāras</s> comes the cessation of <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness); from the cessation of <s>vijñāna</s> comes the cessation of <s>nāmarūpa</s> (name-and-form); from the cessation of <s>nāmarūpa</s> comes the cessation of the <s>ṣaḍāyatanas</s> (six sense-bases); from the cessation of the <s>ṣaḍāyatanas</s> comes the cessation of <s>sparśa</s> (contact); from the cessation of <s>sparśa</s> comes the cessation of <s>vedanā</s> (feeling); from the cessation of <s>vedanā</s> comes the cessation of

body.text:
bhikṣavaḥ ātmārthaṃ samanupaśyadbhiḥ parārthaṃ cobhayārthaṃ ca idaṃ pratisaṃśikṣitavyaṃ: kaccin naḥ pravrajya amoghā bhaviṣyanti kriyāḥ saphalāḥ sukhodayāḥ sukhavipākāḥ; yeṣāṃ ca paribhokṣyāmahe cīvarapiṇḍapātaśayanāsanaglānapratyayabhaiṣajyapariṣkārān teṣāṃ te kārāḥ kṛtāḥ atyarthaṃ mahāphalā bhaviṣyanti mahānuśaṃsāḥ mahādyutayaḥ mahāvistārāḥ ity evaṃ vo bhikṣavaḥ śikṣitavyam
  yadā te bhikṣavo bhagavatā svāgatavādena supravrajitavādena samudācaritāḥ tadā teṣāṃ yat tad abhūn madgutvaṃ kaukṛtyam ālekhaḥ vilekhaḥ vipratisāraḥ tat sarveṇa sarvaṃ prativigataṃ; tato 'nye bhikṣavaḥ saṃśayajātāḥ sarvasaṃśayacchettāraṃ buddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ papracchuḥ: kiṃ bhadanta bhagavatā karma kṛtaṃ yasya karmaṇo vipākena bhagavataḥ śrāvakasaṃgho bhinnaḥ iti; bhagavān āha: tathāgatenaiva bhikṣavaḥ pūrvam anyāsu jātiṣu karmāṇi kṛtāny upacitāni pūrvavad yāvat phalanti khalu dehinām
body.translated_text:
<s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving); from the cessation of <s>tṛṣṇā</s> comes the cessation of <s>upādāna</s> (clinging); from the cessation of <s>upādāna</s> comes the cessation of <s>bhava</s> (becoming); from the cessation of <s>bhava</s> comes the cessation of <s>jāti</s> (birth); from the cessation of <s>jāti</s>, <s>jarāmaraṇa</s> (aging-and-death), sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair cease. Thus there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering. Therefore, monks, considering your own welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both, you should train in this: "May our going forth not be fruitless; may our actions be fruitful, yielding happiness, ripening in happiness. And may the gifts of those whose robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines for the sick we consume — may those gifts become exceedingly fruitful for them, of great benefit, of great splendor, of great extent." Thus, monks, should you train.'
  When those monks were greeted by the <s>Bhagavān</s> with words of welcome and well-going-forth, whatever shame, remorse, embarrassment, distress, and regret they had felt was entirely dispelled. Then other monks, having doubts, questioned the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, the cutter of all doubts: 'What <s>karma</s>, Venerable Sir, did the <s>Bhagavān</s> perform, by the ripening of which the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s community of disciples was split?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'By the <s>Tathāgata</s> himself, monks, in former births, <s>karmas</s> were performed and accumulated — as before, up to — indeed they ripen for embodied beings.'

body.text:
The story of a ṛṣi living in the country
(concerning a previous birth of the Buddha and Devadatta)
body.translated_text:
The story of a <s>ṛṣi</s> living in the country
(concerning a previous birth of the <s>Buddha</s> and <s>Devadatta</s>)

body.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavaḥ anyatamasminn āśramapade mūlapuṣpaphalasalilasaṃpanne nānāvṛkṣopaśobhite anekapakṣigaṇaniṣevite ṛṣiḥ prativasati paṃcānām ṛṣiśatānāṃ pramukhaḥ; yāvad anyaḥ ṛṣiḥ janapadacārikāṃ caran tadāśramapadam anuprāptaḥ; sa tena ṛṣiṇā na samyak pratimānitaḥ; tena saṃjātāmarṣeṇa tasya parṣad bhidyate: ayaṃ pāpecchaḥ ṛṣir na kiṃcid api jānīte; kimartham asya sakāśe tiṣṭhatha? āgacchata; mayā sārdhaṃ gacchata; ahaṃ yuṣmān paṃcasv abhijñāsu pratiṣṭhāpayāmi iti; tena bhidyamānās te tasya ṛṣer avavādena avatiṣṭhante; tena ṛṣiṇā saṃlakṣitam: anena pāpakāriṇā mamaite ṛṣayo bhinnāḥ iti; sa tam upasāntvayitum ārabdhaḥ: mā āyuṣman parṣadbhedaṃ kuru; naiṣa ṛṣidharmaḥ iti; tathāpy asau bhinatty eva, nāvatiṣṭhate iti sa ṛṣir durmanāḥ upāyasaṃvidhānena avasthitaḥ; asati buddhānām utpāde pratyekabuddhā loka (
body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in a certain hermitage endowed with roots, flowers, fruits, and water, adorned with various trees, frequented by flocks of many birds, a <s>ṛṣi</s> (sage) dwelt as the chief of five hundred <s>ṛṣis</s>. Then another <s>ṛṣi</s>, wandering on a tour of the countryside, arrived at that hermitage. He was not properly honored by that <s>ṛṣi</s>. Filled with resentment, he began splitting that one's assembly: 'This evil-intentioned <s>ṛṣi</s> does not know anything at all! Why do you stay in his presence? Come! Go with me! I shall establish you in the five <s>abhijñās</s> (superknowledges).' As he was splitting them, they remained firm through the admonition of their <s>ṛṣi</s>. That <s>ṛṣi</s> realized: 'This evil-doer has split my <s>ṛṣis</s>.' He began to pacify him: 'Venerable one, do not cause a split in the assembly. This is not the way of the <s>ṛṣis</s>.' But even so, that one kept splitting and would not desist. That <s>ṛṣi</s> became despondent and stood pondering a stratagem. In the absence of the arising of <s>Buddhas</s>, <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s> arise in the world —

body.text: SBV II 211
body.translated_text: SBV II 211

body.text: sarvasaṃśayacchettāraṃ buddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ papracchuḥ: paśya bhadanta devadattena sabāhyān abhyantarīkṛtya abhyantarāṃś ca bāhyīkṛtya parṣad hāritā iti; bhagavān āha: na bhikṣava etarhi, yathā atīte 'py adhvany anena sabāhyān abhyantarīkṛtya abhyantarāṃś ca bāhyīkṛtya parṣad hāritā; tac chrūyatām
body.translated_text: questioned the <s>Buddha</s> <s>Bhagavān</s>, the cutter of all doubts: 'See, Venerable Sir, <s>Devadatta</s> has corrupted the assembly by making outsiders into insiders and insiders into outsiders.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Not only now, monks — in the past too, he corrupted an assembly by making outsiders into insiders and insiders into outsiders. Listen to that.'

body.text:
The story of a jackal, Śatadru by name
(concerning a previous life of Devadatta)
body.translated_text:
The story of a jackal, <s>Śatadru</s> by name
(concerning a previous life of <s>Devadatta</s>)

body.text: bhūtapūrvaṃ bhikṣavaḥ anyatamasmin pradeśe sṛgālaḥ prāṇī prativasati; sa atilolupaḥ araṇye paryaṭati grāme 'pi; so 'nupūrveṇa paryaṭan nīlarajakagṛhaṃ praviṣṭaḥ; nīlakuṇḍe patitaḥ; tena ghṛṇā gṛhītā; tasya nātidūre ūṣasya puñjas tiṣṭhati; sa tasmin patitaḥ pārśvena pārśvaṃ luṭhitaḥ; sa bhūyasyā mātrayā śarīraṃ jugupsamānaḥ pānīye patitaḥ; utthāya saṃprasthitaḥ ādityaraśmispṛṣṭaḥ mecakavarṇo jātaḥ; yāvat sṛgālair dṛṣṭaḥ; te samantād vidrutāḥ; dūre sthitvā kathayanti: kas tvaṃ? kuto vā abhyāgataḥ? iti; sa kathayati: (
body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in a certain region, a jackal — a living creature — dwelt. He was exceedingly greedy, roaming about in the forest and in the village too. Wandering about gradually, he entered a dyer's house. He fell into a vat of indigo dye. He was seized with disgust. Not far from him stood a pile of ashes. He fell into it and rolled from side to side. Disgusted even more with his body, he fell into water. Rising up, he set out. Touched by the sun's rays, he became dark-blue in color. Then he was seen by jackals. They scattered in all directions. Standing at a distance, they said: 'Who are you? And from where have you come?' He said:

body.text: SBV II 212
body.translated_text: SBV II 212

body.text: ) ahaṃ śatadrunāmā śakreṇa devendreṇa catuṣpadānāṃ rājye abhiṣiktaḥ iti; sṛgālāḥ saṃlakṣayanti: apūrvarūpo 'yaṃ; nūnam evaṃ bhaviṣyati iti; sṛgālaiḥ sarvacatuṣpadānāṃ niveditaṃ; siṃhāḥ saṃlakṣayanti: ko 'sāv asmat prativiśiṣṭo yaś catuṣpadānāṃ rājā bhaviṣyati? gacchāmas tāvat; svasya yūthapater nivedayāmaḥ iti; teṣāṃ yūthapatir anyatamasmin parvataikadeśe nivasati; sa kesarī paṭṭadhārī; tais tasya niveditaṃ; tenānyacatuṣpadasya ājñā dattā: gaccha catuṣpadādhipatiṃ nirīkṣasva kim asau kenacic catuṣpadena dṛṣṭo na vā iti; sa tena gatvā pratyavekṣitaḥ apūrvadarśanaḥ; sarvaiś catuṣpadaiḥ parivṛtaḥ sthāpayitvā siṃhān; tena tasya yathādṛṣṭaṃ gatvā niveditaṃ; sa śrutvā siṃhayūthaparivṛtaḥ tasya sakāśam abhigataḥ; so 'nekacatuṣpadaparivṛtaḥ hastiskandhābhirūḍhaḥ anvāhiṇḍate; taṃ parivārya siṃhā gacchanti; tato vyāghrāḥ; tato 'nye catuṣpadāḥ; teṣāṃ bahir dūreṇa sṛgālāḥ; tasya mātā anyasmin parvatakuñje prativasati; tasyās tena sṛgālaḥ preṣitaḥ: āgaccha putrarājyaṃ pratyanubhava iti; sā kathayati: kīdṛśaḥ tasya parivāraḥ? iti; sa kathayati: siṃhavyāghrā hastinaś ca abhyantaraparivāraḥ; vayaṃ tu bāhyāḥ iti; sā kathayati: gaccha; vinaṣṭaḥ sa iti; sā gāthāṃ bhāṣate
body.translated_text: ) 'I am named <s>Śatadru</s>. I have been anointed by <s>Śakra</s>, Lord of the Gods, to the kingship over quadrupeds.' The jackals considered: 'This one is of an unprecedented appearance. Surely it must be so.' The jackals informed all the quadrupeds. The lions considered: 'Who is this one, superior to us, who will be king of the quadrupeds? Let us go and report to our pride-leader.' Their pride-leader dwelt on a certain mountainside. He was a maned lion, wearing a diadem. They reported to him. He gave a command to another quadruped: 'Go and examine the lord of the quadrupeds — has he been seen by any quadruped or not?' That one went and observed him — of unprecedented appearance, surrounded by all quadrupeds except lions. Having gone, he reported what he had seen. Having heard, the lion, surrounded by his pride of lions, approached his presence. That one, surrounded by many quadrupeds, rode on the back of an elephant, going about. Lions went surrounding him; then tigers; then other quadrupeds. Outside them, at a distance, went the jackals. His mother dwelt in a certain mountain-cave. A jackal was sent to her by him: 'Come and enjoy the royal estate of your son.' She said: 'What is the nature of his retinue?' He said: 'Lions, tigers, and elephants are the inner retinue. But we are outsiders.' She said: 'Go. He is doomed.' She spoke a verse:

children.translated_text: I live happily in the cave of this mountain,
at ease, drinking cool water. /
He rides happily on that elephant
only so long as he does not hear the jackal's cry. //

body.translated_text: In the past, monks, in a certain region, there dwelt a bull-elephant, lord of the herd. There, a certain elephant's cow-elephant was much beloved. She was exceedingly attached to a certain young elephant-calf. She said to the calf: 'Let us flee.' He said: 'What is the stratagem by which we might flee?' She said: 'I know a stratagem.' She said to the bull-elephant: 'Let us bathe; let us go down into the lake.' He went down. She said: 'Let us see which of us two can remain submerged longer.' That mass of delusion submerged in the water with her. She rose up and fled with the young elephant. That elephant, after remaining submerged a long time, rose up and did not see her. He thought: 'I shall submerge again, lest I suffer defeat.' He submerged again, dug in his tusks, and stayed. After a very long time, his life-breath nearly gone, he came up and did not see that cow-elephant. He began to churn that lake this way and that. By this, many fish, turtles, frogs, and other creatures there met with calamity through his folly. A deity spoke a verse: (

body.translated_text: ) She was brought up, nurtured, and grew up. The archery teacher thought: 'This girl of mine shall not be given to anyone merely on account of his looks, character, or wealth. Rather, whoever masters the five disciplines in my presence, to him shall I give her.' Two young men had trained in archery under him. One of them became skilled in the five disciplines; the second became skilled only in cutting. To the former he gave the girl. The other, filled with resentment, joined a band of thieves and became the commander of five hundred thieves. He set up a road-block at a certain place. The first one, having married the girl, placed her in a chariot and set out for home. A caravan, fearing thieves, stopped ahead of him. He said: 'Sirs, go! Why are you standing?' They said: 'Thieves have blocked the road.' He said: 'Good sirs, go. What will they do?' He set out. The caravan-merchants said: 'Sirs, let him go. Let us wait. It is likely that he will get himself killed and will have his wife taken.' The thieves, having climbed trees and stationed themselves as lookouts, saw him approaching on his chariot. They said: 'Sirs, a man is coming on a chariot.' The thief-commander sent a messenger: 'Turn back your chariot.' He said: 'Sirs, give a hero the respect due to a hero.' They said: 'We too are heroes.' The commander sent five thieves. He slew them. Thus twenty came — he slew them too. Until all were slain. The commander alone remained. He took his sword and stood in front. The archer began to shoot arrows. The commander cut them with his sword. Until the entire quiver of five hundred arrows had been shot. The commander cut them all with his sword. One arrow remained. He did not release it. The girl said: 'Release the arrow! Why do you hesitate?' He said: 'This one alone remains. If this one is released and misses, I shall be killed and you shall be taken.' Then the girl, yawning, began to tie up her braid. The thief-commander, as she glanced about, began to stare at her. He struck the commander in the vital spot with that arrow. As he was dying, he spoke a verse: (

Then King <s>Māgadha Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra</s> addressed <s>Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta</s>: 'Well, <s>Jīvaka</s>, why are you silent? Why do you not speak?' He said: 'On this moonlit night, Your Majesty, on the full-moon night of <s>Āṣāḍha</s>, the night of the rains-invitation — well-known, recognized, full, at the full moon — this lord, the <s>Bhagavān</s>, is a leader of a community, a leader of a group, an instructor of a group, one regarded as virtuous by many people, attended by a large following, and has entered the rains right here in <s>Rājagṛha</s>, in our very mango grove. May Your Majesty attend upon him. This I consider Your Majesty's duty.'

  9. At that time, King <s>Māgadha Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra</s> was at war with the <s>Vṛjis</s>.   11. At that time, the <s>Bhagavān</s> was seated in the midst of the community of monks — clear, serene, and undisturbed, like a lake. Then King <s>Māgadha Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra</s>, passing through the enclosure, addressed <s>Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta</s>: 'Where, <s>Jīvaka</s>, is the <s>Bhagavān</s>?' 'This, Your Majesty, is the <s>Bhagavān</s>, seated in the midst of the community of monks — clear, serene, and undisturbed, like a lake.' Then King <s>Māgadha Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra</s> approached the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Having approached, he arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and joining his palms toward the <s>Bhagavān</s>, said this to the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'May the <s>Bhagavān</s>, Venerable Sir, be endowed with the taming and calming of the mind, and the community of monks likewise be endowed with the taming and calming of the mind — may <s>Udāyibhadra</s> the prince be well!' 'Excellent, excellent, great king! Your love shall be eloquent; sit, great king, upon your own seat.'

<s>Arhats</s> in the world who have gone rightly, who have practiced rightly, who have realized this world and the other world by their own higher knowledge in this very life, and declare: 'Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done; I know there is no more of this state of existence.' Right here the living being lives; after death, he is cut off and perishes — he does not exist after death. The body is composed of the four great elements. At the time of death, the earth-element of his body returns to earth; the water-element to water; the fire-element to fire; the air-element to air; the sense-faculties pass into space. Four men with the bier as fifth carry the person, proceeding to the charnel ground. Beyond the cremation, nothing is known. The bones remain, dove-colored; the oblations become ash." Generosity is a doctrine conceived by fools; acceptance is a doctrine conceived by the wise. Those who speak of existence all babble empty, vain, and false words. Both the fool and the wise — these two, after death, are cut off, perish, and do not exist after death.

'Just as, Venerable Sir, one asked about mangoes would answer about breadfruits, or asked about breadfruits would answer about mangoes — even so, <s>Pūraṇa Kāśyapa</s>, when asked by me about the visible fruit of the ascetic life, answered with nihilism. Then this thought occurred to me: "It is not proper for one such as I, a knowledgeable person, to publicly contradict an ascetic or <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> who is regarded as virtuous and dwelling in my domain." ) without cause or condition; there is no cause, there is no condition for the arising of ignorance among beings — without cause or condition, ignorance arises among beings; there is no cause, there is no condition for the arising of knowledge among beings — without cause or condition, knowledge arises among beings. There is no strength, no effort, no power of strength, no human exertion, no striving, no exertion-and-striving. There is no action by self, no action by others; all beings are without vigor, without power, without will, without effort, without striving — determined by the fixed course of destiny and circumstance, they experience pleasure and pain according to the six classes of birth.'
  19. Just as, Venerable Sir, a person asked about mangoes would answer about breadfruit, or asked about breadfruit would answer about mangoes — even so <s>Maskarī Gośāliputra</s>, when asked by me about the visible fruit of the ascetic life, expounded the doctrine of no-causation. The thought occurred to me: 'How could a discerning person like myself openly disparage an ascetic or <s>brāhmaṇa</s> dwelling in the realm who is regarded as virtuous?' So I neither rejoiced in nor censured the words of <s>Maskarī Gośāliputra</s>. Neither rejoicing nor censuring, I rose from my seat and departed.

They perform their respective work through their own crafts and occupations, give gifts, make merit, and support their dependents; and endowed with and possessing the five qualities of sensual pleasure, they sport, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves. Is it possible to designate a visible fruit of the ascetic life for such people?'

Thus addressed, <s>Ajita Keśakambala</s> said this to me: 'I, great king, hold this view and this doctrine: these seven bodies are uncreated, not made by a creator, not fashioned, not produced by a fashioner, indestructible, immovable, standing firm like a pillar. Which seven? Namely: the earth-body, water-body, fire-body, air-body, pleasure, pain, and the life-principle as the seventh. These seven bodies are uncreated, not made by a creator, not fashioned, not produced by a fashioner, indestructible, immovable, standing firm like a pillar. They do not move; they do not change; they do not harm one another — neither for merit nor for demerit, neither for merit-and-demerit, neither for pleasure nor for pain, neither for pleasure-and-pain. Even the person who cuts off another person's head — he too does no harm to anything in the world, whether moving or stationary. Through these eighty-four thousand great aeons, both the fool and the wise one, having wandered and transmigrated, make an end of suffering — just as a light ball of thread cast upward into the sky unwinds until it reaches the earth, even so through these eighty-four thousand great aeons, both the fool and the wise one, having wandered and transmigrated, make an end of suffering. sa evam āha: aham asmi mahārāja evaṃdṛṣṭir evaṃvādī; yat kiṃcid ayaṃ puruṣapudgalaḥ prativedayate sarvaṃ tat pūrvahaitukam iti purāṇānāṃ karmaṇāṃ tapasā vāntībhāvaḥ; navānāṃ karmaṇām akaraṇasatusamudghātaḥ; evam āytyām anavasravaḥ; anavasravāt karmakṣayaḥ; karmakṣayād duhkhakṣayaḥ; duḥkhakṣayād duḥkhasyāntakriyā bhavati iti
  28. tadyathā bhadanta puruṣaḥ āmrāṇi pṛṣṭo lakucāni vyākuryāt, lakucāni vā pṛṣṭaḥ āmrāṇi vyākuryād evam eva mayā bhadanta nirgrantho jñātiputraḥ sāndṛṣṭikaṃ śrāmaṇyaphalaṃ pṛṣṭaḥ pūrvakṛtahetutām eva vyākārṣīt; tasya mama bhadanta etad abhavat; na mama pratirūpaṃ syād yad ahaṃ sādhurūpasaṃmataṃ viṣayanivāsinaṃ śramaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā saṃmukham avasādayeyam iti; so 'haṃ nirgranthasya jñātiputrasya bhāṣitaṃ nābhinandāmi na pratikrośāmi; anabhinandya apratikrośya utthāyāsanāt prakrāntaḥ
body.translated_text:
He spoke thus: 'I, Great King, hold this view and proclaim this doctrine: whatever this individual person experiences, all that is due to previous causation. Through austerity comes the exhaustion of old deeds; through the non-performance of new deeds comes their termination. Thus, in the future, there is no further influx. From the absence of influx comes the destruction of <s>karma</s>. From the destruction of <s>karma</s> comes the destruction of suffering. From the destruction of suffering comes the making of an end to suffering.'
  28. Just as, Venerable Sir, if a person asked about mangoes were to explain about breadfruit, or if asked about breadfruit were to explain about mangoes — even so, Venerable Sir, when I asked <s>Nirgrantha Jñātiputra</s> about the fruit of the ascetic life visible in this world, he explained only in terms of previous causation. Then, Venerable Sir, this occurred to me: 'It would not be fitting for me to directly rebuke a respected ascetic or <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> dwelling in my realm.' So I neither rejoiced in nor censured <s>Nirgrantha Jñātiputra</s>'s words. Without rejoicing and without censuring, I rose from my seat and departed.

) "it is not or not; it is not indeed or not" — when asked such a question, I would answer "It is not or not; it is not indeed or not, the next world."
  31. Then I reflected, Venerable Sir: 'Of all those who have gone forth and dwell here in <s>Rājagṛha</s>, this one is the most foolish, the most stupid, and the most dull-witted — namely, <s>Kakuda Kātyāyana</s>.' Then this occurred to me: 'It would not be fitting for me to directly rebuke a respected ascetic or <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> dwelling in my realm.' So I neither rejoiced in nor censured <s>Kakuda Kātyāyana</s>'s words. Without rejoicing and without censuring, I rose from my seat and departed.

29. I then approached <s>Kakuda Kātyāyana</s>. Having approached, I said this to <s>Kakuda Kātyāyana</s>: 'There are, Venerable <s>Kātyāyana</s>, these various worldly crafts and occupations — such as garland-makers, reed-workers, confectioners, barley-workers, charioteers, elephant-riders, horse-riders, chariot-warriors, spearmen, archers, servants, slaves, alms-eaters, fierce warriors, heroes, scouts, great naked ascetics, princes, workers, barbers, and bath-attendants. They perform their duties through their respective crafts and occupations, give gifts, perform meritorious deeds, and support their dependents. Endowed and furnished with the five strands of sensual pleasure, they sport, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves. Is it possible to declare the fruit of the ascetic life visible in this world for such people?'
  30. Thus asked, <s>Kakuda Kātyāyana</s> said this to me: 'I, Great King, hold this view and proclaim this doctrine: if anyone were to approach me and ask thus — "Does the next world exist?" — and if it were the case that the next world exists, then when asked the question "Does the next world exist?" I would answer "The next world does not exist." "The next world both exists and does not exist; it neither exists nor does not exist; it is thus or not; it is otherwise or not; it is not or not; it is not indeed or not" — (

  36. 'No, Venerable Sir. On the contrary, I myself would approach him for an audience. And the respect, salutation, rising, and reverential greeting that he formerly showed to me — I myself would show to him. And I would invite him for life with the four requisites: robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicine and provisions for the sick.'
  'What do you think, great king? Since this is so, have I not shown you a visible fruit of the monastic life?'
  'Indeed, Venerable Sir. Since this is so, the <s>Bhagavān</s> has shown a visible fruit of the monastic life.'
  37. 'Here, great king, a Teacher arises in the world — a <s>Tathāgata</s>, <s>Arhat</s>, perfectly awakened one, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Charioteer of Persons to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, <s>Buddha</s>, <s>Bhagavān</s>. He teaches the <s>Dharma</s>, good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete, perfect, pure, and utterly refined. He proclaims the holy life. A householder or a householder's son hears that <s>Dharma</s>. Having heard it, he examines the Teacher's purity in three respects — namely, in the domain of greed, in the domain of hatred, and in the domain of delusion: "Does this venerable one have that greed which is unabandonded, uncomprehended, unextinguished, unremoved, overwhelmed by which, with a mind overcome, while not knowing he would say 'I know,' while not seeing he would say 'I see,' or would lead others in such a way that it would be to their long-lasting harm, non-benefit, and suffering? Or does this venerable one not have that greed which is unabandonded, uncomprehended, unextinguished, unremoved, overwhelmed by which, with a mind overcome, while not knowing he would say 'I know,' while not seeing he would say 'I see,' or would lead others in such a way that it would be to their long-lasting harm, non-benefit, and suffering?" He concludes: "This venerable one does not have that greed which is unabandonded, uncomprehended, unextinguished, unremoved, overwhelmed by which, with a mind overcome, while not knowing he would say 'I know,' while not seeing he would say 'I see,' or would lead others in such a way that it would be to their long-lasting harm, non-benefit, and suffering." For what reason? For the bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations of this venerable one are those of one free from greed.

What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron-colored robes, and rightly and with faith go forth from the household life into homelessness?' Having thus considered, abandoning a large or small mass of wealth, abandoning a large or small circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron-colored robes, and rightly and with faith goes forth from the household life into homelessness. Having thus gone forth, he lives endowed with moral conduct; restrained by the restraint of the <s>Prātimokṣa</s> (code of monastic rules), accomplished in conduct and domain, seeing danger in the slightest faults, he trains himself, taking up the training-rules. He abandons the taking of life and abstains from taking life; he has laid down the rod, laid down the weapon, is modest, compassionate, dwelling with concern for the welfare of all living beings and creatures, abstaining from taking life down to even an ant or a small insect.

What you have asserted has been overturned too hastily. Your thesis has been refuted — argue your point! Remove the thesis to be free from the argument! You are caught — extricate yourself!   63. Endowed with this noble aggregate of moral conduct and with this guarding of the sense-doors, he experiences internally a blameless happiness. He becomes one who acts with clear comprehension in going forward and returning, in looking ahead and looking around, in bending and stretching, in wearing the <s>saṅghāṭī</s> robe, bowl, and robes, in going, standing, sitting, lying down, waking, speaking, being silent, and in dispelling drowsiness and fatigue — he becomes one who acts with clear comprehension. Endowed with this noble aggregate of moral conduct, with this guarding of the sense-doors, and with this supreme mindfulness and clear comprehension, he experiences internally a happiness free from harm. Endowed with this noble aggregate of moral conduct, with this guarding of the sense-doors, and with this supreme mindfulness and clear comprehension, he resorts to secluded dwelling places — forests, tree-roots, and empty houses. Having gone to the forest, or to a tree-root, or to an empty house, he sits down, crossing his legs, straightening his body, and establishing mindfulness before him. Having abandoned covetousness toward the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness. He purifies the mind of covetousness. Having abandoned ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-worry, and doubt toward the world, he becomes one who has crossed beyond doubt. Free from doubt and uncertainty regarding wholesome states, he purifies the mind of doubt.

He would then pay off that loan, and there would remain enough of his own wealth to support his wife. The thought would occur to him: 'Having taken a loan, I engaged in business. My business ventures succeeded, not failed. With that, I have paid off the loan. And I have enough of my own wealth to support my wife.' On that account he would experience joy.

  66. Suppose a man were a slave — a servant, menial, bondsman, one who goes not at his own command. At a later time, he would no longer be a slave — no longer a servant, bondsman, or one who goes not at his own command. The thought would occur to him: 'I was formerly a slave, a servant, menial, bondsman, one who goes not at his own command. Now I am no longer a slave, no longer a servant, bondsman, or one who goes not at his own command.' On that account he would experience gladness.
  67. Suppose a man were bound in a prison, fettered with his hands tied behind his back in tight bonds. He would then be released from that, safely, securely, and without loss. The thought would occur to him: 'I was formerly bound in a prison, fettered with my hands tied behind my back in tight bonds. I have been released from that, safely, securely, and without loss.' On that account he would experience gladness.
  68. Suppose a man, having been in danger, would become happy; having endured famine, he would arrive at abundance. The thought would occur to him: 'I am happy, having been in danger. Whereas I formerly had famine, now there is abundance.' On that account he would experience happiness, would experience joy.

There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded, not permeated by the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
